source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.5.1: Explain why changes of vision are possible yet rare and costly — they arrive either as sudden "road to Damascus" conversions or as gradual erosion that leaves no record and perhaps no awareness in the person changed, while the centuries-long persistence of both visions, the anguish of the apostate (from within as well as from former comrades), and the religious vocabulary — conversion, apostasy, heresy — borrowed for secular creeds all testify to the emotional commitment visions evoke.
learning_objectives.5.2: Explain why the familiar contrasts between the visions — trade-offs versus solutions, incentives versus dispositions — are suggestive but not decisive, and how the two criteria that are decisive, the **locus of discretion** and the **mode of discretion**, actually place a theory: deliberate decisions by surrogates on explicitly rationalistic grounds for the common good in the unconstrained vision, social decisions evolving systemically from innumerable individuals' self-interested discretion in the constrained — with a philosophy unambiguously placed only when both criteria consistently align (a central planning commission or an activist judge can make trade-offs; it is the *systemic mode* of trade-offs that is the heart of the constrained vision).
learning_objectives.5.3: Explain why acknowledging man's inherent limitations does not by itself place a thinker in the constrained vision — the need for food, the reality of death, and the ignorance of newborns are readily conceded in the unconstrained vision — and what the constrained vision additionally requires: that individuals will not voluntarily accept socially commensurate limits, so constraints must be conveyed to each individual, the wisest thinker included, by systemic mechanisms such as prices and moral traditions; a world whose trade-offs are freely accepted has turned them into solutions and is the *unconstrained* vision (Godwin and Condorcet on population: "an abstract trade-off but a practical solution").
learning_objectives.5.4: Given a previously unseen social theory, policy argument, or movement, apply the twin criteria — locus of discretion and mode of discretion — to place it as constrained, unconstrained, or outside both, judging by where discretion sits and how it operates rather than by trade-off vocabulary, limits-talk, policy conclusions, or left-right position (Rawls's trade-off theme with surrogate "society" as chooser; Bentham reaching laissez-faire by articulated reasons rather than Smith's; a surrogate locus whose mode is not articulated rationality).
learning_objectives.5.5: Explain how Marxism combines the two visions without inconsistency — history up to and including capitalism analyzed in the constrained vision's terms (systemic causation in which "what emerges is something that no one willed," capitalists controlled by the economy rather than controlling it, even the bourgeois regime a "temporary necessity" because nothing better was then possible), the communist future conceived in the unconstrained vision's terms ("real" freedom defined as a result, not a process) — because its theory of history is precisely that constraints, set by material production rather than by fixed human nature as in Smith and Burke, lessen as science and technology advance.
learning_objectives.5.6: Contrast the two different ways utilitarianism is a hybrid: Bentham, who split by domain — an incurably selfish man (the moral constraint) joined to vast intellectual horizons, operationally unconstrained in law and politics yet laissez-faire in economics, and even there not always for Smith's reasons — versus Mill, who deliberately sought a hybrid and paired bold assertions from the unconstrained vision with provisos from the constrained one (distribution "a matter of human institutions solely," yet its consequences having "the character of physical laws"), leaving his overall classification ambiguous.
learning_objectives.5.7: Explain why the constrained-unconstrained dichotomy cannot be equated with political right and left — Marxism epitomizes the left but not the unconstrained vision; libertarianism contains both Godwin and Ayn Rand; the constrained vision justifies individual freedom and property not by the individual's moral claims against society but by the social efficiency of systemic processes (Smith on fire regulations, Holmes on the public welfare) — and what actually divides the visions: not value premises, since every camp makes the common good paramount, but differing empirical assumptions about human nature and about cause and effect.

Chapter 5 → Varieties and Dynamics of Vi.text: Earlier chapters treated the two visions as pure types, but there are degrees within each, hybrid and inconsistent forms, and visions change. A shift may arrive suddenly, one event reorienting everything, or imperceptibly, like water on rock, leaving no record and perhaps no awareness beyond knowing things look different now. That both persisted for centuries suggests change is hard: the apostate suffers inwardly and from former allies alike, and the vocabulary — conversion, apostasy, heresy — is borrowed from religion.

Chapter 5 → Operational Definitions.text: No vision is wholly one or the other, and the pair does not exhaust the possibilities. The familiar contrasts — trade-offs against solutions, incentives against dispositions — are suggestive without being decisive, because a central committee or a judge ruling from the bench can weigh one good against another too. Two things decide placement: where discretion sits and how it operates. Choice by surrogates reasoning for the common good marks one vision; outcomes emerging from countless self-interested individuals mark the other.

Chapter 5 → Hybrid Visions.text: Marxism and utilitarianism combine the visions in different ways. Marxism reads history as constrained — causation systemic, outcomes nobody willed, an earlier order defensible because nothing better was then possible — while placing communism in the unconstrained register, because it holds constraints to come from material production rather than fixed human nature, and so to recede. Utilitarianism splits by domain instead: an incurably selfish man joined to vast intellectual reach, unconstrained in law yet laissez-faire in economics.

Chapter 5 → Summary and Implications.text: Many characteristic differences — articulation, incentives against dispositions, fidelity against sincerity — mark the visions without defining them. What defines them is whether human capability allows a society's choices to be settled collectively by surrogates reasoning toward a chosen result. So the dispute is less about what is wanted than about what can be achieved: a question of cause and effect rather than of values. It follows that the pair maps onto neither political left nor right.

items.stem: According to the chapter, a person's vision can change in which two ways?
options: As a deliberate re-examination of one's own premises, or as a surrender to the public arguments of the opposing camp
As a response to a shift in one's own economic interests, or as an accommodation to the pressure of one's social circle
As an abandonment of visions altogether in favor of practicality, or as a merger of the two visions into a hybrid of both
As a sudden conversion in which one event reorients a person's thinking, or as a slow wearing away that goes unnoticed
items.source_anchor: Chapter 5 → Varieties and Dynamics of Visions

items.stem: According to the chapter, the terms in which changes of social vision are discussed - conversion, apostasy, heresy - are borrowed from religious history, and they apply equally to secular creeds because such creeds evoke similar emotional commitments.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 5 → Varieties and Dynamics of Visions

items.stem: The chapter notes that some people who lose their faith in a vision continue its outward observances, or quietly withdraw if they can. What does it present this as evidence of?
options: The role of social pressure, which sustains a vision after conviction has gone
The power visions hold over adherents and the pain involved in changing one
The insincerity of many professed adherents, who never genuinely held the vision
The way gradual erosion erases any record of when or how a vision was lost
items.source_anchor: Chapter 5 → Varieties and Dynamics of Visions

items.stem: Why can the gradual kind of vision change leave no clear record of when or how it happened, and perhaps no awareness of it in the person changed?
options: Because gradual change comes only to the weakly committed, and a commitment too weak to defend is also too weak to be worth noting as it slips away
Because people whose visions erode conceal the shift deliberately, preferring quiet withdrawal to the condemnation that an open apostate faces
Because a vision operates below awareness from the start, so its departure is no more visible to its holder than its presence was
Because one vision imperceptibly wears away and changing implicit assumptions take its place, so the person knows only that things look different
items.source_anchor: Chapter 5 → Varieties and Dynamics of Visions

items.stem: According to the chapter, which two criteria are decisive for classifying a social philosophy as constrained or unconstrained?
options: The locus of discretion and the mode of discretion
Elaboration of premises, and isolated remarks on human nature
Left-right position, and the priority given to the common good
Trade-offs versus solutions, and incentives versus dispositions

items.stem: The chapter calls the trade-offs-versus-solutions contrast 'suggestive but not decisive' for placing a vision. Why does the presence of trade-offs fail to settle the classification?
options: Trade-offs freely accepted are essentially solutions, so the two categories collapse into each other and the contrast has nothing left to distinguish
Few writers spell out their premises explicitly, so whether a theory rests on trade-offs or on solutions usually cannot be read from its text at all
No theory is literally 100 percent constrained or unconstrained, so the difference between the visions is one of degree rather than a difference in kind
Trade-offs can be made deliberately by surrogates too; the mark of the constrained vision is trade-offs arising systemically, not trade-offs as such

items.stem: Rawls's A Theory of Justice takes as its central theme the trade-off between equality and the need to produce material well-being. By the chapter's account, how is the theory placed, and on what ground?
options: As constrained — a trade-off standing at the centre of a theory is an acceptance of inherent limits on what man can directly achieve
As a hybrid — constrained in its account of existing society, unconstrained in the future its principles are meant to produce
As outside both categories — the trade-off theme and the collective chooser point opposite ways, so the twin criteria never align
As unconstrained — discretion lies with a surrogate 'society', whose principles are derived in explicitly rationalistic terms

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, a social philosophy that assigns social decisions to surrogate decision-makers can presumably be classified as an unconstrained vision on that basis alone.
options: True
False

items.stem: Which of the following states the chapter's position on man's inherent limitations, such as the need for food or the reality of death?
options: Only the constrained vision acknowledges inherent limitations; the unconstrained vision denies that any exist
Both visions acknowledge inherent limitations in man, differing over the nature and degree of those limitations
The unconstrained vision concedes limitations only for the masses, holding its intellectual pioneers exempt from them
Neither vision treats man's inherent limitations as relevant to how a social theory should be classified

items.stem: Sowell notes that thinkers in the unconstrained vision readily concede the need for food, the reality of death, and the ignorance of newborns. Why does conceding these inherent limitations not place a thinker in the constrained vision?
options: Because a concession places a thinker only when he spells out his assumptions explicitly, and few writers in either vision systematize them as Godwin did
Because the constrained vision further requires that individuals will not voluntarily accept limits commensurate with what is socially available
Because the constrained vision rests on the scarcity of external resources relative to desires, not on any limitation internal to human beings
Because such limitations are conceded only in the abstract for mankind, and a vision is placed by what its holder accepts for himself in the concrete

items.stem: Godwin and Condorcet both acknowledged that man's biological capacity to generate an ever-larger population carried the potential for catastrophic poverty. Why does Sowell treat their handling of this danger as the mark of an unconstrained vision?
options: They premised that draconian impositions during a transitional period would contain the danger until mankind had advanced enough to relax them
They premised that advancing science and technology would push back the material constraints faster than population could outrun them
They premised that surrogate decision-makers would restrain population growth until the mass of mankind could make social decisions directly
They premised that rational foresight of the consequences would contain the danger, a trade-off in the abstract but a solution in practice

items.stem: According to the chapter, a world in which individuals voluntarily accept the trade-offs that scarcity makes necessary is the world of the unconstrained vision.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what are the two key criteria for deciding whether a social vision is constrained or unconstrained?
options: The position on the political left and on the political right
The pursuit of trade-offs and the pursuit of solutions
The reliance on incentives and the reliance on changed dispositions
The locus of discretion and the mode of discretion

items.stem: True or false: in the chapter's account, the constrained and unconstrained visions between them presumably cover the whole spectrum of social philosophies, so that applying the twin criteria will place any theory in one camp or the other.
options: True
False

items.stem: Why does the chapter call the contrast between trade-offs and solutions 'suggestive but not decisive' for placing a thinker in one vision or the other?
options: Trade-off language appears chiefly in economic writing, while a vision can be placed only after its stances in law and politics have been examined.
Surrogates like a planning commission or an activist judge can make trade-offs too; the constrained vision's mark is trade-offs arising systemically.
The unconstrained vision denies that genuine trade-offs exist at all, so the vocabulary arises on only one side and cannot distinguish the camps.
Few writers state their premises explicitly enough for trade-off reasoning to be detected, outside systematic thinkers such as Godwin or Condorcet.

items.stem: The central theme of Rawls's A Theory of Justice is the trade-off between equality and the production of material well-being. Why does the chapter nonetheless classify it as an unconstrained vision?
options: Its account treats producing material well-being as costless once society adopts the correct principles of justice.
Its principles rest on hypothetical beings — the unborn in the 'original position' — rather than on real people's behavior.
Its egalitarian conclusions align it politically with thinkers the chapter identifies as exemplars of the unconstrained camp.
Its trade-off is chosen collectively by the surrogate 'society,' on principles derived in explicitly rationalistic terms.

items.stem: The city of Arden has chartered a permanent Parkland Stewardship Council. Each spring the council alone decides how the city's limited green space is divided among sports fields, community gardens, and quiet woodland, and it publishes a reasoned justification for every allocation: what each use gains, what the others must give up, and why the balance struck serves the city as a whole. The council's charter opens soberly — space given to one purpose is always taken from another, no arrangement can please everyone, and painful sacrifices will remain a permanent fact of life in a crowded city. Into which of the chapter's categories does the council's program fall?
options: A hybrid of the two visions
The constrained vision
Outside both visions
The unconstrained vision

items.stem: Mara Voss heads the world federation for a centuries-old strategy board game. Asked about the game's future, she is exuberant: an era of play richer than anything yet seen is coming, she says — styles no committee could have invented, from players no one has heard of yet. Her federation certifies tournament conditions — honest clocks, open entry, no cheating — publishes the results, and stops there: it will not rule on which openings are sound, which schools of play deserve students, or which styles ought to spread. That, Mara says, is settled board by board, by millions of players each chasing their own wins. Into which of the chapter's categories does Mara's program fall?
options: The unconstrained vision
A hybrid of the two visions
The constrained vision
Outside both visions

items.stem: The Meridian Atelier, an international arts collective, runs residencies, a school, and shared studios. Every decision — who is admitted, what is taught, which works are exhibited — rests with the founder, Celeste Marchetti, and a small inner circle she selects for the refinement of their eye. Celeste teaches that every member carries immense creative capacity waiting to be released. But the Atelier's direction, she insists, can never be argued out: proposals are judged by how they strike the circle's trained instinct, and a member who asks for reasons is told that the request itself shows an eye still undeveloped. Into which of the chapter's categories does the Atelier's program fall?
options: Outside both visions
A hybrid of the two visions
The constrained vision
The unconstrained vision

items.stem: According to the chapter, in what way does Marxism combine the constrained and unconstrained visions?
options: It splits by domain, operating in the unconstrained vision's terms in law and politics while remaining laissez-faire in its economics.
It pairs bold assertions drawn from the unconstrained vision with immediate provisos drawn from the constrained vision on the same issues.
It casts history up through capitalism in the constrained vision's terms and the communist future in the unconstrained vision's terms.
It invokes the constrained vision's symbols of loyalty and authority while negating the systemic processes that give those symbols meaning.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Marx was not inconsistent in analyzing history up through capitalism in the constrained vision's terms while conceiving the communist future in the unconstrained vision's terms, because his theory of history holds that constraints lessen as science and technology advance.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter notes that Marx, like Smith and Burke, believed in inherent constraints on man. According to the chapter, what separated Marx's conception of those constraints from theirs?
options: Marx denied them any moral force, judging every past arrangement by timeless standards rather than by what its era made possible.
Marx located them in material production, whose frontiers science and technology push back, rather than in a fixed human nature.
Marx held that sufficiently committed leadership could override the constraints at any time, regardless of the era's stage of development.
Marx confined them to the masses, holding that the intellectual pioneers of the present already stood outside them.

items.stem: When Marx described the 'real' freedom to be realized under communism, the chapter says his language became that of the unconstrained vision. According to the chapter, what makes this conception of freedom belong to that vision?
options: It holds that each individual becomes free only apart from the community, once social compulsion over him is removed.
It defines freedom as the negative power to avoid this or that, a power that past regimes had deliberately withheld from the worker.
It makes freedom conditional on the stage of economic development, achieved by degrees as the productive forces expand.
It defines freedom as a result, the positive power to assert one's true individuality, rather than as a process characteristic.

items.stem: In Sowell's account, Jeremy Bentham's vision of man joined a severe moral constraint -- man as thoroughly, relentlessly, and incurably selfish -- to what second element?
options: A confidence that man's intellect was vast enough to rationally structure the social universe
A conviction that moral traditions and social pressures were the only workable restraints on conduct
A belief that human dispositions could gradually be improved until selfishness gave way
A theory that the march of science and technology progressively loosens material constraints

items.stem: Sowell calls utilitarianism a hybrid vision 'to a different degree in its two chief proponents.' On his account, how does Bentham's hybridity differ from Mill's?
options: Bentham held different visions in different domains, while Mill deliberately worked opposing visions into the same positions
Bentham sought out an opposing school as a corrective, while Mill reached Smith's conclusions without accepting Smith's reasons
Bentham cast the past in one vision and the future in the other, while Mill split production from distribution along the same line
Bentham's position resists placement in either camp, while Mill matched the unconstrained commitment of Godwin and Condorcet

items.stem: Mill declared the distribution of output 'a matter of human institutions solely' -- mankind can do with goods as it likes. Sowell writes that this seems a clear statement of the unconstrained vision, 'but it only seems so.' What makes it only seem so?
options: Mill at once added that the consequences of such rules escape man's control, having the character of physical laws
Placing a thinker requires the twin criteria of discretion, not a survey of his isolated economic remarks
Bentham had already established, for articulated reasons that Mill accepted, that legislators should not redistribute wealth
The declaration concerned economics alone, while Mill's constrained commitments governed his work in law and politics

items.stem: Since Bentham repeatedly declared himself a believer in Adam Smith's laissez-faire economics -- even chiding Smith for not carrying it far enough on usury laws -- his opposition to letting legislators redistribute wealth presumably rested, like Smith's, on the conviction that doing such things properly lay beyond man's intellectual and moral capabilities.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter argues that the constrained-unconstrained dichotomy cannot simply be equated with political right and left. Which philosophy does it name as epitomizing the political left while not being the unconstrained vision?
options: Libertarianism
Marxism
Fascism
Fabian socialism

items.stem: On what ground does the constrained vision, as the chapter presents it, justify allowing the individual great freedom and secure property rights?
options: The premise that the individual's own benefit, not the common good, is the end a social philosophy should serve
The expectation that free individuals will voluntarily direct their property toward the care of their fellow man
The individual's morally superior claims against society, which no appeal to the common good can override
The efficiency of making social decisions through systemic market incentives rather than by central planning

items.stem: The chapter puts William Godwin and Ayn Rand at opposite poles on moral responsibility to one's fellow man, yet counts both among the contributors to libertarianism. Why can both be included?
options: Both reject government control, and libertarianism leaves open whether freedom serves altruistic or purely personal ends
Both reason from the same constrained account of human limitations that runs from Adam Smith to F. A. Hayek
Both reach free-market conclusions, and shared policy conclusions are what mark a shared underlying vision of man
Both combine the two visions in one hybrid, reading the past in constrained terms and the hoped-for future in unconstrained terms

items.stem: According to the chapter, what ultimately divides the constrained and unconstrained visions is not a moral value premise about the common good but differing empirical assumptions about human nature and about social cause and effect.
options: True
False

bank_meta.status: UNVETTED (instructor review still required) - assembled by tools/bank_pipeline.py. THE INVARIANT FIRST, because every count here is a dated measurement: no item in this chapter keys a verdict on whether a policy is good, works, or is just -- the charged material appears only as a position the chapter attributes to a vision, a figure or a Justice. Owner-ruled buildable 2026-10-28 (ledger item 27, ch6 half). COVER TEST RUN 2026-10-28, 3 Sonnet judges (Fable authored; spec v3.10 author-judge separation), majority rule: 3 scenarios judged, ALL 3 COLLAPSED, 0 survived, and all 9 judge picks landed ON THE KEY -- the exact mirror of ch5's 0 of 9, which remains the project's best result. 6.7 is CAPPED, topped at Tier 2 with 5 Tier-2 items (floor 3). The bank ships 31 items, 8 T1 / 23 T2 / 0 T3, 0 errors 0 warnings. A chapter with no Tier-3 is a normal outcome here, as ch1 and ch4 already are. WHY, AND IT IS NOT ch4's REASON -- that is what makes this panel worth reading. ch4 failed because its stems STATED the discriminating fact. These stems do not: they describe a scheme's features (who decides, what is equalized, what happens to the residue) and no speaker explains themselves in vision-theoretic terms, which is precisely what s4a prescribes and what the spec for this LO demanded in writing. The leak is not in the stem at all. IT IS IN THE OPTION LABEL. All three judges independently reported that "constrained" and "unconstrained" carry their ordinary English senses and that those senses track the structural discriminator: keeping the existing rule and applying it as written reads as "constrained", while standing up a new expert board, overriding the old arrangement and accepting a cost reads as "unconstrained". Judge 2: "'unconstrained' reads as free to redesign and 'constrained' as bound to the existing rule, pointing to Mara=constrained/Deniz=unconstrained without needing the concept." Judge 3: "the ordinary sense of the two words alone points to this pairing over the other three." Judge 1 on all three: "reads as 'the constrained vision' by ordinary word meaning alone." SO s4a HAS A GAP, AND THIS PANEL FOUND IT. Its unbuildable test asks whether the SCENARIO can set up the case without stating the concept's variable. It never asks whether the OPTION LABEL already encodes that variable. The test was run before authoring and recorded in the LO spec as "authorable", and it was answered correctly on its own terms -- the stems really do describe only features. The missing question is s4's opaque-label clause, which asks whether a reader can decode the label without having learned it ("creative destruction", "internally stimulated" pass; an ordinary English adjective does not), and which s4a does not carry into its structural test. THE DECOY WAS AIMED AT THE WRONG VARIABLE, which is the author-side half of the same error. The spec directed the decoy at AFFECT -- dismissiveness about ordinary people reads constrained and belongs to the unconstrained tradition; indignation at unmerited rewards belongs to both camps -- and the scenarios disarmed it well. NO JUDGE USED AFFECT. All three reasoned from rule-fixity versus redesign, which is the concept's own variable in plain words, and which nothing misdirected. WHY ch5's 5.4 SURVIVED ON THE IDENTICAL LABELS, and this is the usable rule rather than the anecdote: in 5.4 the surface reading pointed AWAY from the key, because Sowell's own thesis there is that trade-off vocabulary, optimism and limits-talk do NOT place a vision, so a word-mapper was actively led wrong and every judge was pulled to a distractor. Here the surface reading pointed AT the key. So for this book a "which vision is speaking" item is buildable only when the scenario's plain reading leads AWAY from the key -- a materially stricter condition than s4a's, and the one to apply before spending scenarios on 7.6, 7.7, 8.5 or 9.7. THE PREDICTION WAS PRE-REGISTERED AND WRONG, in the optimistic direction: 2 of 3 surviving, written into the LO spec before the panel ran, per guide s4's calibration rule. That rule exists so a failure can be told apart from a misread item, and this was the former -- the reasoning was wrong, not the reading. The authoring agent's own independent forecast (choir ~2 in 3, irrigation moderate, weaver weakest) agreed with it and was equally wrong, so this is two independent optimistic errors rather than one, and neither party identified the label as the risk.

source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.6.1: Contrast what each vision holds is to be equalized — treatment by the same rules of the process, whatever results follow (Burke's "equal rights; but not to equal things," Hayek's equal treatment regardless of which group fares better), versus the results themselves, to one degree or another (Godwin's shared output of society) — so that the dispute between the visions is never over the degree of equality, which both recognize in degrees, but over what it is that is to be equalized.
learning_objectives.6.2: Explain why "equality of opportunity" and "equality before the law" still divide the two visions even though both endorse the words — prospective equality can mean prospects of being treated a given way by the rules, or equalized probabilities of achieving given results — and how the second reading generates compensatory advantages (Condorcet's "real equality" mitigating even natural differences; Shaw's ridicule of formal opportunity) that the constrained vision resists as a floodgate to new inequalities beyond anyone's intention or control, so that the two Justices in the preferential-treatment case "argued past each other."
learning_objectives.6.3: Contrast the two visions' causal accounts of why inequality exists and persists — in the unconstrained vision some have little *because* others have much (Godwin's taking, Shaw's profit-as-overcharge and parasitic empire, Bellamy's defrauded co-heirs of inherited knowledge), while in the constrained vision many exponents explain unequal results not at all, the market mitigates a common misfortune and chiefly benefits ordinary people (Friedman), and attempts to equalize economic results breed a greater and more dangerous inequality of political power (Hayek's Road to Serfdom, where humane democratic socialists pave a road others complete).
learning_objectives.6.4: Explain why the constrained vision rejects "social justice" without defending existing inequalities as just or merited — the particulars of a spontaneous order cannot be just or unjust, since only a deliberately created entity such as government can be morally judged; merit justifications belong to repudiated secondary figures (Smiles, Alger, Sumner); unmerited rewards are conceded and accepted as a trade-off on the conviction that no solution is possible; and the unconstrained vision's moral principles are rejected as irrelevant to the choices actually available, and dangerous in the concentration of power their pursuit implies, rather than as wrong.
learning_objectives.6.5: Explain why shared premises did not produce shared conclusions: Smith believed in innate human equality more than anyone (the philosopher and the porter) and despised the worship of the privileged, Godwin agreed with him point for point yet demanded drastic change, and Smith and Friedman were as offended by gross inequities as Godwin and Dworkin — because the visions part on the plane of causation, over what can be done at what cost and danger, not on fundamentally different moral principles, so that devotion to processes is not favor toward unequal results.
learning_objectives.6.6: Explain how the two visions' estimates of human capability invert the expected picture — the unconstrained vision holds the higher estimate only of human *potential*, while of people as they currently exist it estimates the elite-mass gap as far wider (the sweeping dismissals of ordinary people come from Godwin, Rousseau, Condorcet and Shaw, while the constrained tradition holds elite and mass closer together) — and why the more general and pervasive that differential is thought to be, the stronger the case for surrogate decision-makers, so that the constrained vision prizes equality of discretion where the unconstrained prizes equality of condition.
learning_objectives.6.7: Given an unfamiliar voice on an equality question, determine which vision is speaking — placing it by the structure of the position (whether the capability gap it asserts between the advanced and the ordinary is general and pervasive or confined to specialties a layman can hire; whether a conceded inequity is accepted as the by-product of a process no one designed, or discounted as a cost the demand for change outweighs) and never by surface affect, since dismissive estimates of ordinary people's current state belong to the unconstrained tradition and indignation at unmerited rewards belongs to both.

Chapter 6 → Visions of Equality.text: Equality sits with freedom and justice: a property of processes in one vision, of outcomes in the other. Burke and Hayek count identical treatment under general rules as equality however unevenly results fall; Godwin wants society's output shared out. Both admit degrees, so the quarrel is not how much but what. Even "equal opportunity" divides: prospects of being judged by one set of rules, or evened-out chances of arriving — the second inviting compensatory advantages the first calls a floodgate.

Chapter 6 → Causation.text: Why inequality persists divides them. Many constrained thinkers never explain unequal results at all; for the other side the disparity is central and causal — the few hold much because they took it, from landlords and employers to empires and disinherited heirs. Friedman replies that markets soften a common misfortune and chiefly lift ordinary people; Hayek, that equalizing outcomes concentrates dangerous political power. Neither side calls existing rewards merited: one concedes unmerited ones as a trade-off, believing no remedy exists.

Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Ineq.text: Smith held innate human equality as firmly as anyone — a philosopher parted from a porter only by upbringing — and mocked the worship of rank, yet reasoned his way to laissez-faire. Godwin granted every one of those premises and demanded upheaval; they differed about causes, not morals. On capability as it actually stands, the unconstrained vision rates the spread far wider, and its bluntest verdicts on common people come from Godwin, Rousseau, Condorcet and Shaw.

Chapter 6 → Summary and Implications.text: The visions part less over people as they are than over what they might become: the distance from actual to potential is wider in the unconstrained vision, and so is the distance between the advanced few and everyone else. Estimates of present capability differ in spread, not average — and spread is what argues for deciding on another's behalf. Where the shortfall is confined to specialties, a layman can hire expertise; where it is general, they cannot judge what they need.

items.stem: According to the chapter, equality belongs to a different category of thing in each vision, just as freedom and justice do. Which statement identifies the two categories?
options: It is a matter of degree in the constrained vision and an absolute, all-or-nothing demand in the unconstrained vision.
It is a characteristic of results in the constrained vision and a characteristic of processes in the unconstrained vision.
It is a characteristic of processes in the constrained vision and a characteristic of results in the unconstrained vision.
It is a guarantee of the law in the constrained vision and an aspiration of morality in the unconstrained vision.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the dispute between the two visions is over what is to be equalized, not over the degree of equality; each side recognizes equality in degrees.
options: True
False

items.stem: Why, in the chapter's account, does the constrained vision define equality as a characteristic of processes rather than of results?
options: Results vary too much from case to case to be judged against any fixed standard, while the rules of a process hold still long enough to be examined and compared.
The outcomes of a fair process are presumed to reflect the merit of those who obtain them, so the pattern of results stands in no need of a correcting standard.
Applying the same general rules to everyone is expected to yield roughly equal outcomes in the long run, so a separate standard aimed at results would add nothing.
A results standard would demand more intellectual and moral capacity than this vision grants to man; equal treatment under general rules lies within human reach.

items.stem: The chapter notes that Godwin himself allowed certain advantages to talent and wealth to stand. What does that allowance show about the unconstrained vision of equality?
options: That Godwin stood apart from the main unconstrained tradition, which refused any departure from strictly equal shares of society's output.
That the vision can admit equalization by degrees while still holding that results, not treatment by the rules, are the thing to be equalized.
That the vision quietly adopts the constrained camp's standard whenever absolute equality of outcome proves impossible to defend in practice.
That the vision in fact measures equality by contribution, with larger shares owed to those whose talents add the most to the common output of society.

items.stem: The chapter observes that both visions endorse "equality of opportunity" and "equality before the law," yet the phrases still mean different things in each vision. It distinguishes two readings of this prospective kind of equality. What are the two readings?
options: The same treatment under the process's rules, or the same likelihood of reaching a given result
The same guarantees in formally written law, or the same protections in unwritten social custom
The same voice in political decisions, or the same share in the economy's material rewards
The same standing when a rule is adopted, or the same standing once its outcomes are known

items.stem: The chapter presents the constrained vision's case against compensatory preferences as resting not on a claim that specified inequalities are impossible to reduce one at a time, but on the claim that the process of reducing them generates new inequalities -- beyond anyone's intention or control -- that defeat its purpose.
options: True
False

items.stem: In the preferential-treatment case the chapter recounts, one Justice held that ranking ethnic groups by historic injustice demands a kind of sociological and political analysis beyond what courts can competently perform, while the opposing Justice set out those injustices at length as grounds for compensatory preferences. Why does the chapter say the two "argued past each other"?
options: They accepted a shared conception of equality but read the historical record differently, so the dispute was over the facts of past discrimination
One treated equality as a legitimate aim for law while the other denied that equality was a proper constitutional value at all
Both agreed the preferences would equalize prospects and divided only over whether courts or legislatures should be the branch to order them
They reasoned from rival conceptions of prospective equality -- equal handling by the process's rules versus equalized prospects of results

items.stem: On the unconstrained vision's reading, the chapter explains, "equality of opportunity" can call for compensatory measures -- special schooling, hiring preferences, publicly funded counsel. Why do measures that treat people differently follow from a principle of equal opportunity, on that reading?
options: Because opportunity on that reading attaches to groups rather than persons, individuals must be treated unequally so that whole groups end up placed the same
Because compensation is owed for historic wrongs as a matter of desert, whatever any measure does to a person's present chances of success
When opportunity means an equal probability of achieving a result, one standard applied to people in radically different circumstances leaves their chances unequal
Because no rule of a process can be framed neutrally in the first place, any uniform standard already favors some group, and offsets merely cancel that built-in bias

items.stem: According to the chapter, what causal claim about wealth and poverty has run through the unconstrained vision for centuries?
options: Large fortunes chiefly reflect superior talent and effort, so the rewards of the rich are individually merited.
Some have little because others have much: the wealth of the rich was gained by taking from the poor.
Inequality is a misfortune common to every economic system, one that markets soften where they operate.
Unequal results are simply the natural default of social life, calling for no special causal account.

items.stem: The chapter presents the argument of Hayek's The Road to Serfdom as the constrained vision's central warning about equalizing economic results, noting that Hayek took democratic socialists to be genuinely humane people without the ruthlessness their goals would demand. Within the argument as the chapter renders it, what work does that point about the reformers' character do?
options: It shows the program collapsing harmlessly: reformers without ruthlessness never carry the equalization through, and the social order is left roughly as it was.
It narrows the danger to infiltration: the movement's decency could be preserved if vigilant screening kept a handful of ruthless actors from capturing it.
It locates the danger in the process itself: equal treatment by law and limits on power give way, and more ruthless movements complete what the humane began.
It functions as a charge of hypocrisy: the humane language masks reformers who mean to hold the concentrated power themselves once it exists.

items.stem: The chapter quotes Bellamy insisting that when people incapacitated for work are denied a full share of society's output, they are robbed rather than merely treated uncharitably. In his argument as the chapter gives it, what turns the denial into robbery?
options: Producers systematically charge more than their goods are worth, so the poor are robbed in every purchase they make — as customers rather than as heirs.
Most of what a producer makes comes of inherited knowledge and machinery, and the incapacitated are co-heirs to it — the share withheld was theirs already.
Aid reaches them so grudgingly and so publicly that it humiliates; offered freely and generously, the same provision would have wronged no one.
Their own earlier labor helped build the tools and workshops now in use, so wages withheld from them in the past remain owed to them in the present.

items.stem: In the account the chapter attributes to Friedman, the achievements of modern capitalism have presumably flowed mainly to the wealthy, with ordinary people sharing only incidentally in the gains.
options: True
False

items.stem: What place did merit justification - the defense of unequal rewards as individually deserved - hold in the constrained vision's tradition, as the chapter tells it?
options: It was rare, mostly confined to secondary figures, whom leading thinkers such as Hayek explicitly repudiated.
It was applied to fortunes earned in a lifetime but withheld from inherited wealth, which was treated separately.
It was standard early in the tradition but abandoned once Social Darwinism made desert arguments disreputable.
It was the tradition's main line of defense, with leading thinkers holding that rewards broadly track achievement.

items.stem: The chapter reports Hayek holding that moral judgment applies to what a government does, but not to the particular results a spontaneous order hands to individuals. What grounds the distinction?
options: Justice verdicts presuppose an intention behind the outcome, and only a deliberately created entity can act on one.
The order's results are vindicated by the general prosperity they generate, which outweighs the particular hardships.
Rewards in the order track contribution closely enough that verdicts of injustice misread what actually happened.
A government's decisions are recorded and traceable, while an order's outcomes are too tangled for anyone to reconstruct.

items.stem: According to the chapter, on what footing does the constrained vision reject the moral principles behind demands for 'social justice'?
options: As insincere, voiced by an elite more concerned with its own authority than with the lot of the masses.
As irrelevant to the choices actually open, and dangerous in the power their pursuit would concentrate.
As sound in principle but premature, waiting on gains in human knowledge and administrative capacity.
As morally false, resting on an egalitarian ideal that the vision's account of human nature refutes.

items.stem: In the chapter's account, Hayek's defense of the market presumably extends to holding that its distribution of benefits and burdens would still be just if a deliberate allocator had assigned the very same shares.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell presents William Godwin as agreeing with Adam Smith that human beings are innately equal, that the gap between wealth and poverty was enormous, and that privilege bred arrogance, yet Godwin demanded drastic change where Smith did not. Where does the chapter locate the actual difference between the two men?
options: In their preferred methods: whether change should come peacefully or by force
In their moral principles: the weight each man assigned to equality as an ideal
In their factual premises: how far each man accepted that people are innately equal
In their beliefs about causation: what could be done, at what cost and danger
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: In Sowell's account, Smith and Friedman were as offended by the gross inequities of their eras as Godwin and Dworkin were; the camps parted over causation, over what could be done about those inequities and at what cost and danger, not over fundamentally different moral principles.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell notes that a constrained-vision thinker may favor a disadvantaged group's advancement, may even have personally worked toward it, and yet fight hard against process changes designed to aid that very advancement. How does the chapter explain the combination?
options: A private preference for unequal results, concealed behind a public language of equal treatment
A devotion to processes such as free choice and the rule of law, with results a secondary concern
A conviction that formal equal treatment had already given the group genuine equality of opportunity
A belief that existing rewards are individually merited, so that aiding one group wrongs the deserving
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: Sowell relays a scholar's quip that entire socialist orations could be stitched together from Adam Smith's own words: Smith believed in innate human equality more than anyone, scorned businessmen, and mocked the foolish worship of the privileged. Why, on Sowell's account, did these premises carry Smith to laissez-faire capitalism rather than toward equalization?
options: He read the masses' worship of the privileged as proof that ordinary people were content with the social order as it stood
He concluded that the large fortunes of his era were mostly earned, so redistribution would strip the deserving of what merit had won
He held that unequal results, however real, did not matter enough to override the freedom of civil and economic processes
He expected free economic processes to erode unequal results on their own, making deliberate equalization unnecessary
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: Which statement matches the chapter's comparison of the two visions' estimates of human intelligence?
options: The unconstrained vision runs higher only on potential intelligence, not on current.
The unconstrained vision runs higher on both potential intelligence and current intelligence.
The two visions diverge on current intelligence but agree in their estimates of potential.
The constrained vision runs higher on potential intelligence, the unconstrained on current.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: Since the unconstrained vision takes the welfare of the masses as its central concern, the harshest dismissals of ordinary people as they now exist have presumably come from the constrained tradition, which arguably sees the wider gap between the capabilities of the elite and those of the mass.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: In the chapter's account, why does the unconstrained vision's estimate of people as they currently exist strengthen the case for surrogate decision-makers?
options: It expects material equalization itself to lift the masses, and only sustained direction by the advanced can hold conditions equal while that improvement arrives.
It holds that most people actively prefer inequality, so that popular choices would undo any equalization unless overridden by those who know what a better world is.
It sets the average rationality of the whole of mankind so low that nearly every choice, made by nearly anyone, requires guidance from someone better placed to judge.
It holds the differential in rationality between the advanced and the ordinary to be general and pervasive, not confined to specialties a layman could hire.

items.stem: Which kind of equality does the constrained vision rank above equality of condition, and on what ground?
options: Equality of potential — innate capacities differ far less than upbringings do, so policy should equalize the points where people start rather than where they finish.
Equality of opportunity — results can never be fully equalized, so the rules of the process should give every person identical prospects of reaching any given result.
Equality of discretion — no group has a superiority general enough to warrant deciding for others, so each person exercises his own, guided by widely shared experience.
Equality of esteem — the worship of rank is an unearned psychic windfall for the privileged, so honor should be detached from wealth and spread across the community.

items.stem: The chapter surveys contemptuous verdicts on what ordinary people are presently capable of — the peasant likened to an oyster, the masses to an invalid. From which quarter, on Sowell's account, have such verdicts characteristically come?
options: Only the explicitly racist and Social Darwinist writers
Writers in the constrained tradition
Both traditions in roughly equal measure
Writers in the unconstrained tradition
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: According to the chapter, leading thinkers of the constrained vision concede that many rewards in society go to people who have not personally earned them.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell reports that Smith and Friedman were moved by the same gross disparities of wealth that outraged Godwin and Dworkin. Why, on the chapter's account, does this shared reaction tell us nothing about which vision a thinker holds?
options: Because the visions part over causation — what produced the disparity, and what remedy is open at what risk — not over moral principles.
Because each camp reserves its indignation for a different target, inherited privilege on one side of the divide and commercial profit on the other.
Because the constrained thinkers' expressions of concern are merely rhetorical, masking a settled conviction that existing rewards are deserved.
Because only secondary figures in either tradition voiced such reactions, while each tradition's leading exponents stayed silent on inequity.

items.stem: Both visions, the chapter says, concede that people's developed capabilities are unequal. What, in its account, actually determines how strong the case for surrogate decision-makers becomes?
options: How low the average capability of the ordinary person is estimated to be, measured across the society as a whole.
How sincerely the elite is thought to have made the well-being of the ordinary masses its central concern.
Whether innate potential is believed to be spread equally across all individuals and across social groups.
How wide the capability gap between different sets of people is taken to be, rather than its average level.

items.stem: A town choral society pays small honoraria to its soloists, and the solo roster has been filled by the same dozen voices for years. Two members address the annual meeting. Mara calls several current soloists coasting beneficiaries of the society's habits, no finer than the rank and file, and wants the audition rule enforced exactly as written for every singer, with any member who wishes engaging the retired opera coach in town for lessons at their own expense and judgment. Deniz calls most of the membership unable, for now, to hear their own faults, and wants a standing board of the three conservatory-trained members to assign every singer's parts, repertoire and practice plan, granting that dues must rise and some singers will quit, a price he counts well worth paying. Which pairing correctly places the two speakers?
options: Both speakers constrained
Both speakers unconstrained
Mara unconstrained; Deniz constrained
Mara constrained; Deniz unconstrained

items.stem: A hill village's irrigation association meets after a dry summer; under rotations handed down for generations, a few households draw far more water than the rest. Four members speak. Tamsin is incensed that the largest draws water the meadows of families who have not cleared a ditch in years, wants the rotation bell rung by the book for every household, and would have disputing farmers split the cost of a hired surveyor whenever a channel's fall is doubted. Odo wants the old rotation captains stood down and every question of a draw or a ditch put to a show of hands of the full membership, each household casting one vote alike whatever its acreage, and the tally posted in the hall that same evening. Petra wants a permanent board of the two agronomy-schooled farmers and the schoolhouse engineer to set each household's draw, cropping and channel repairs season by season, conceding that the meters and a clerk's wage will cost the village dearly and counting that cost slight beside the gains. Mina wants the driest crofts carried through hard summers by a standing subscription that the better-watered households are invited, never compelled, to join, with the rotation itself left exactly as the elders set it and the next dry year met in the same way. Which speaker's position belongs to the unconstrained vision?
options: Petra
Tamsin
Odo
Mina
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: A retired master-weaver writes to her guild about the journeyman's medal, whose stipend has gone for a generation to apprentices of the same three workshops. Any child set young to a loom, she writes, could have matched most of the medalists, the difference lying in the bench and not the blood; and several recent winners she names outright as no credit to the craft, carried to the stipend on their workshop's reputation. She opposes the committee's plan to rotate the medal among the workshops by turns until each has had its share; asks instead that the judging rules be read aloud unchanged and applied alike to every bolt entered, and that the two judges who last year let a famous name sway their marks be put off the panel; and remarks that any shop wanting the medal badly can buy winters of the pattern-drawer's teaching, as two of the winning three once did. Which vision is the letter speaking from?
options: Neither vision
The constrained vision
The unconstrained vision
Both visions equally
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

bank_meta.status: UNVETTED — Tier-3 CONFIRMED on LO 1.3 by a 3-judge blind Sonnet panel after ONE REPAIR ROUND, 2026-09-24 (spec v3.10 author≠judge: authored by Fable, judged by Sonnet, judges restricted to the blinded prompt and forbidden the chapter, the bank and the LO doc). All three scenarios now survive. THIS BANK'S HISTORY IS THE USEFUL PART, so it is recorded rather than smoothed. The FIRST panel collapsed TWO of the three scenarios UNANIMOUSLY (3/3 each): fly-c1-014 and fly-c1-016. All six judge verdicts gave the same reason — the KEY'S REFERENT was described more fully, more vividly and more specifically than the alternatives. Measured afterwards, the per-case word counts were 19/20/26/15 and 17/34/24/15, with the key holding the longest description in both. Because the options in these items are bare names, the stem's descriptions of each case ARE the option set, so authoring_guide §3 parity applies to them and a character count on the option strings reports parity while the item is wide open. One judge named it outright: 'that disproportionate elaboration reads as the item-writer's tell.' Written up as LEARNED_2026-09-24_authoring_parity-applies-to-the-referents-not-the-options.md and as the new authoring_guide §3a. THE REPAIR was a presentation fix only — same four labels, same keys, same discriminating logic, verified by assertion. Referent descriptions equalised to 32/32/32/31 and 34/34/33/34 words, the stem's own framing phrases moved off the key and onto distractors, and the most vivid case made a wrong answer in both (Cal; Ashby, with its itemised pay-stub line). The surviving scenario fly-c1-015 was left byte-identical. THE RE-PANEL USED THREE FRESH JUDGES AND A HARDER PROMPT than the first, explicitly directing them to hunt for referent-description asymmetry — a repair that only passes a gentler test has not been shown to work. Result: fly-c1-014 clean 0/3 (judges took Cal, Ben and Dee, all distractors), fly-c1-015 clean 0/3, fly-c1-016 one dissent of three. WEAKEST SURVIVOR, AND A REFINEMENT THE REPAIR ITSELF CAUSED. fly-c1-016 drew its single collapse vote from a judge that narrowed the field to Ashby-or-Bell because the repair had given those two a VERBATIM IDENTICAL closing clause ('they now drop everything in exam week'), then called the choice 'roughly a coin flip between them' and guessed the key at confidence 0.40. So parity is not monotonically good: making the key and exactly one distractor word-identical cuts a blind guess from one-in-four to one-in-two. Spread equalising language across three or four cases, never exactly two. If a later edit disturbs fly-c1-016, re-run the panel rather than assuming the tier holds. SINGLE ANCHOR: this chapter has no subsection headings, so all 26 items carry 'Chapter 1 → The Cabbie's Tale' and one 76-word excerpt serves all five LOs — the most compressed excerpt in the project, and the practical cost of a chapter with no internal structure. LO 1.1 is deliberately recall-topped and thin: this is an introduction whose mechanisms live in later chapters. TWO SOURCE INCONSISTENCIES FOUND HERE, both recorded as never-key in docs/flynn_los.md. (7) This chapter contradicts itself on the spending ratio six paragraphs apart — '75 percent less per person' (US = 4x) against 'nearly three times as much per person' (US = 3x); across the book the ratio appears as 4x, 3x and ≈2.6x. Never key a computed ratio. (8) This chapter ranks Singapore FIRST in maternal mortality while chapter 3 says three countries beat it and chapter 3's own table shows one of those three doing worse — three mutually incompatible accounts of one statistic. Never key Singapore's maternal-mortality standing anywhere in this book. Grounded on a private staged copy (sources/, gitignored) verified against the read-only reference library at 0.0 percent word-count drift. Excerpt is paraphrase, ≤80 words, longest run shared with the source 3 words. Instructor review required before release.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.1.1: Identify the kinds of evidence Flynn offers for his claim that Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare at the world's lowest cost — published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and a week of first-hand observation undertaken because the numbers seemed too good to be true to a self-described cynical economist.
learning_objectives.1.2: Explain what Flynn's pairing of outcome rankings with spending comparisons is meant to establish: that the United States pays far more per person than Singapore and still trails it on every outcome he cites, so the gap is a failure on both axes rather than a price-for-quality trade-off — and that the countries usually offered as US models, Canada and the United Kingdom, also spend far more than Singapore.
learning_objectives.1.3: Explain how, on Flynn's reading, the cabbie's complaint that he has to go to the gym because he would bear much of the cost of developing diabetes is evidence the system works rather than a flaw: personal cost exposure, explicitly not a government mandate, produces the sustained preventive effort US professionals mostly just talk about.
learning_objectives.1.4: Explain why Flynn treats the US origin of Singapore's components — price tags and health savings accounts, developed in America decades earlier — together with their use by Whole Foods and by Indiana, as answering his opening question of whether the approach could work back home: the US merely invented, while Singapore implemented.
learning_objectives.1.5: Explain why Flynn expects reform on Singapore's model to be thankless but not fruitless: beneficiaries stop perceiving a good system and complain about the very incentives that make it work, while the payoff he claims accrues whether or not anyone notices.

Chapter 1 → The Cabbie's Tale.text: A sceptical economist flew out for a week because the reported pairing of top results with the lowest spending seemed implausible. He found a well-run neighbourhood clinic whose staff saw nothing remarkable in it, and a driver who resented exercising because he would meet much of the cost of falling ill — pressure no rule imposed. The components, he notes, were American inventions that another country merely applied. Reform, he predicts, would go uncredited without going unrewarded.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Flynn fly to Singapore to examine its healthcare system in person?
options: No published figures on Singapore's system existed, so he had to gather the basic data himself.
He was convinced the statistics were false and went to document the system's hidden flaws.
The statistics he had read seemed too good to be true, and he wanted to confirm they were not lying.
Singapore's health ministry had invited him on an official visit to evaluate its neighborhood polyclinics.

items.stem: According to the chapter, on what kinds of evidence does Flynn rest his claim that Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare at the world's lowest cost?
options: Published outcome rankings, a week of observing the system himself, and cost projections from his own economic model.
Published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and the results of Whole Foods' and Indiana's programs.
Published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and a week of observing the system himself.
A week of observing the system himself, per-person spending comparisons, and an official evaluation by its health ministry.

items.stem: Flynn reports gathering first-hand evidence during his week in Singapore. According to the chapter, which of the following was part of that effort?
options: Meeting the health ministry's leadership to review the government's own official outcome statistics.
Comparing the annual budgets of several polyclinics with those of comparable clinics in the United States.
Touring the country's leading private hospitals rather than its government-run neighborhood clinics.
Asking doctors, former public health officials, cabbies, and shop clerks what they thought of the system.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Bloomberg Businessweek ranking Flynn cites is presumably a measure of per-person healthcare spending rather than of health outcomes.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does per-person healthcare spending in the United States compare with Singapore's?
options: The US spends about one and a half times as much per person as Singapore.
The US and Singapore spend about the same amount per person on healthcare.
The US spends somewhat less per person than Singapore does.
The US spends nearly three times as much per person as Singapore.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the United States edges out Singapore on at least one of the three measures of healthcare effectiveness that Flynn calls most important, even though it trails on the others.
options: True
False

items.stem: Flynn presents Singapore's outcome rankings alongside per-person spending comparisons. According to the chapter, what is that pairing meant to establish about the United States?
options: That its extra spending buys strengths the three headline measures miss and only a broader index can reveal.
That its results would rise to Singapore's level if it were willing to spend more per person on healthcare.
That Singapore's low spending is offset by weaker results on some measures, so each country trades price against quality.
That it pays far more than Singapore yet gets worse results, so the gap is not a matter of paying more for better care.

items.stem: Suppose Flynn had reported only the outcome rankings, with the United States trailing Singapore on each measure, and said nothing about spending. According to the chapter's line of argument, which reply to Flynn's case would that leave open?
options: That the outcome statistics are too good to be true and cannot be taken at face value.
That the US is simply spending less than Singapore and getting the level of care it pays for.
That Singapore's results rest on policies foreign to the US that could not be transplanted here.
That the three measures are too narrow to judge a whole system, so the ranking proves little on its own.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does Flynn extend the spending comparison beyond the United States to Canada and the United Kingdom?
options: They spend about what Singapore spends per person, which leaves the United States as the lone high-cost outlier.
They rank ahead of Singapore on Bloomberg's broader index, which makes them the fairer benchmark for outcomes.
They, rather than the United States, developed the price tags and savings accounts Singapore later implemented.
They are the usual models offered for US reform, and even they spend far more per person than Singapore.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did Flynn react once the cabbie explained why he hated Singapore's healthcare system?
options: He pressed the cabbie for other flaws that outsiders might have missed
He smiled, taking what the cabbie called a problem to be an answer
He told the cabbie that regular exercise was a small price for his health
He noted the complaint as his first sign that the statistics had been oversold

items.stem: According to the chapter, when Flynn asked whether the government forced him to go to the gym, the cabbie said no; he went because he would have to pay much of the cost himself if he got fat and developed diabetes.
options: True
False

items.stem: On Flynn's reading, why does the cabbie's complaint count as evidence that Singapore's system is working rather than as a report of a flaw in it?
options: What he resents is an exercise rule that the government applies evenly to every citizen
What he resents is trivial next to the treatment costs he would otherwise face
What he resents is the sort of thing people find to complain about under any arrangement
What he resents is the sustained preventive effort the system exists to produce

items.stem: According to the chapter, what struck Flynn about the cabbie's habit was that Singapore had found a way to get an ordinary citizen to comply with a government exercise requirement, something US healthcare professionals had only talked about doing.
options: True
False

items.stem: A delivery company changes one thing about breakdowns: when a van fails on its route from a fault the driver could have caught on a morning walkaround, the tow and the lost day come out of that driver's quarterly bonus. Six months in, a consultant asks four drivers what they think of it. Ben: 'I hate it. Since the bonus thing my supervisor has us sign a twenty-point sheet every morning, and I do every line, because he is at the gate checking twice a week.' Cal: 'I hate it. In March a fuel pump quit on me halfway through my route, no warning at all, and the tow and the lost day came out of my bonus anyway.' Ana: 'I hate it. Belts, hoses, tires, my own routine now, every day before I pull out. It beats paying for a tow, but I have been late to my first stop twice.' Dee: 'It's fine. The shop fixes things properly now instead of patching them, my van has not been off the road once all year, and it has never cost me a cent.' Which driver's response is the counterpart of the cabbie's in Flynn's chapter?
options: Cal
Ana
Dee
Ben

items.stem: A housing co-op has long paid for burst-pipe repairs out of its shared reserve and has run a well-attended winterizing workshop every October. Two years ago the board changed one thing about billing: a unit now pays for repairs to its own frozen pipes. The workshop continues. At this year's annual meeting a resident who says she has no interest in home maintenance tells the board she hates the change, because every October she now has to crawl under her deck to shut off the outside tap and drain the line. She adds that the workshop taught her how years ago. Several neighbors nod. The board asks what to do. If the board reasons about her the way Flynn reasons about the cabbie, what does it do?
options: Drop the billing change and expand the workshop
Leave the billing change and the workshop as they are
Make the October shutoff a bylaw with a fine for missing it
Return frozen-pipe repairs to the shared reserve

items.stem: Four colleges at one university want final grades submitted on time. At Ashby a late grade sheet costs the instructor a hundred dollars a day, itemized as a line on the next pay stub, and instructors grumble that they now drop everything in exam week. At Bell nothing is deducted; the registrar no longer covers for late grades, so a late instructor sorts out every resulting enrollment hold, and instructors grumble that they now drop everything in exam week. At Cole the dean circulates a memo every term on the importance of timeliness and presents a plaque to the most punctual department at the faculty meeting, and instructors grumble about the memo. At Dunn a staff member in the records office quietly handles whatever late grades produce, as she has for years; nobody is charged and nothing is said, and instructors do not grumble at all. A visiting economist who reasons as Flynn does about the cabbie is asked which college has built what the cabbie was describing. Which does she name?
options: Cole
Ashby
Bell
Dunn

items.stem: According to the chapter, where does Flynn say the major components of Singapore's healthcare system, such as price tags and health savings accounts, were originally developed?
options: In Canada and the United Kingdom, the countries often proposed as models for US reform
In the United States, in many cases decades before Singapore made use of them
In the United States, but only recently and in response to Singapore's results
In Singapore, by officials designing a system to suit its own population

items.stem: According to the chapter, when Flynn says the United States 'merely invented, while Singapore implemented,' the inventions he has in mind are mainly medical technologies, such as drugs and devices, that Singapore then adopted.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn went to Singapore wanting to know, among other things, whether what it was doing 'might also work back home.' After returning, he discovered that Singapore's major components had originally been developed in the United States. How does Flynn treat that discovery in relation to his question?
options: As answering it yes: the ideas are already American and should have produced the result here first, so all that is missing is implementation
As answering it no: Singapore succeeded only by reworking American ideas that had already failed at home, so re-importing them would repeat that failure
As changing it: since the ideas were American, Flynn argues the United States deserves the credit for Singapore's results rather than needing to copy them
As leaving it open: who invented a policy says nothing about whether it works, so Flynn falls back on the outcome statistics to settle the question

items.stem: According to the chapter, having argued that Singapore's components were invented in America, Flynn then points to Whole Foods Market and to former Indiana governors as Americans who, he says, have already implemented such policies. What work does this citation do in his argument?
options: It supplies his main evidence: detailed cost and outcome figures from these programmes, which replace the Singapore statistics as proof
It concedes a limit: private firms and state governments can adopt such policies, but Flynn doubts a national system could
It names the inventors: Flynn credits Mackey, Daniels and Pence with originally developing price tags and health savings accounts
It moves the claim from 'could work here' to 'has already been done here': Americans can implement, not only invent

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn writes that the United States 'merely invented, while Singapore implemented.' Which reading best captures the contrast he is drawing?
options: The policies were developed in America as voluntary options, while Singapore made them work by having the government compel their use
The policies were developed in America but never used to build its healthcare system, while Singapore built its system on them
The policies were developed in America in rough form, and only Singapore's later refinements turned them into something that could work
The policies were developed in America and adopted in both countries, but Singapore has run them more effectively than the United States

items.stem: At the close of the chapter, Flynn tells anyone who signs on to implement Singapore-style reform in the United States what to expect. According to the chapter, what does he predict?
options: Reform will probably be fruitless, but reformers would still be thanked.
Reform will probably be thankless, but it won't be fruitless.
Reform will be appreciated once Americans notice how much better it is.
Reform will be resisted until the government mandates regular exercise.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn expects that a few years after a Singapore-style reform took effect, most Americans would probably remember how bad the old system had been and thank the reformers for the change.
options: True
False

items.stem: Flynn closes the chapter by predicting that reform on Singapore's model would probably be 'thankless' but would not be 'fruitless.' According to the chapter, what distinction is he drawing?
options: Whether Americans invent the components is separate from whether they implement them.
Whether the reform pays off depends on whether people notice and appreciate it.
Whether people complain about the reform shows whether it has failed to deliver.
Whether people credit the reform is separate from whether it delivers its benefits.

items.stem: Flynn writes that 'a fish doesn't know that it's living in water,' and earlier he describes a senior polyclinic nurse who could not understand why anybody would be impressed by her clinic. According to the chapter, what point do these two illustrations make?
options: People complain about a system's incentives even when the incentives work.
People who benefit from a well-run system stop noticing how good it is.
People resent being photographed or studied by outsiders.
People in poor neighborhoods have access to modern, well-run public clinics.

items.stem: In his closing prediction, Flynn writes that, 'as with my cabbie in Singapore, people will find things to complain about.' According to the chapter, what does invoking the cabbie add to his prediction that reform would be thankless?
options: Some beneficiaries would find genuine flaws in the system that outsiders cannot see.
Some beneficiaries would need a government mandate before they changed their habits.
Some beneficiaries would resent the very incentives that make the system work.
Some beneficiaries would stop noticing the system because they were used to it.
