source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.2.1: Explain how the chapter establishes that Singapore's rise since independence was exceptional: the reversal of its standing relative to the United States, matched by comparable gains in health and environment, and its ranking as the richest nation once oil, banking and gambling economies are set aside.
learning_objectives.2.2: Explain how the chapter makes the PAP's electoral dominance the enabling condition for Lee's long-horizon policymaking, including the feedback loop by which policy success extended that dominance.
learning_objectives.2.3: Explain how meritocratic schooling and integrated, owner-occupied public housing were designed to give every ethnic and religious group an equal chance at advancement and a real stake in the economy.
learning_objectives.2.4: Apply Lee's carrot-and-stick logic for escaping the middle-income trap to a novel case, predicting whether a proposed policy pairing would make low-productivity production unprofitable enough to push firms to upgrade.
learning_objectives.2.5: Explain the role of the Central Provident Fund in Singapore's development: how compulsory saving at high combined rates supplied domestic capital in place of borrowing from foreign investors, and why Lee put its investment under engineers and technocrats rather than bankers.
learning_objectives.2.6: Explain how Singapore's tax design — low, flat, almost no deductions, with credits only for research and development, training, high-efficiency equipment and intellectual property — makes innovation, investment and entrepreneurship the only route by which a firm can reduce its taxable income.

Chapter 2 → The Colony of Singapore.text: A trading settlement founded under a British company in the early nineteenth century, drawing labourers from China and elsewhere, it prospered by sitting at the narrow point every east-west voyage through the region must pass. Independence arrived late and poor, with income per head roughly a fifth of the American figure. Within half a century that relationship had inverted, and among countries with varied economies none was richer.

Chapter 2 → Rich, Green, and Prosperous.text: Gains were not confined to income. Where cholera and typhoid once circulated and waste ran untreated into the water, the city is now unusually clean and densely planted, topping assessments of urban greenery. Most residents own their homes, a far larger share than in America, and a tenth of households hold wealth above a million dollars, behind only an oil state and a banking centre.

Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?.text: The explanation offered is governance. The governing party won by margins wide enough, on this account, to free the first prime minister from bargaining with rivals, factions or interest groups, leaving him to pick whichever policies he judged best. Success then made that party more popular still and secured further terms — a loop the chapter credits with letting ministers spend their time solving problems rather than campaigning, and so plan further ahead.

Chapter 2 → Policies for Prosperity?.text: Schooling was made excellent and advancement made to follow measured achievement, so every community shared one route upward. Flats were built with subsidy and then sold rather than let, with quotas keeping each block mixed, which gave residents both an asset and a stake. To escape stalling at low-wage manufacturing, owners were offered generous help buying better machinery and training staff, while a charge on wages made staying cheap unprofitable.

Chapter 2 → Savings and Wealth.text: A compulsory savings scheme, the Central Provident Fund, was inherited from the colonial administration and expanded until worker and employer each put in a quarter of pay — an extraordinary rate by rich-world standards. That pool funded roads, schools and firms, sparing the country dependence on foreign lenders, and engineers rather than financiers were entrusted with investing it. Taxes stayed low and flat, with relief only for research, training, equipment and intellectual property.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did Singapore's standard of living compare with that of the United States at independence, and again by the 2010s?
options: Roughly level with the United States at independence; almost 20 percent above it by the 2010s.
About 80 percent below the United States at independence; almost 20 percent above it by the 2010s.
About 20 percent below the United States at independence; almost 80 percent above it by the 2010s.
About 80 percent below the United States at independence; still roughly 20 percent below it by the 2010s.

items.stem: According to the chapter, by the 2010s Singapore had become, by a modest margin, the world's richest nation as measured by GDP per person.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter ranks Singapore seventh in the world in GDP per person by the 2010s, yet calls it the richest country 'among nations with diversified economies'. According to the chapter, what do the six countries ranked above it have in common that justifies setting them aside?
options: Each is a microstate whose tiny population inflates its per-person figure, making the comparison with Singapore statistically unfair.
Each was already wealthy at the time of Singapore's independence, so it never had to make the climb from poverty that Singapore made.
Each is an oil state, a banking haven, or a gambling destination, rich from one narrow source rather than a broad-based economy.
Each reports GDP without adjusting for cost of living, so its figure overstates what its residents can actually afford to buy.

items.stem: After describing Singapore's economic rise, the chapter turns to health and the environment. What does that section add to the chapter's case that the rise was exceptional?
options: It concedes that environmental quality lagged for decades and was cleaned up only once the country was already rich.
It argues that the health gains came first and drove the income gains, since a healthier workforce is more productive.
It reports that health and environmental conditions improved as dramatically as incomes did over the same period.
It shows that the new wealth went mainly into public amenities such as greenbelts rather than into household incomes.

items.stem: The chapter compares Singapore's GDP per person with that of the United States at independence and again about five decades later. According to the chapter, what does that pair of comparisons establish?
options: That Singapore did not merely close the gap but reversed it, from far poorer than the United States to richer within fifty years.
That Singapore's later figure owes much to the cost-of-living adjustment, which flattered its standing relative to the United States.
That the United States stagnated over the period, which is what allowed a small trading economy to draw level with it and then pass it.
That Singapore's growth, though rapid, had brought it only to roughly the same standard of living as the United States enjoyed.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what do the PAP's near-certain election victories allow Singapore's government to do?
options: Adjust its program after each election to match the concerns that voters raised most often during the campaign.
Promote only the brightest and most accomplished graduates into the government's administrative positions.
Take the long view, with ministers spending their terms on solving problems rather than on getting reelected.
Fund its investments by borrowing abroad rather than by drawing on the compulsory savings of its own citizens.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?

items.stem: On the chapter's account, the PAP's near-certain election victories mainly gave Lee's government better timing, letting it schedule unpopular measures for the period just after each election.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?

items.stem: Which statement best captures how the chapter relates the PAP's strength at the polls to the success of Lee's policies?
options: The two are separate: Lee's firm belief that Singapore could become a first-world nation explains the policies, and the party's early standing explains its margins.
Wide margins freed Lee to pursue the policies he judged best; their success then made the PAP more popular, which extended his freedom to keep implementing them.
The policies succeeded because the PAP was already popular; the party's wide margins at independence were enough on their own to account for Singapore's rise.
The PAP's margins were the product of the policies' success; popular support was a result of good governance rather than a condition that made good governance possible.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?

items.stem: The chapter contrasts government ministers who spend their terms 'focused on solving problems' with ministers focused 'on getting reelected.' According to the chapter, what produces the first kind in Singapore?
options: Lee's own firmly held belief that Singapore could become a first-world nation and that he was placed to bring that about.
The meritocratic practice of promoting only the brightest and most accomplished graduates into government administrative positions.
The placement of engineers and technocrats, rather than bankers and financiers, in charge of the investment decisions made with the country's savings.
The near-certainty that the PAP will win the next election, which removes reelection as a constraint on how ministers spend a term of office.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?

items.stem: The chapter answers its own question, 'How did Singapore get from there to here?', with 'good governance.' What role does the PAP's electoral dominance play in that answer, as the chapter presents it?
options: It is the good governance itself: the PAP's repeated wide election margins are the main evidence offered that Singapore was well run under Lee.
It is a rival explanation set aside: schools, housing and compulsory saving, not who held office or by what margin, are what account for the rise.
It is a by-product noted in passing: successful policies made the PAP popular, but the explanation of the rise rests on the specific policies and nothing else.
It is what made that governance possible: wide margins left Lee free to pursue the policies he judged best rather than those likeliest to win reelection.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?

items.stem: According to the chapter, Lee's effort to make Singapore a meritocracy rested on which two elements?
options: World-class schools, plus promotion of only the most accomplished graduates to government administrative posts
Low flat tax rates, plus generous credits for research, worker training and high-efficiency equipment
Subsidized apartment construction, plus quotas keeping every building and neighborhood racially and religiously mixed
Compulsory retirement saving by every worker, plus a wage surtax on firms that declined to upgrade their factories

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Housing and Development Board mostly rented out the apartments it subsidized rather than selling them to residents.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Lee have the Housing and Development Board sell its subsidized apartments to residents rather than rent them?
options: He held that owning a home gave people a real stake in the economy and a reliable vehicle for long-term saving
Owners, unlike tenants, could be held to the quotas that kept each building racially and religiously mixed
Sales recovered the construction subsidies quickly, which freed up public money for the next round of apartment building
Ownership gave children of every ethnic and religious group an equal chance at advancement

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did making Singapore a meritocracy help to ease racial tensions?
options: Government administrative posts were apportioned among the ethnic and religious groups in proportion to their share of the population
Families of every background lived side by side as neighbors in apartment buildings the housing board had integrated
A steady flow of well-educated graduates let firms upgrade their factories, raising productivity and wages for everyone
Advancement went to the most accomplished graduates, so children of every ethnic and religious group had an equal chance at it

items.stem: On the chapter's account, what were the Housing and Development Board's integration quotas designed to accomplish?
options: Reserve a share of the units in every building for low-income households, so that affordable housing reached even the poor
Give graduates promoted into government service first choice of units, so that merit was rewarded in housing as well as in careers
Keep any ethnic group from becoming geographically isolated, so families of all backgrounds lived as neighbors and shared schools
Show the foreign investors Lee was courting that the island was socially stable and its property rights were secure

items.stem: According to the chapter, what did Lee's government do to a clothing manufacturer who turned down the upgrade subsidies and kept paying sweatshop wages?
options: Demanded a surtax matching every wage the manufacturer paid
Fined the manufacturer for each month it ran without approved equipment
Ordered the manufacturer to raise wages to a government-set minimum
Revoked the manufacturer's licence until it accepted the subsidies

items.stem: According to the chapter, at what stage do countries caught in the 'middle-income trap' get stuck?
options: Urban trading, unable to build a manufacturing base of any kind
Heavy industry, unable to develop a cutting-edge service sector
Agriculture and resource extraction, unable to industrialise at all
Light industry, unable to move on to heavy or high-tech industry

items.stem: On Lee's logic as the chapter presents it, why did the wage surtax lead low-productivity factory owners to accept the upgrade subsidies rather than carry on as before?
options: It made carrying on without the subsidies a breach of the law
A steady supply of well-educated graduates made upgrading easy
It raised labour costs until the low-tech factory no longer paid
It funded the subsidies from the pockets of the low-wage firms themselves

items.stem: On Lee's logic as the chapter presents it, the subsidies for higher-tech equipment and worker training were arguably enough on their own to move light-industry owners off low-productivity production.
options: True
False

items.stem: A hospital group buys laundered linen and sterile packs from a network of small local suppliers, most of which still run labour-intensive operations on low pay. The group announces the largest supplier programme in its history: it will pay most of the cost of automated washing and packing lines for any supplier that wants them, and will train the supplier's staff to run the new equipment. The offer is open for a fixed window, after which it closes for good. Suppliers that decline stay on their current contracts at current prices. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the group expect most of its suppliers to do?
options: Drop out of the network
Keep running as they are
Automate as the window closes
Take the offer and automate

items.stem: A port authority licenses a dozen private firms to load and unload cargo on its quays. Most still work the old way, with large gangs of low-paid casual labour rather than the container cranes and automated yards used at rival ports. The authority announces the toughest package it has ever adopted: a charge on every hour of low-paid casual labour worked on the quays, large enough that the old way stops paying, together with a well-funded scheme, open to dockworkers rather than to the firms, that retrains anyone whose job disappears and places them with other employers. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the authority expect most of the firms to do?
options: Buy cranes at their own cost
Buy cranes using the scheme
Carry on and pay the charge
Hand back their licences

items.stem: In the weaving district of Orlan, in the country of Halveria, most workshops still run hand-fed looms with low-paid operators. The district council adopts two measures at once. The first is a grant covering most of the cost of modern looms and of training operators to run them. The second, the first of its kind in the district's history, is a levy on every hour of low-paid work; the workshop owners' association has denounced it as an attack on the trade. The levy is set at the level needed to cover the council's cost of processing grant applications. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the council expect most workshops to do?
options: Re-equip without the grant
Close rather than re-equip
Take the grant and re-equip
Carry on as they are

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did the Central Provident Fund (CPF) come into being, and what was Lee Kuan Yew's part in it?
options: It began as a program of the Malaysian federation, which Singapore kept after its expulsion, leaving the contribution rates as they were.
The Housing and Development Board created it to finance apartment construction, and Lee later widened it to retirement saving.
Lee created it shortly after full independence, as one of his first economic measures, and set its contribution rates high from the outset.
It was set up under British colonial administration, before independence; Lee's contribution was to raise its rates over time.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did the savings rate produced by the CPF's peak contribution rates compare with the personal savings rate of the United States?
options: It roughly matched the highest US rate of the postwar decades, but Singapore sustained that level for far longer than the United States did.
It fell short of the peak US rate, because contributions made by employers were not counted as personal saving by the worker.
It was far above the highest rate the United States has ever recorded, and beyond anything Western Europe or Japan has reached.
It exceeded the long-run US average in most years, but stayed below the highest US rates that were recorded over the same period.

items.stem: The chapter calls the cash generated by the CPF 'essential' to Singapore's development. On the chapter's account, why was it essential?
options: It showed foreign investors that Singaporeans were thrifty and disciplined savers, which drew in the foreign capital that financed most of the country's growth.
It guaranteed every worker a retirement income, which relieved the government of having to fund support for the elderly out of general tax revenue.
It gave Singapore its own pool of capital to invest in infrastructure, schools and businesses, instead of the foreign borrowing many poor nations rely on.
It held down household consumption, which kept inflation low enough for the currency to be fully backed by international assets and remain strong.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Lee put the CPF's investments in the hands of engineers and technocrats rather than bankers and financiers?
options: He worried bankers would park the money in safe, low-yield reserves, leaving the fund too little growth to pay out workers' retirement benefits when they came due.
He feared bankers would lend the fund's money to borrowers abroad at higher interest, draining away the domestic capital that compulsory saving had been built to accumulate.
He wanted the money steered into productive technologies, infrastructure and education, not into the short-run profits financiers might be tempted to chase.
He expected engineers to estimate the costs of ports, roads and housing more accurately, which would keep the fund's construction projects within their budgets.

items.stem: On the chapter's account, Singapore financed its development in much the same way as many poor nations, largely by borrowing from foreign investors, with the CPF serving mainly as a retirement scheme for its workers.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is the only way a business in Singapore can reduce its taxable income?
options: By keeping wages low enough to avoid the government's surtax
By engaging in innovation, investment, or entrepreneurship
By claiming the ordinary business deductions the flat tax allows
By paying the required contributions into its workers' CPF accounts

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore kept its taxes low in order to attract foreign investment and to let local companies reinvest more of their profits.
options: True
False

items.stem: On the chapter's account, why is engaging in innovation, investment or entrepreneurship the only way a business in Singapore can reduce its taxable income?
options: Because the rates are already so low, firms have little tax left to reduce, and the credits are the only reductions still worth the effort of claiming.
Because the flat tax allows almost no other loopholes or deductions, the credits tied to those activities are the only reductions left to claim.
Because the wage surtax claws back whatever a firm saves through ordinary deductions, the credits are the only reductions that actually survive it.
Because the credits are so generous, firms prefer them to the ordinary business deductions that the code continues to make available to them.

items.stem: On the chapter's account, why is the near-absence of other deductions essential to the incentive? That is, why would the credits for R&D, training, high-efficiency equipment and intellectual property, on their own, not make those activities the only route to a lower taxable income?
options: With ordinary deductions still available, firms would use them to offset the wage surtax and keep their low-productivity factories profitable.
Without closing the other deductions, the code would lose the simplicity and transparency that the chapter says is what draws foreign investors to Singapore.
With ordinary deductions still available, firms could cut taxable income without innovating, and the credited activities would be one option among several.
Without closing the other deductions, the government could not afford credits as generous as the chapter describes, so it would have to scale them back.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what makes innovation, investment and entrepreneurship the only way for a Singapore firm to reduce its taxable income is mainly the low level of its tax rates; the flat structure with almost no deductions serves mostly to keep the system simple and transparent.
options: True
False

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.3.1: Explain why the chapter ranks Singapore, not Japan, as the world's best healthcare system: Japan edges it on life expectancy and infant mortality, but among nations of a million or more — a cutoff adopted to drop tax-haven microstates — Singapore alone sits in the top five on all three outcome measures, does so year after year, tops Bloomberg's twenty-one-metric ranking, and spends less per person than any other developed nation.
learning_objectives.3.2: Explain why the chapter says a policy-maker weighing the United States against a much poorer country as a cost-benefit question would miss the real action: the choice is a false dichotomy between spending too much for mediocre results and spending too little into an early grave, and the real question is whether a country can live longer while spending less.
learning_objectives.3.3: Given a new candidate explanation of Singapore's results and a set of comparison countries, determine which comparison the chapter's method uses to rule it out and on what ground — a country with the trait that performs poorly, or a country lacking it that performs well — so that the cause must lie elsewhere.
learning_objectives.3.4: Explain how Table 3.2 establishes Singapore's efficiency — the world's best outcomes from fewer physicians and nurses per 1,000 than any other rich nation and only two hospital beds per 1,000 — and why the same inputs-against-outcomes reading marks the United States inefficient.
learning_objectives.3.5: Explain why the chapter treats hospital beds per 1,000 people as a summary measure of a system's total physical capital rather than a count of beds: each bed arrives bundled with equipment, rooms, buildings, surgical suites, utilities and maintenance, so a low bed count signals modest physical inputs across the board.
learning_objectives.3.6: Explain why the chapter's diagnosis — that America's performance comes down to institutions and incentives, the incentives that produce efficiency rather than the naive answer of efficiency itself — is also its ground for hope: institutions and incentives, unlike genes, diets, geography or population size, are transferable between countries.

Chapter 3 → World-Class Outcomes.text: Three outcome measures — how long people live, how many infants die, how many mothers die — are set against what each country spends, with the wealthy-nation average as a yardstick. One very poor country reaches sixty-three years on almost nothing; America pays vastly more for eighty. Weighing only those two, the chapter argues, frames a choice that was never the sole option, since it overlooks the places reaching the longest lives for less than America already pays.

Chapter 3 → Addressing the Real Question.text: The better questions ask what the longevity leaders spend, and whether a country might live longer while paying less. Across every nation Singapore sits third, trailing two microstates whose gambling and offshore-banking wealth makes them peculiar. Dropping countries below a million residents removes those two and leaves Singapore second, a matter of weeks behind Japan, on a health budget that no wealthy nation undercuts — which is what makes it the leader in value for money.

Chapter 3 → Consistent Excellence.text: Among nations above a million residents Singapore places second, second and fourth on the three measures, and is alone in reaching the leading five on every one — holding that overall lead year upon year even when it heads no single category. A separate ranking built on twenty-one metrics agreed, while placing a nearby prosperous former colony far below. How is this done so cheaply? Not by efficiency itself, the chapter answers, but by what produces it.

Chapter 3 → How It Happens.text: Efficiency means drawing much output from little input. Singapore employs fewer doctors, and fewer nurses and midwives, for every thousand residents than any other wealthy country, and keeps two hospital beds per thousand. Beds gauge all physical capital, because each arrives with monitors, supplies, rooms, buildings and upkeep. America uses more of all three inputs and ranks far lower on results. Iceland, neither Asian nor large, also outperforms America, and the tiniest states are not the cheapest.

Chapter 3 → Let's Be Better.text: Stereotypes about ethnicity or culture, and appeals to a country's territory or headcount, cannot account for results and costs as poor as America's. What remains, on the chapter's account, is how healthcare institutions are arranged and what they reward. This is offered as grounds for optimism rather than despair: such arrangements travel between countries far more readily than diets, inherited traits or a convenient size, so the chapter holds that what Singapore built could be built elsewhere.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does it exclude countries with populations under one million before ranking healthcare outcomes?
options: To leave out very poor countries such as Haiti and India, whose tiny health budgets would distort the cost comparison
To drop tax-haven microstates such as Monaco and Macau, whose economies and demographics are peculiar
To remove small countries whose size gives them lower healthcare costs than Singapore can reach with 5.4 million people
To restrict the comparison to the thirty-four OECD member nations, most of which are high-income like Singapore

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does Singapore's per-person healthcare spending compare with that of other developed nations?
options: It spends more per person than Japan but far less than the United States
It spends about the same per person as the average OECD nation
It spends roughly what Canada and the United Kingdom spend per person
It spends less per person than any other developed nation

items.stem: The chapter concedes that Japan edges Singapore on both life expectancy and infant mortality. On the chapter's criterion, why does Singapore rather than Japan still earn its title of the world's best healthcare system?
options: Singapore spends less per person than Japan, which the chapter treats as the tiebreaker between two near-equal systems
Singapore is the only nation in the top five on all three measures, and it holds that overall lead year after year
Singapore trails Japan in life expectancy by only about five weeks, a gap the chapter treats as too small to matter
Singapore tops each of the three measures every year, whereas Japan leads on some of them only in certain years

items.stem: The chapter anticipates an objection: three outcome indicators are too few to justify calling any nation's healthcare system the world's best. According to the chapter, what answers that objection?
options: Singapore repeats its top-five showing on the three indicators year after year
A separate Bloomberg ranking that used twenty-one health metrics also put Singapore first
The three indicators come from authoritative sources, the CIA World Factbook and the OECD
Singapore reaches those outcomes while spending less per person than any other developed nation

items.stem: According to the chapter's walk through the life-expectancy rankings, dropping nations of fewer than one million people leaves Singapore in first place.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is wrong with a policy-maker asking whether the United States' roughly seventeen extra years of life expectancy over Haiti are worth its vastly larger lifetime healthcare bill?
options: It uses life expectancy alone, when the chapter treats infant and maternal mortality as the measures that decide the case
It compares lifetime totals, when the chapter says only annual per-person spending can be compared fairly
It rests on Haitian figures the chapter regards as too unreliable to support any cost-benefit conclusion
It poses a false dichotomy: spend too much for mediocre results, or too little on the way to an early grave

items.stem: According to the chapter, the lesson of comparing the United States with Haiti is presumably that seventeen extra years of life expectancy are worth the far larger American lifetime healthcare bill.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, Japan and Singapore each spend less than half of what the United States spends per person on healthcare, roughly $4,400 and $3,700 against about $9,500, and their people live about five years longer. What does the chapter say these figures establish about the US-versus-Haiti cost-benefit question?
options: That its two alternatives were never the only ones: a country can outlive the US while spending far less
That the right target is a spending level midway between the United States and Haiti, with outcomes to match
That Haiti's low spending, rather than American overspending, is the real anomaly the framing conceals
That spending and outcomes are essentially unrelated, so the cost-benefit question has no answer at all

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do the questions it says a policy-maker should ask in place of the US-versus-Haiti comparison turn specifically to Japan and Singapore?
options: They are the two developed nations that spend the least on healthcare, so their figures show the lowest level of spending on offer
They are the two systems most often presented as models for American health reform, so their costs are already on the table
They lead the world on the very outcome the question was pricing, so their spending shows what the best result costs
Their spending falls closest to the midpoint between American and Haitian levels, making them the fairest test of the trade-off

items.stem: A university is choosing between two advising models. Professional advisers cost about $1,900 per student a year and are associated with 82 percent second-year retention; faculty-only advising costs about $300 and is associated with 64 percent. The provost frames it as a purchase: is eighteen points of retention worth $1,600 per student? Peer records are on the table. Aldercroft, widely admired as the gold standard, reaches 86 percent at about $2,600. Corwin reaches 83 percent at about $1,150. Dunmore spends about $150 and retains 58 percent. A consultant urges the Brennan State approach, 73 percent at about $1,100, as the balanced path between the two extremes, and most of the committee is leaning that way. Which institution's record, if accurate, exposes the provost's question as a false dichotomy?
options: Brennan State
Dunmore
Corwin
Aldercroft

items.stem: A grocery chain's board is choosing a carrier for its inbound produce lane. Meridian Freight delivers 97 percent of loads on time at $2,400 a load; Lowline Haulage delivers 81 percent on time at $1,300. The finance director puts it as a purchase: is sixteen points of on-time delivery worth $1,100 a load? The operations director calls that a false choice and produces Crossway Carriers, 88 percent on time at $1,780 a load, as proof that a middle way exists and the board was never limited to two options. What does Crossway's record establish about the trade-off the finance director priced?
options: It leaves the trade-off intact
It shows the premium is overpriced
It shows the trade-off was never real
It shows the premium is worth its price

items.stem: A city council is weighing two proposals for its water utility. A new treatment plant would cost households about $260 a year more than today and is projected to cut boil-water advisories from eleven per decade to two; continuing to patch the old plant would cost about $50 more and leave the count near eleven. The finance committee puts it as a purchase: is nine fewer advisories per decade worth $210 per household per year? A neighboring town, often cited as running the leanest utility in the county, charges about $40 less per household than the city does today. One council member replies that the committee's question misses the real action. Which figure would she ask for first?
options: The cost per avoided advisory under each of the two proposals
What the utilities with the fewest advisories charge households
The advisory count at the neighboring town's lean utility
The advisory count a budget midway between the proposals would buy

items.stem: According to the chapter, Hong Kong ranks seventeenth on Bloomberg's twenty-one-metric list of the world's healthiest countries. What does the chapter say that rank rules out as the explanation for Singapore's excellence?
options: Having healthcare institutions and incentives that push its providers and patients toward efficiency
Being one of the tiny, wealthy tax-haven microstates that the chapter drops from its rankings
Being a prosperous, geographically small, formerly British society that eats a mostly Asian diet
Spending less per person on healthcare than any other developed nation in the comparison

items.stem: According to the chapter, Iceland's strong outcomes at modest spending tend to support the idea that Singapore's success is at least partly a matter of being a small country.
options: True
False

items.stem: On the chapter's method, what makes Hong Kong's showing on Bloomberg's twenty-one-metric ranking the telling case against the explanation that Singapore's results come from being a prosperous, geographically small, formerly British society with a mostly Asian diet?
options: It has none of those traits, yet performs well enough to show that a country can reach the top of Bloomberg's list without any of them
It is one of the larger, white-majority, Western-diet countries that the chapter uses to show that an Asian diet is not required at the top
It ranks second behind Singapore on Bloomberg's list, exactly where the chapter says a country with those traits would land if they mattered

items.stem: On the chapter's method, why does Iceland's performance count against the explanation that Singapore's results come from Asian genes or an Asian diet?
options: Iceland is a small country that performs well, which confirms that small size rather than diet is Singapore's real advantage
Iceland has neither trait yet performs well at far lower spending than the United States, so its success must lie elsewhere
Iceland spends less per person than Singapore, which shows that low spending rather than diet is what produces good outcomes

items.stem: Ashby's schools post the best reading scores in their county, and the Ashby board credits the thirty-minute silent-reading period that every one of its schools runs each day. A researcher lines up four other districts. Bramble runs the same daily period, and its scores are a close second to Ashby's. Cutler runs the same daily period, and its scores sit in the middle of the county. Dorset has no such period, and its scores rival Ashby's. Elton has no such period, and its scores are near the bottom. Which district plays the part that Hong Kong plays in the chapter's argument?

Cutler
Dorset
Bramble

items.stem: Meridian Freight moves containers at the lowest cost per box of any carrier in its port, and rival carriers put that down to Meridian running a single class of ship. A consultant pulls the records of four other carriers. Osprey Shipping also runs a single class of ship; it has the port's worst on-time record, and its cost per box is nearly as low as Meridian's. Pelican Marine also runs a single class of ship; it has the port's best on-time record, and its cost per box is among the highest. Heron Carriers runs a mixed fleet; its on-time record is poor, and its cost per box is among the highest. Kestrel Lines runs a mixed fleet; both its on-time record and its cost per box sit mid-pack. On the chapter's method, which carrier's record settles what the rivals' claim is worth?

Osprey Shipping
Pelican Marine
Heron Carriers

items.stem: Harbor City has won its regional league in six of the last eight seasons. Rival supporters say it buys titles with one of the league's three biggest payrolls; the club's chairman credits its new stadium, its coach hired from abroad and the youth academy the club runs. A journalist pulls the records of four other clubs. Redfern: a top-three payroll, a new stadium, a home-grown coach, an academy of its own; usually finishes second. Sablewood: a top-three payroll, an old ground, a coach from abroad, no academy; finishes mid-table. Tarrow: a modest payroll, a new stadium, a coach from abroad, no academy; finishes near the bottom. items.stem: According to the chapter, what does it mean to call a healthcare system efficient?
options: It gives doctors and hospitals the right incentives
It produces a lot of output from only a little input
It spends less on healthcare than most other rich nations

options: Because those modest inputs are producing the world's best health outcomes, so Singapore is getting more from less
Because Singapore's staffing is also lower than America's on both counts, and the United States is the chapter's real target

Why does the chapter read these figures as showing that the United States is inefficient?
options: Because the United States already spends more per person than any other nation, so any added input must be waste
Because the largest American excess is in hospital beds, the one column the chapter reads as a measure of physical capital
Because it uses more of every input than Singapore and still ranks far below Singapore on all three outcomes

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's low input figures in Table 3.2 (its physicians, nurses and midwives, and hospital beds per 1,000 people) would establish its efficiency on their own, regardless of how its outcomes compared with those of other nations.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, the number of hospital beds per 1,000 people is presented as a summary measure of which kind of healthcare input?
options: Physical inputs, such as wards, surgical suites, and equipment
Financial inputs, such as per-person healthcare spending
Human inputs, such as physicians, nurses, and midwives
Health outputs, such as life expectancy and infant and maternal mortality

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, a system's hospital-bed count tells you about the physical capital it must pay to maintain, utility bills and maintenance costs included, and not only about the beds themselves.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does a low number of hospital beds per 1,000 people indicate that a healthcare system uses modest physical inputs across the board, rather than merely that it owns few beds?
options: Because beds are not bought in isolation: each comes with its own equipment, and more beds mean more rooms, bigger hospitals, larger surgical suites, and higher upkeep
Because international statistics report physical capital only through bed counts, so no other measure of a system's equipment, buildings, and upkeep is available for comparison
Because a bed cannot be used without staff assigned to it, so the bed count also captures the physicians, nurses, and midwives that a healthcare system employs
Because beds are the single costliest item a hospital purchases, so their count dominates the total value of the physical capital a healthcare system holds

items.stem: The chapter reports that Singapore uses 2.0 hospital beds per 1,000 people while the United States uses 2.8, about 40 percent more. According to the chapter, what does Singapore's lower figure show?
options: That Singapore's hospitals run much closer to full occupancy, so each of its beds serves more patients in a year than a bed in an American hospital does
That Singapore achieves its outcomes with a smaller overall stock of physical capital, such as equipment, buildings, and surgical suites, not merely with fewer beds
That Singapore achieves its outcomes with fewer physicians, nurses, and midwives per person, since staffing levels rise and fall with the number of beds a hospital keeps in use
That Singapore spends less per person on healthcare than any other developed nation, since fewer beds translate directly into a smaller national healthcare bill each year

items.stem: True or false: Since a hospital bed is useless without someone to staff it, the chapter arguably reads a low bed count as evidence of low human inputs, meaning few physicians, nurses, and midwives, as well as low physical inputs.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, when it asks how Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare while spending so much less than other countries, what does it give as the 'correct answer' in place of the 'naive answer'?
options: A small population eating a mostly Asian diet
Incentives that lead to efficiency
Efficiency in turning inputs into outputs
Fewer physicians and hospital beds per person

items.stem: The chapter's closing section suggests that Singapore's healthcare advantage rests largely on features of its geography and population that other countries could not expect to copy.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter says the 'naive answer' to how Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare while spending so much less is efficiency, and then gives a different 'correct answer.' On the chapter's argument, what is wrong with the naive answer?
options: It overstates how few physicians, nurses and hospital beds Singapore uses
It attributes Singapore's results to a trait the chapter has already ruled out
It credits Singapore's spending level rather than its outcomes for the ranking
It names the result that needs explaining rather than what produces it

items.stem: The chapter's closing section says its diagnosis of America's poor performance gives hope to all other countries. On the chapter's argument, why do its earlier eliminations - Asian genes and diet, small geographic size, small population, and being a prosperous former British colony - matter for that hope?
options: They prove the United States outspends every other nation, so there is ample room for it to cut
They show Singapore's lead is consistent year after year, which is what earns it the top ranking
They remove every explanation another country could not readily adopt, leaving one that it could
They demonstrate that Singapore's efficiency comes from fewer inputs, which any country could copy

items.stem: Four students summarize the chapter's account of why Singapore gets the world's best outcomes at the lowest cost of any developed nation. Which summary orders the explanation the way the chapter does?
options: Modest inputs are the incentive, and using fewer physicians and beds is what produces the top outcomes
Efficiency leads to the right incentives, and those incentives are what keep spending below other rich nations'
Low spending forces efficiency, and efficiency in turn is what the chapter means by good institutions
Institutions and incentives lead to efficiency, and efficiency delivers top outcomes from modest inputs

bank_meta.status: UNVETTED — assembled by tools/bank_pipeline.py. Chapter 4 re-presents chapter 3's verdict as figures and adds two new moves: the benchmark-choice argument and the Poland correction. Within this chapter Singapore's quality standing is ASSERTED rather than argued, so items ground only in this chapter's attributed claims and never import chapter 3's tables. TWO ANCHOR ZONES because the chapter carries exactly one subsection heading; its unheaded opening two thirds collapses to a chapter-level anchor. Both figures are images and students never see them, so no item keys a value visible only in a chart -- every load-bearing figure is restated in prose. THREE NEW SOURCE INCONSISTENCIES, all never-key. The prose introduces Figure 4.1 as 2012 data for thirty-four countries while its caption says 2015 and thirty-two, and every later number is 2015. 'We spend 75 percent more per person than Singapore' is the book's FOURTH incompatible version of that ratio and is refuted by this chapter's own per-person figures, which give about 160 percent more; the standing rule hardens to never key any US-to-Singapore spending multiple anywhere in this book. And the claim that Singapore spends less per person than any other rich nation is contradicted in the same paragraph, which names Poland as spending less out of the same high-income set -- so only the share-of-GDP form is safe, and 'Singapore comes in last' must never be juxtaposed with the per-person table, where it does not. Instructor review required before release. TIER-3 PANEL RUN 2026-09-30 and BOTH application LOs are CONFIRMED, which the forecast did not expect. LO 4.4 was forecast to collapse at 0 to 1 survivors of 3 because 'emulate the winner' is guessable from any advocacy framing; fly-c4-016 did collapse unanimously and is demoted here, but 4.4 holds at the floor with two survivors. LO 4.5 survives 3 of 3 CLEAN, its best-in-chapter forecast of about 0.65 again erring low. That is the eighth consecutive pessimistic forecast in this project. fly-c4-017 and fly-c4-018 each carry one dissent of three and so hold on a minority verdict with no margin; if a later edit disturbs either, re-run the panel rather than assuming the tier holds. KNOWN WARNING, and it is a false positive in the shared validator rather than a defect in the item: validate_bank.py reports fly-c4-016's key as the lone longest at 9 characters against 8, which is a one-character difference between BARE LABELS where length is an accident of spelling. Guide 3a is the applicable rule there and it puts parity in the stem's description of each case, which no character count can measure. Reported to the dev lane; not silenced here.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.4.1: Identify the standings the chapter reports for healthcare spending as a share of national income among the high-income OECD nations plus Singapore: the United States first and far above second-place Switzerland; the countries usually mooted as US models -- France, Sweden, Canada and the United Kingdom -- clustered well below the United States; and Singapore last, spending substantially less than even the next most frugal country, Luxembourg.
learning_objectives.4.2: Explain why the chapter tells Americans they should want to come in last rather than first on this table: the ranking measures healthcare value for money, so the top spot marks the least efficient system and the bottom spot marks the best, which is why a margin over the neighbouring country compounds the embarrassment at one end and the achievement at the other.
learning_objectives.4.3: Explain how the chapter's Health Spending Sprint analogy works and what it is built to do: Singapore's spending share is set equal to a world-record hundred-metre time and every other country's time slows in proportion to its spending, which converts percentage-point differences a reader might shrug at into a margin the reader can feel.
learning_objectives.4.4: Apply the chapter's benchmark-choice argument -- that the experts' usual models for US reform, Canada and the United Kingdom, are mid-pack finishers in the very race they are asked to coach, so a country that wants to learn to run should emulate the one that finishes first -- to a novel case, determining which candidate plays the part Canada and the United Kingdom play in the chapter's telling.
learning_objectives.4.5: Apply the chapter's distinction between spending the least and affording effective medicine cheaply, determining which of several described systems pursues the goal the chapter attributes to Singapore -- retaining modern medicine's expensive but effective treatments while spending far less than other rich nations -- rather than the outright-minimum position the chapter assigns to Poland.

Chapter 4 → America's Healthcare Humilia.text: Plotted as a share of national income, American health spending stands highest of the wealthy nations and Singapore's lowest, with the countries usually proposed as models sitting between them. Because the measure is value for money, the chapter argues the top of this table is the worst place to be. Rendering the gap as sprint times rather than percentage points is meant to make a difference a reader might shrug at feel like a rout.

Chapter 4 → It's Time to Catch Up.text: Reform advocates, the chapter says, point to mid-ranking countries as models when they should point to the leader. Per person, American spending exceeds every other wealthy nation's, though Singapore is not the thriftiest of all — one poorer member spends less. That matters to the argument: the goal attributed to Singapore was never to spend the least, which would mean giving up costly but effective treatment, but to afford such treatment cheaply.

According to the chapter, what does coming in last on that figure mean?
options: Reporting the worst health outcomes of all the countries shown, since the figure orders the nations from healthiest down to sickest
Dropping out of the comparison entirely, since only members of the OECD can appear anywhere on the figure
Devoting the smallest share of national income to healthcare, the position the chapter crowns 'the true winner of this race'
Spending so little that a nation must give up the expensive but effective treatments modern medicine now provides

items.stem: Beyond the bare order of finish, the chapter dwells on two gaps in its figure of healthcare spending as a share of national income: the United States comes in 'way higher' than even second-place Switzerland, while Singapore spends 'substantially less' than even the next most frugal country, Luxembourg. According to the chapter, what do these margins over the neighbouring country add to the story?
options: They forecast the standings: a country far clear of its nearest neighbour is still pulling away, so each gap shows where the table is heading in the years ahead
They nominate the runners-up as models: Switzerland and Luxembourg each sit nearest to an extreme of the table, close enough to study without actually occupying it
They vouch for the data: countries separated by gaps that wide could not have swapped places through measurement error, so the standings themselves can be trusted
They amplify each verdict: with the podium read upside down, distance from the runner-up deepens the disgrace at one end and enlarges the achievement at the other

items.stem: Flynn calls it 'an utter embarrassment that the United States is first in healthcare spending' on his figure of spending as a share of national income. According to the chapter, why does first place on this figure call for embarrassment rather than pride?

The countries most often mooted as models for American reform all finish well below the United States, which shows that the top spot could have been avoided
First place means healthcare is crowding out everything else: the chapter's complaint is the schools, roads and other goods a nation must forgo to fund its outsized share
The figure ranks what healthcare takes from each nation's income, so its top spot marks the least efficient system, the worst bang for the buck in the chapter's phrase

Brixhaven sits mid-table, and harbor-association guides have held it up for twenty years as the port to study. Ostrava, a small utility under an unfamiliar charter, posts the survey's best quality marks while charging less than any other utility with top marks. items.stem: Four companies tour musicals on the same national circuit. Starlight Runs carries no orchestra, replacing every score with polished recorded tracks, books bare venues with inventive staging, and spends the least of any company on the circuit. Grand Pavilion carries a full pit orchestra on every date, books landmark venues with lavish staging, and spends the most of any company on the circuit. Harbor Light carries a half-size ensemble on its larger dates only, books mid-range venues with standard staging, and spends close to the average for the circuit. Grand Pavilion

items.stem: Four grain cooperatives farm the same valley. County extension reports credit modern self-propelled combines, the costliest equipment a co-op can own, with saving more of a harvest from storm loss than any other purchase. Cedar Bend brings in its grain with late-model combines kept running season after season, shares crews among member farms, and its outlays rank far below most co-ops in the valley. Willow Creek brings in its grain with refurbished pull-behind rigs and extra field crews, reports yields it says match anyone's, and its outlays rank the lowest of any co-op in the valley. Iron Ridge brings in its grain with factory-new combines traded in each season and fitted with every option, and its outlays rank the highest of any co-op in the valley. Dry Fork brings in its grain with one aging combine backed by rented equipment in the peak weeks, and its outlays rank near the middle of co-ops in the valley. items.stem: A regional airline is founding a pilot-training academy and is weighing four build-out plans. The Voss plan equips desktop trainers and projection screens in place of simulators, houses classes in a renovated terminal wing, and would put the academy's budget under every comparable school. learning_objectives.5.1: Identify the gains the chapter claims the United States would realize by matching Singapore's results: the benefits it says you cannot place a dollar value on -- about five more years of average lifetime longevity, infant deaths cut by more than half, maternal deaths cut by roughly four-fifths -- and the one benefit it prices, annual healthcare savings it sizes at about $2.4 trillion, or 13.6 percent of GDP.
learning_objectives.5.2: Explain how the chapter computes its headline savings figure: hold US GDP fixed, ask what the United States would spend if healthcare took only Singapore's share of GDP (4.2 percent) instead of its own (17.8 percent), and subtract that counterfactual spending from actual spending -- so the claim is about matching Singapore's spending RATE, not copying its dollar outlays.
learning_objectives.5.3: Explain what the chapter's stack of size comparisons -- more than four times the defense budget, enough to balance the federal deficit many times over, bigger than the GDP of all but six nations, enough to run 139 smaller countries at once, and a share of GDP beside which defense, Social Security and the deficit are each dwarfed -- is meant to establish: that the money at stake exceeds the scale of every budget item and budget fight Americans usually treat as large.
learning_objectives.5.4: Explain why the chapter surveys conservative and progressive spending priorities before Flynn states his own preference: the stakes claim is built to stand no matter the reader's political persuasion, and he makes the separability explicit, so the argument that the savings are worth pursuing does not depend on accepting his answer to who should keep them.
learning_objectives.5.5: Apply the chapter's account of how the savings would reach workers without any mandate -- competitive labour markets shifting the freed-up share of total compensation from employer insurance premiums into take-home pay, and incentivised health-savings-account contributions accumulating as the worker's own property -- to a novel case, determining whether a described arrangement would actually land the savings with workers.

Chapter 5 → What We Could Do If We Copie.text: Matching Singapore's results would buy gains the chapter declines to price — years of life, fewer infant and maternal deaths — and one it does price: hold national income fixed, spend only Singapore's share of it, and the difference is an annual saving larger than the defence budget or the deficit. The case is built to survive disagreement about who keeps the money, which the author would hand to workers through competitive pay and accounts they own.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.6.1: Identify the three parties in the chapter's framework and the payment flow that defines third-party payment: the patient as first party, the provider as second, and the payer -- Medicare, Medicaid or private insurance, involved in neither providing nor receiving care -- as third, with payments flowing from third parties to second parties for services delivered to first parties, rather than directly from consumer to producer as when hiring a lawyer or a mechanic.
learning_objectives.6.2: Explain how, on the chapter's account, the route a payment takes determines whether a provider must care about the customer: in a two-party market first parties spending their own money take their business elsewhere, so competition forces a retailer to deliver value rather than poor service at inflated prices, and routing healthcare payment through third parties removes exactly that pressure.
learning_objectives.6.3: Explain how the chapter's motorised-wheelchair example shows that free to individuals does not mean free to society: because a third party -- the taxpayer -- foots the bill, the user gets the benefits while bearing none of the costs, so costs and benefits become isolated from one another and people acquire more equipment than anyone facing the true cost would.
learning_objectives.6.4: Explain why the chapter calls physicians pushovers on requests like wheelchairs and antibiotics: approval costs the doctor nothing while denial is time-consuming under patient-volume pressure and risks losing the patient, complaints, or a malpractice suit -- an asymmetry whose large-scale form is defensive medicine, with unnecessary imaging, blood panels, biopsies and prescriptions whose costs are dumped onto third parties.
learning_objectives.6.5: Apply the chapter's analysis of share-of-volume compensation to a novel case, predicting whether an intermediary paid a roughly fixed share of the spending it processes will police that spending or grow it -- the reasoning by which the chapter rejects as short-term thinking the obvious expectation that insurers profit by denying claims.
learning_objectives.6.6: Explain why, on the chapter's account, government insurers cannot control costs even without a profit motive: as legal entitlements they must lean in favour of paying claims, and their one lever -- cutting reimbursement rates -- is offset by providers who respond by billing a larger number of procedures, or a different set, extracting as much as before.
learning_objectives.6.7: Given a novel payment arrangement, determine which party is positioned to restrain wasteful spending, by locating where the incentive to economise and the information to judge necessity coincide, as against the party that merely holds payment authority -- the chapter's diagnosis being a system that entrusts payment decisions to those with the least information while the two informed parties have no incentive to restrain.

Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare Sys.text: The chapter blames the route money travels. Patient, provider and payer are numbered first, second and third; in healthcare the payment runs from the third to the second for something the first received. Where a buyer pays directly, a seller who offers poor value loses that buyer, and competition disciplines it. Insert a payer who neither receives nor provides the service and that discipline disappears, which the chapter says is the road American healthcare took.

Chapter 6 → The False Promise of \"Free\.text: Advertising for subsidised medical equipment leads with what it costs the user rather than with what it does, because almost nothing is as persuasive as nothing. The claim is accurate and the conclusion still wrong: costless to the person is not costless to everyone, since a payer absorbs the difference, and here that payer is the public. What looks like a gift is a transfer whose price nobody at the counter sees.

Chapter 6 → First-Party Incentives.text: Take the price away from the person choosing and you take away the comparison. Someone weighing a purchase against a short remaining need would decline it at full price and accept it at none, so the equipment is ordered and the public billed. The chapter's point is not extravagance but severance: benefits accrue to the chooser while costs land elsewhere, and once the two are detached there is nothing left to weigh.

Chapter 6 → Second- and Third-Party Ince.text: Saying yes costs a clinician nothing; saying no costs time, goodwill, possibly the patient, possibly a lawsuit. That asymmetry, the chapter argues, produces agreement rather than scrutiny, and at scale becomes tests and prescriptions ordered to be safe. Nor will the payers restrain it: one earns a share of whatever volume it handles, so shrinking the volume shrinks the earnings, and the other is an entitlement that must lean toward paying.

Chapter 6 → Who's in the Know?.text: Authority and knowledge sit in different places. The patient and the clinician know the case; the distant payer decides. Cutting what it pays per procedure does not help, because providers answer a lower rate with more procedures or different ones. So judgement rests with the party least able to judge, while the two who could judge have no reason to economise, and the waste survives everyone's good intentions.

That a buyer facing the full price and knowing their own situation would decline a purchase that sails through when a third party pays
That advertising the equipment as free is deceptive, since the machines are in fact billed to Medicare at their full price
That Medicare ought to prorate what it pays to the period of actual use rather than reimbursing the full purchase price of the equipment

items.stem: According to the chapter, doctors are incentivized to be 'pushovers' when patients request items such as motorized wheelchairs. Which of the following states a reason the chapter gives?
options: Doctors genuinely believe that nearly every patient who asks for such a device has a lasting medical need for it.
Verifying that a patient truly needs the device takes time the doctor does not have, while approving the request takes none.
Doctors earn a commission from the device maker on each motorized wheelchair they prescribe, so approvals raise their income.
Insurers direct doctors to approve such requests because processing a denial creates more paperwork than paying the claim.

items.stem: The chapter supposes, for the sake of argument, that a detailed mobility exam could be done quickly and at low cost - and argues that a doctor would still lean toward approving a wheelchair request. According to the chapter, why?
options: Hospital administrators push doctors to keep approval rates high so that the facility's overall billing volume keeps growing.
A refused patient will probably seek approval from another doctor, and the refusing physician may lose that patient for good.
State regulators can sanction a physician whose denial is later judged to have blocked medically necessary equipment.
Medicare rules treat mobility devices as entitlements, leaving the physician no legal authority to refuse a qualifying request.

items.stem: According to the chapter, physicians go along with patients' demands for antibiotics to treat colds because acquiescing is easier than dealing with complaints to hospital administrators or the threat of baseless but costly malpractice lawsuits.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter calls a physician's decision to practice defensive medicine - ordering extra imaging, blood panels, biopsies, and prescriptions - 'understandable.' According to the chapter, what calculation makes it understandable?
options: Extra tests raise a practice's billing revenue, and under fee-for-service payment more procedures mean more physician income.
Upsetting a patient could cost the physician dearly, while the whole cost of the useless care is passed along to a third party.
Medical training drills physicians to exhaust every diagnostic avenue, so ordering everything reflects professional thoroughness.
The extra tests sometimes catch dangerous conditions early, so their medical benefit outweighs the annoyance and expense involved.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how do private health insurance companies actually make their profit?
options: Fees collected from providers for handling their billing paperwork
About five percent of the gross medical billing they process
Investment earnings on premiums held until claims come due
Whatever remains of the premiums after the year's claims are paid

items.stem: According to the chapter, what do private insurers mostly rely on for larger profits year after year?
options: Drawing customers away from rival insurers
Cutting what they spend on their own operations
Raising premiums year after year
Denying a larger share of claims each year

items.stem: According to the chapter, why is it short-term thinking to expect private insurers to boost their profits by ruthlessly denying claims?
options: Because they lack the information to tell valid claims from invalid ones
Because larger profits require the billing they handle to keep growing
Because regulators oblige them to pay every claim that is medically valid
Because denied patients would defect to rival insurers that approve more freely

items.stem: According to the chapter, a private insurer's surest route to larger profits is presumably to deny as many claims as it can.
options: True
False

items.stem: A manufacturing group hands all of its employee travel to Traverline, an outside firm that books every flight and hotel and reviews each trip against the group's travel rules. Traverline is paid a small fixed share of every travel dollar it books. The board brought Traverline in after shareholders complained loudly about travel waste, its contract renews each year unless the board ends it, and each autumn Traverline proposes the size of the coming year's travel programme for the board to approve. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the board expect Traverline to do over the next several years?
options: Propose bigger programmes each autumn
Cut travel until the waste is gone
Refuse every doubtful trip request
Keep the programme at its present size

items.stem: The city of Ardenmoor repairs its streets and bridges from a fund whose annual size is fixed for the next ten years by the covenants of a bond issue, which no official can amend. Contractors bill the fund as repairs arise; in some years their invoices fall short of its limit and in others press against it. Kelbrook Associates reviews the invoices and pays the approved ones, earning a small fixed share of every dollar it pays out, and it won the contract on its record of rooting padded invoices out of client accounts. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the city expect Kelbrook to do?
options: Pay almost every invoice it gets
Slow payments to make the fund last
Strip the padding from the invoices
Push the fund's size up over time

items.stem: When the farm-equipment maker Drummond wound up its extended-service plans, the regulator required it to leave behind an escrowed fund to cover the plans' remaining claims, with anything unspent at closure returning to Drummond. Hartley Clearing, an outside firm appointed by the regulator, processes those final claims and is paid a small fixed share of every dollar it pays out of the fund. Once the last claim closes, the programme ends for good and Hartley's appointment ends with it; no claimant will ever deal with Hartley again. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should be expected of Hartley?
options: Pay out most of what remains
Deny most of what remains
Settle each claim for less than billed
Approve small claims, fight large ones

items.stem: According to the chapter, why must government insurers such as Medicaid and Medicare 'always lean in favor of paying claims'?
options: Because their benefits are entitlements established in law
Because they can grow only by approving ever more claims
Because they employ no adjustors or investigators of claims
Because they earn a profit on the billing volume they process

items.stem: The chapter says Medicaid and Medicare try to keep a lid on costs by repeatedly cutting their reimbursement rates for specific procedures — yet it argues this tool cannot hold spending down. Why not, on its account?
options: Patients respond to the lower rates by seeking more visits, since their share of the bill shrinks
The cut lowers the price per procedure, while providers choose the number and mix billed
Congress soon restores the old rates once providers and patient groups lobby against the cuts
The cuts reach so few procedures that most of what providers bill stays at the old rates

items.stem: Flynn argues that Medicare and Medicaid are worse positioned than private insurers to say no to wasteful claims: they lack even the short-term profit motive to deny them, and as legal entitlements they must lean in favor of paying.
options: True
False

items.stem: In its discussion of reimbursement-rate cuts, the chapter remarks that 'second parties are not potted plants.' What point is the remark making?
options: Providers outnumber the field investigators that insurers can afford to send out
Providers, unlike distant insurers, see each patient's actual condition firsthand
Providers adjust what and how much they bill when their payment terms change
Providers abandon any payer whose rates stop covering the costs of their practice

items.stem: According to the chapter, who has the most information about a patient's actual condition, and where does the ultimate authority for payment approval and cost control sit?
options: The claims adjustors in the field have the most information, while approval authority sits with the treating physician
The hospital billing departments have the most information, while approval authority sits with the patient and the doctor jointly
The patient and the doctor have the most information, while approval authority sits with insurers and government payers
The government payers have the most information, while approval authority sits with the patient selecting among competing providers

items.stem: According to the chapter, even with claims adjustors in the field and lawsuits against those caught in fraud, the more than $2 trillion in claims handled each year leaves Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers unable to discover whether most of the claims they pay are medically valid.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter's 'Who's in the Know?' discussion grants that third parties hold the ultimate authority to approve payments and control costs. Why, on its account, is that authority not enough to stop wasteful claims?
options: Operating under entitlement law, they are barred from refusing any claim that a licensed physician has signed, whatever their investigators find
Operating far from the patient, they cannot affordably gather the facts that separate needed care from waste, so they largely pay on trust
Handling too few claims to see patterns across providers, they cannot tell which second parties are systematically inflating their bills
Collecting a share of every claim they approve, they would see each denial they issue come straight out of their own annual revenue

items.stem: According to the chapter, the patient and the doctor are the two people with the most information about whether a treatment is really needed. Why does it conclude that neither of them will act as a brake on spending?
options: Because the payer's reviewers see thousands of similar cases a year, both defer to its judgment about what a condition requires
Because legal restrictions on patients' medical information keep both of them from passing what they know to the payer
Because neither can predict what the insurer will finally reimburse, both order generously while the approval window stays open
Because the bill lands on neither of them, the knowledge to judge necessity sits with parties who gain nothing by refusing

items.stem: Kestrel Parcel runs its delivery vans under the following arrangement. The drivers note what is wrong with the vans they take out each morning, and repair charges never touch their pay. Ostrander Garage determines what work each van that reaches it needs, and it invoices Kestrel's account for every job performed. Halloway Fleet Services approves or rejects every repair invoice from its office two states away, and it draws one flat yearly fee. The depot manager picks which vans go in as she works the yard, and repair charges come out of her fixed budget. Lately, invoices have been arriving for brake overhauls on vans barely a year old. Applying the chapter's analysis of payment arrangements, which party is positioned to restrain wasteful repair spending?
options: The depot manager
Ostrander Garage
Halloway Fleet Services
The drivers

items.stem: A private foundation is funding a three-year study at Ellsworth College under the following terms. The bench technicians run and calibrate every instrument daily, and the equipment budget is not theirs to keep or lose. Veridian Instruments advises the lab on what each experiment could use, and it is paid for each machine it places. The foundation's program officer must countersign every purchase before funds release, and she reviews each request against the approved category list from another city. The lab director set the study's methods at the start, and funds left at close-out stay with her lab for its next projects. Midway through, a proposal circulates to order a second imaging unit like the one already installed. On the chapter's analysis of spending restraint, which party can be relied on to turn down equipment the study does not need?
options: The bench technicians
Veridian Instruments
The lab director
The foundation's program officer

items.stem: Hartwell Corporation moves about forty employees a year under the following arrangement. The transferring employees choose services from a set menu before each move, and none of the charges appears on their side of the ledger. Copeland Movers performs the packing and hauling it has listed for each household, and it bills for every service line it enters. Crestline Relocation clears each mover invoice for payment from Hartwell's funds, and its reviewers judge the paperwork from a processing center out of state. Hartwell's finance office has ordered two across-the-board cuts to the moving allowance, and it examines the program's total spending every year. Invoices routinely list full-service packing for lightly furnished apartments, and the program's total has not fallen. On the chapter's diagnosis, which party's position explains why the waste persists?
options: Crestline Relocation
Hartwell's finance office
Copeland Movers
The transferring employees

Chapter 7 argues that the fall in out-of-pocket costs caused the rise in US healthcare spending, and it argues it TWICE by elimination -- once over time (supplier-induced demand, new technology and malpractice costs are all real but did not change enough to explain a change) and once across countries (an MRI costs the same in France; other nations' out-of-pocket rates were continuously low and static, so they cannot explain a divergence). That change-versus-constancy mechanic is the chapter's best Tier-3 substrate and is DELIBERATELY DISTINGUISHED from the confirmed LO 3.3, which turns on presence/absence controls instead. NEVER-KEY: this chapter says only the United States has ever exceeded about 12 percent of GDP, which chapter 4 contradicts by putting Switzerland at 12.1 percent, so the threshold is never keyed and only the argument's shape is tested.
