source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.14.1: Identify what the chapter says the original MediShield was — a low-cost catastrophic plan run by the CPF, covering hospitalization and expensive outpatient treatments (dialysis, chemotherapy, radiation) at public facilities, payable from MediSave — and the fact Flynn stresses as the key point: although participation was purely voluntary from the early 1990s until MediShield Life, the vast majority of residents enrolled, most adding paid supplementary coverage on top.
learning_objectives.14.2: Explain how, on the chapter's account, the S$2,000 annual deductible and the Ministry of Health's posted percentile cost data work together to create a competitive healthcare market — first parties spending their own money weigh cost against benefit and judge "Quality v. Price" themselves, so a provider who gets lazy on either loses the business — and why the chapter says that feedback is mostly absent in America, where third-party payment obscures both price and quality.
learning_objectives.14.3: Apply MediShield's cost-sharing structure — everything out of pocket below the annual deductible, then a copay on every dollar above it, shrinking but never reaching zero — to a novel patient situation, determining what share of the next healthcare dollar the patient bears and the incentive the chapter says this creates.
learning_objectives.14.4: Explain how the chapter argues MediShield's administration keeps a lid on prices and wasteful spending: a non-elected CPF bears the actuarial risk and decides coverage without the special-interest lobbying the chapter says plagues US state insurance regulators, while daily, annual and lifetime claims limits discipline providers' pricing and remind patients that MediShield "is not a bottomless common pool."
learning_objectives.14.5: Given a novel supplemental-insurance market design, determine which of the chapter's three Integrated Shield safeguards it preserves or omits and what the chapter's logic says follows — the MediShield-first rule that stops insurers cherry-picking the healthy out of the common pool, near-standardized coverage that forces competition onto premiums, or the cap on the number of plans against consumer information overload.
learning_objectives.14.6: Explain why the chapter calls MediShield "self-reinforcing and self-perpetuating" — high deductibles and meaningful copays create the competition that lowers prices, low prices allow the low premiums that induce mass participation, and mass participation sustains the competition — so that premiums far below the US average are presented as an outcome of the design itself.
learning_objectives.14.7: Given a proposed change to one link in a self-reinforcing insurance design — for instance reducing cost sharing to make a plan more generous — predict the downstream consequence the chapter's logic implies, tracing it through the chain that runs from cost sharing to competition to prices to premiums to participation rather than from generosity straight to take-up.

Chapter 14 → MediShield and the Right In.text: The insurance leg began as a low-cost plan against catastrophe, administered by the same body that holds the compulsory savings and payable from them. It covered hospital stays and a few costly outpatient courses, at public facilities only. The point the author stresses is take-up: enrolment was voluntary for roughly two decades and the great majority joined anyway, most of them buying additional private cover on top.

Chapter 14 → Coverage That Facilitates C.text: Below an annual deductible the patient pays everything, from saved funds or elsewhere, which gives a reason to weigh cost against benefit and creates a market the patient can walk away from. To make comparison possible the health ministry publishes percentile bill sizes for common procedures, so a quotation can be checked against the national spread. A patient may still choose the dearer surgeon with the better reputation; the point is that providers must attend to price and quality together.

Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Ga.text: Above the deductible the patient still bears a share of every further dollar. That share shrinks as spending rises but never reaches zero, so the calculation never disappears — unlike plans where sharing stops at a ceiling, after which the insurer bears everything and the reason to shop vanishes. Programmes with little sharing remove it from the first dollar. Patients also pay their own premiums from their own balances, so cover is never mistaken for free.

Chapter 14 → Politically Independent Adm.text: The savings body runs the insurance and carries its actuarial risk, setting the deductible and the sharing thresholds. Unelected, it decides coverage without the lobbying the author attributes to American regulators. Limits by day, year and lifetime cap what may be drawn. Supplementary private plans are governed by three rules: the public plan must be held first, which stops insurers selecting the healthy; cover is near-standardised, so competition falls on premium; and plan numbers are capped against overload.

Chapter 14 → Shockingly Low Premiums.text: The chapter closes on cost, arguing the plan would be pointless if it were ruinous. The author sets the average American individual premium beside the published premiums for the public plan and finds the latter a small fraction of it. He presents this as a product of the design rather than a subsidy: real cost-sharing produces competition, competition lowers prices, low prices permit low premiums, and low premiums bring in nearly everyone, which sustains the competition.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what kind of program was the original MediShield?
options: A low-cost catastrophic plan run by the CPF, covering hospitalization and expensive outpatient treatments at public facilities
A mandatory savings account managed by the CPF, set aside for routine medical expenses rather than for insurance coverage
A comprehensive first-dollar plan run by private insurance companies, covering routine checkups and everyday care at any clinic
A supplementary plan sold by private companies, covering upgraded wards and medical treatments at private hospitals and clinics
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → MediShield and the Right Incentives

items.stem: The chapter makes what it calls a key point about participation in the original MediShield program, before it became MediShield Life. What is that point?
options: Participation stayed low for years until the government finally made enrollment compulsory for every resident
Most residents turned the coverage down, preferring to pay for their healthcare out of their own savings
Enrollment was compulsory from the program's start, which is what produced its high participation rate
Even though enrollment was entirely voluntary, the vast majority of residents signed up for the coverage
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → MediShield and the Right Incentives

items.stem: According to the chapter, most of the people enrolled in the original MediShield also chose to pay extra for supplementary coverage, such as Integrated Shield plans, on top of their basic MediShield policy.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → MediShield and the Right Incentives

items.stem: According to the chapter, what cost information does Singapore's Ministry of Health post on the internet so consumers can make informed choices about medical procedures?
options: Quality ratings of individual surgeons compiled from government inspections
The 50th and 90th percentile bill sizes for common hospital procedures
A list of providers disciplined for charging above the national average
A government-approved fee schedule that caps what each provider may charge

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Ministry of Health posts 50th- and 90th-percentile cost data for common procedures. In Flynn's account, how does that posted data help create a competitive healthcare market?
options: It allows the government to identify and penalize providers whose prices run far above the posted percentiles
It replaces the need for out-of-pocket exposure, since informed patients economize even when a third party pays
It steers every patient toward the lowest-priced provider, driving all providers to converge on one price
It lets a patient judge whether a quoted price is competitive, so first parties can take their money elsewhere

items.stem: According to the chapter, why is the competitive feedback of "Quality v. Price" mostly absent in American healthcare?
options: Third-party payment obscures price and quality alike, so providers feel no pressure from the patients they treat
Too few providers compete in most American markets, so patients have no alternative to take their business to
Regulations prevent American providers from advertising their prices, keeping consumers in the dark about costs
American patients lack the expertise to judge clinical quality on their own, no matter who is paying the bill

items.stem: Flynn presents the S$2,000 annual deductible and the Ministry of Health's posted cost data as working together: spending below the deductible comes out of the patient's own pocket, which supplies the motive to shop carefully, while the posted percentile data supplies the information that makes careful shopping possible.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does a MediShield policyholder pay for healthcare spending below the annual deductible?
options: Entirely out of pocket, from a MediSave Account or any other personal funds
In full through MediShield, which reimburses the bills once claims are filed
Through government subsidy, with the cost recovered later from payroll taxes
Through a fixed percentage split between the patient and the MediShield fund

items.stem: According to the chapter, a MediShield policyholder who has spent well past the annual deductible still pays a share of every additional dollar of covered spending.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Game

items.stem: The chapter emphasizes that MediShield's copays shrink as annual spending rises but never disappear. According to the chapter, why is the design built so that no level of spending is ever free to the patient?
options: So patients are steered toward supplementary Integrated Shield plans with fuller coverage
So MediSave balances are drawn down slowly enough to last through a member's retirement
So the fund collects enough patient revenue to keep its premiums from rising over the years
So patients keep weighing costs against benefits however much they have already spent
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Game

items.stem: The chapter arguably implies that because MediShield's copay rate shrinks as spending rises, the incentive to spend prudently largely fades away at the highest levels of spending.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Game

items.stem: A software firm is choosing how product teams will pay for the cloud-computing resources they consume, and four cost-allocation schemes are on the table. Under Alder, a team pays its own usage in full to a yearly floor, then a portion of each further dollar that steps down in stages yet never reaches zero. Under Birch, a team pays its own usage in full to a yearly floor, then nothing at all: the firm absorbs every dollar past it, however ruinous the year becomes. Under Cedar, a team pays its own usage in full to a yearly floor, then one flat portion of each dollar until its outlay hits a ceiling, the firm absorbing the rest. Under Rowan, the firm simply absorbs every dollar of cloud usage from the first, so a team never sees a charge against its own budget at any spending level. Which scheme reproduces the cost-sharing structure the chapter attributes to MediShield?
options: The Rowan scheme
The Birch scheme
The Cedar scheme
The Alder scheme
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Game

items.stem: A filmmakers' cooperative covers members' equipment-repair costs through a fund whose cost-sharing rules are copied from the chapter's description of MediShield. Mara, a member, has had a ruinous year: a flood destroyed her gear, and her repair bills have run far past the fund's self-pay floor and deep into its highest spending band. Applying the chapter's account of that design, what does Mara owe on the next repair dollar?
options: A larger share than before, since heavy users strain the fund
A smaller share than on her earlier bills, but still something
The whole dollar, exactly as she paid below the self-pay floor
Nothing: at that level the fund bears the whole of each dollar
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Game

items.stem: A trade school's tool-replacement fund for apprentices copies its cost-sharing rules from the chapter's MediShield design: full self-payment up to a yearly floor, then a copay on further spending set on a declining schedule the founders call the design's signature. An outside reviewer proposes two amendments: replace the declining schedule with one uniform copay rate at every spending level above the floor, and cap each apprentice's total yearly outlay as a modest protection against a catastrophic year. Judged by the chapter's reasoning about what keeps spenders prudent, which amendment breaks the design?
options: Neither amendment
Both amendments
The outlay cap
The uniform copay rate
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Game

items.stem: According to the chapter, which body runs MediShield -- taking its actuarial risks onto its own balance sheet and deciding the size of the annual deductible as well as the copay percentages and thresholds?
options: A consortium of private insurance companies
The Ministry of Health
The Central Provident Fund
An elected board of insurance commissioners

items.stem: The chapter emphasizes that the CPF, which runs MediShield, is a non-elected body. According to the chapter, what does that status allow the CPF to do?
options: Decide what is and is not covered without the special-interest lobbying said to plague US state insurance regulators
Raise or lower MediShield premiums each year without needing approval from parliament or from the voters
Invest the premiums it collects alongside other CPF balances, earning returns that hold coverage costs down
Reject questionable individual claims aggressively, since disappointed patients cannot vote its administrators out

items.stem: The chapter says the government set a daily limit on the ward charges -- the room-and-board part of a hospital stay -- that MediShield will cover. On the chapter's account, how does that cap work on providers and on patients?
options: MediShield pays out the full limit however little the ward costs, so frugal patients keep whatever is left over
It applies only to the most expensive ward classes, steering patients toward the cheaper subsidized wards below it
Providers have reason to price ward services at or below it, and patients pay anything above it themselves
Hospitals are legally forbidden to bill ward charges above it, so ward prices settle at the capped level nationwide

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediShield's annual and lifetime claims limits serve a purpose similar to the daily ward-charge cap: they discourage wasteful spending by reminding people that MediShield is not a bottomless common pool from which they can withdraw other people's money, since any spending beyond the limits must be paid entirely out of their own savings.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, the only way anyone can get into an Integrated Shield supplemental plan is to first pay for MediShield coverage.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does Singapore's government limit the number of Integrated Shield plans on the market?
options: To hold every plan's coverage terms close to a common standard
To stop insurers from drawing the healthiest people out of the shared pool
To keep consumers from facing more options than they can sensibly compare
To limit the claims risk the CPF carries on its own balance sheet

items.stem: The chapter says the government allows only minor differences in what each Integrated Shield policy covers and in how each structures its deductibles and copays. According to the chapter, what does this near-uniformity do to the private insurers who sell the plans?
options: It makes premiums the one dimension left open, forcing a hard fight on price
It frees them to compete on coverage options, since prices are effectively fixed
It pushes them to chase the healthiest customers, since benefits cannot differ
It removes their reason to compete at all, since buyers cannot tell policies apart

items.stem: The chapter calls it very important that no one can buy an Integrated Shield plan without first paying for MediShield. According to the chapter, what does this requirement prevent?
options: Consumers stacking up more supplemental coverage than they can keep track of
Private insurers undercutting MediShield's premium and draining its enrollment
Policyholders collecting twice on a single bill from MediShield and a private plan
Insurers enrolling the healthy and leaving only the sickly in MediShield's pool

items.stem: In the country of Lenara, a bar association runs Counsel Assure, a voluntary basic plan that pays members' court costs in return for a flat yearly contribution. The regulator has now opened a market for private premier legal plans that add specialist counsel and faster case handling. Its rules license five premier products, hold their terms nearly identical, post every price on one public comparison page, and allow sale to Counsel Assure members and non-members alike. According to the chapter's reasoning about supplemental plans, what should Lenara expect over time?
options: Shoppers lose track of the field among the five premier products
The basic plan's membership tilts toward those likeliest to make claims
The basic plan's contribution falls as premier plans draw off its heaviest users
The premier insurers turn their rivalry onto what each product offers

items.stem: The island nation of Veyra requires every household to join a public mutual covering basic storm damage to home contents, and private insurers sell optional top-up policies for losses the mutual leaves out. Veyra licenses just four top-up products, lists them all on a single government site, permits their sale only to households current on their mutual contributions, and leaves each insurer to decide what its product covers and how its deductible works. Years on, top-up prices drift upward and few households ever switch products in search of a better rate. Which feature of Veyra's design does the chapter's reasoning point to as the source of the trouble?
options: The latitude insurers have over coverage terms
The requirement of mutual membership before purchase
The single government site listing the products
The regulator's licensing of only four products

items.stem: In the province of Osthollow, every grazier belongs to a compulsory basic livestock-mortality mutual, and private insurers sell top-up policies covering pedigree animals and transport losses. Top-ups may be sold only to mutual members, and all must be written on the regulator's standard terms, which permit few differences between products; any insurer meeting those terms may list one, and forty-one products are currently on sale. The regulator now proposes licensing no more than six. According to the chapter's reasoning about supplemental plans, what effect should the cap have?
options: Price rivalry slackens as the surviving sellers face fewer challengers
The basic mutual's soundest herds get bid away by the survivors
The sellers shift their competition from premiums onto coverage
Buyers can weigh the products again, so price rivalry tightens

items.stem: According to the chapter, how is it possible for MediShield to charge premiums so far below the US average?
options: Government tax revenue quietly covers most of each claim, so premiums only need to fund a small residual share of the costs.
Its high deductibles and meaningful copays create competition that lowers prices, so the plan reimburses claims very cheaply.
Its coverage is limited to minor routine care, so the expensive hospital treatments never reach the plan to be reimbursed.
Participation was compulsory for every resident, so claim costs were spread across the entire population from the very start.

items.stem: The chapter closes its account of MediShield by calling the program 'self-reinforcing and self-perpetuating.' Which of the following best captures what Flynn means by that?
options: Cost sharing creates competition that lowers prices, low prices permit the low premiums that draw mass participation, and that participation keeps the competition strong.
Mass enrollment gives the plan enough bargaining power to dictate reimbursement rates to its providers, and those negotiated discounts are then passed along as lower premiums.
The daily, annual, and lifetime claims limits hold the plan's yearly payouts down, and the underwriting savings that they generate are returned to members as lower premiums.
Low premiums leave more money building up in members' MediSave Accounts, and that growing pool of savings absorbs most medical bills before the plan ever has to pay.

items.stem: Within the cycle the chapter says perpetuates MediShield, what work does mass participation itself do, according to Flynn?
options: It satisfies the MediShield-first requirement, blocking private insurers from drawing healthier members out of the pool.
It demonstrates broad public support, freeing the non-elected CPF to set coverage terms without special-interest lobbying.
It sustains the strong competition among providers, preserving the low prices that make the low premiums possible.
It spreads the actuarial risk across a far larger pool, lowering what each member must contribute toward expected claims.

items.stem: Flynn concedes that Singapore's premium advantage runs out at the top of the market: the country's most expensive supplemental plan — private-hospital coverage with an unlimited lifetime claims limit — is generous enough that its annual premium exceeds what the average American pays for individual coverage through most of adulthood.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why can MediShield charge premiums far below what Americans pay for individual health coverage?
options: Daily, annual, and lifetime claims limits cap what any one member can ever collect from it.
Only younger, healthier residents were allowed to enroll, keeping total claims unusually small.
Its deductible and copays create the competition that holds down the prices it reimburses at.
The government pays most of each claim out of tax revenue, so premiums cover little of the cost.

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediShield is self-reinforcing: its high deductibles and meaningful copays create the competition that lowers prices, those low prices allow the low premiums, and the low premiums induce the mass participation that sustains the competition.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter presents MediShield's low premiums as an outcome of the plan's own design rather than a figure that could simply be decreed. On its account, why do the premiums depend on the deductible and copays?
options: The cost sharing pushes most of every bill onto the patient, so the plan's own share of spending is too small to matter.
The cost sharing sustains the competition that keeps prices low, and those prices are what the premiums rest on.
High out-of-pocket exposure keeps the sickest from enrolling, leaving a pool whose claims are inexpensive to insure.
Deductible and copay receipts flow into the premium fund directly, offsetting what members would otherwise be charged.

items.stem: On the chapter's logic, lowering MediShield's deductible and copays would presumably raise participation, since members would be getting more coverage for the same premium.
options: True
False

items.stem: A farm-machinery repair cooperative in a wheat-growing region charges low annual dues, and nearly every farm in three counties belongs. A member pays the first part of any repair bill and a share of everything above it, choosing freely among a dozen area repair shops; the co-op reimburses the rest. At the annual meeting, the board proposes that the co-op cover every repair bill in full, so that members finally get complete protection in exchange for their dues. According to the self-reinforcing chain Flynn describes, what should the co-op expect if the proposal passes?
options: Membership climbs as fuller coverage draws in the holdout farms.
Bulk reimbursement volume wins the co-op discounts from the shops.
Shop prices rise, and the dues follow them up.
Repair volume swells while shop rates stay where they are.

items.stem: A harbor association runs an engine-repair plan for a commercial fishing fleet. A member pays the first slice of any repair bill and a share of the rest, choosing any of the port's several marine mechanics; the plan reimburses the balance, and its yearly fee has stayed low for a decade. To simplify claims paperwork, the association signs a three-year exclusive deal with the largest yard: every covered repair now goes there, at today's rates locked in writing for the full term. Members' first-slice and share arrangements are left untouched. What does the chain of incentives Flynn describes imply will follow?
options: The yard's workmanship slides during the term.
Members' unchanged cost shares keep the yard sharp.
Pooling the fleet's work wins terms open choice never matched.
The fee's gains hold until the rate lock expires.

items.stem: A county legal-services plan reimburses members' attorney bills after a member pays the first slice and a share of the rest; members may hire any lawyer in the county, dues have been modest for years, and most working households belong because the area's largest union enrolls its members automatically. The union ends automatic enrollment, and the plan's membership falls by half within a year; its first-slice, member-share, and dues terms are unchanged so far. Following the self-reinforcing logic Flynn lays out, what comes next?
options: Attorneys' rates drift up, and the dues follow.
Each remaining member shops as before, so rates hold.
Whether the dues rise turns on which members left.
Fewer members mean fewer claims, so the dues can ease down.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.15.1: Identify the definitions the chapter supplies and the fact its whole argument rests on: age rating (each age cohort charged a premium reflecting its own costs and risks, so the young pay far less than the old), community rating (everyone charged the same premium regardless of age), adverse selection (the tendency for only the sickest to opt into an insurance system while the healthier opt out) -- and that MediShield was a voluntary system until it became MediShield Life in 2015, which is why its designers could not solve adverse selection by compulsion.
learning_objectives.15.2: Explain how adverse selection unravels a voluntary insurance system in the chapter's two worked configurations -- premiums set high for the young and low for the old, and one community-rated premium for everyone: in both, premiums are priced on the assumption that everyone signs up, the young recognize they are being charged far more than people like them cost and stay out, the old sign up in droves, and the result is a doubly bad outcome -- an insolvent system that cannot cover its costly enrollees, and millions of young people uninsured and exposed to bankruptcy -- which is why the chapter says community rating will tend to fail in any voluntary system enrolling participants with different cost profiles.
learning_objectives.15.3: Distinguish the two escapes from adverse selection the chapter lays out and what each leaves a designer still having to ensure: compulsion, the route it attributes to the Affordable Care Act's fines, under which nobody's willingness to join matters and the only remaining constraint is that total premium inflow cover future claims -- a constraint that itself dissolves if the system is subsidized from tax revenues -- versus age rating, the only route open to a voluntary system, under which each cohort's premium reflects its own costs and risks so that each cohort collectively gets back what its members collectively pay in and nobody is overcharged to subsidize another cohort.
learning_objectives.15.4: Explain what the chapter's participation comparison is meant to establish: that MediShield's 94 percent voluntary participation beat both the pre-ACA American rate and the rate the ACA achieved after years of fining non-participants, so a properly designed voluntary system can out-enroll a poorly structured system even after that system adds compulsion -- and why the chapter reads the remaining 6 percent as success rather than failure, since those opt-outs are believed to be well-off people holding employer coverage or wealth enough to self-insure, unlike America's uninsured, who were mostly poor, unemployed, or caught between losing employer insurance and not qualifying for Medicaid.
learning_objectives.15.5: Explain how the chapter argues age rating blocks intergenerational wealth transfer and how Flynn conditions the contrast with the ACA: each cohort's annual premiums are sized to cover that cohort's own spending, so no group's premiums are made artificially high to make another's artificially low, whereas community rating makes the young pay far more than they claim on the implicit promise that they will underpay decades later -- a promise whose fairness assumes politicians will keep the system solvent, which Flynn doubts because election pressure biases them toward overpromising today and underfunding tomorrow, so he offers age rating as protection precisely to readers who share that doubt.
learning_objectives.15.6: Explain how the Ida May Fuller story supports the chapter's Ponzi-scheme characterization of pay-as-you-go programs: the first Social Security recipient drew out vastly more than she paid in because Social Security is not a savings system but a transfer from current workers to current retirees, so falling birth rates threaten the same end a Ponzi scheme meets when withdrawals exceed deposits -- while MediShield, whose age-rated premiums restrict it to operating one year at a time with each cohort's payments fully funding that year's payouts, makes no long-term promise on which it could ever default.
learning_objectives.15.7: Given a novel voluntary arrangement whose would-be participants differ in expected costs, predict whether the chapter's adverse-selection logic says enrollment holds or unravels -- and through which group's exit or entry -- judging by how each group's price compares with what people like them expect to draw out, rather than by how many are signing up.
learning_objectives.15.8: Given a system's reported participation or non-participation figures, determine whether the chapter's reasoning reads them as success or failure, and what must be known about the non-participants -- who they are and what alternatives they hold -- before a headline rate can be read either way.

Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Parti.text: Premiums here differ by age band rather than being one figure for everyone. In a voluntary scheme the single figure collapses: the young see they are charged more than people like them draw out, so they stay away, the old enrol eagerly, and the fund cannot cover them. Compelling everyone is one escape; pricing each band to its own expected costs is the other, and it kept enrolment voluntary and unusually high, with those who declined mostly covered elsewhere.

items.stem: Flynn credits MediShield's premium design with avoiding the adverse-selection problem. According to the chapter, what is adverse selection?
options: The practice of insurers screening out applicants whose age or medical history makes them costly to cover
The pressure on politicians to promise generous benefits today while leaving the system underfunded tomorrow
The habit of actuaries pricing premiums on the assumption that every person in the country will enroll
The tendency for mainly the sickest people to join an insurance plan while healthier people stay out
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does MediShield decide what premium an enrollee pays?
options: Every cohort is charged below its true cost, with tax revenues covering the annual shortfall
The young are charged comparatively high premiums while the elderly are offered low ones
Every enrollee is charged one identical premium, no matter how old or young they are
Each age cohort is charged a premium that reflects the costs and risks of people its own age
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediShield operated as a voluntary system until it became MediShield Life in 2015, so its designers had to make its premiums attractive to every age group rather than rely on compelled participation to defeat adverse selection.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: In the chapter's two-price thought experiment -- a voluntary system charging the young a high premium and the elderly a low one -- the actuaries set those premiums on what assumption about enrollment?
options: That mostly the elderly will enroll, so premiums are sized to their expected claims
That people who decline to enroll will be charged a fine
That every single person in the country will choose to enroll
That any premium shortfall will be covered out of general tax revenues
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do the young stay out in both of its worked configurations -- the two-price system charging them a high premium, and the community-rated system charging everyone the same premium?
options: The young doubt the system will remain solvent long enough to pay out when they are old and finally need it
Their premium far exceeds what people like them typically cost to cover, so joining means funding the old's care
The premiums in both designs are set beyond what most young adults on entry-level incomes can realistically afford
The young expect lawmakers to make enrollment compulsory eventually, so they see no gain in volunteering early
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: In the chapter's two-price example, the elderly sign up eagerly while the young stay away. According to the chapter, why does that surge of willing enrollees leave the system insolvent rather than well funded?
options: The old's low rates never covered their own costs; the design counted on overpayments from young members who never came
Far more elderly people signed up than the actuaries had ever projected, overwhelming a system sized for a much smaller pool
The administrative burden of processing elderly members' frequent claims consumed most of the premium inflow
Many elderly members let their premiums lapse once their health declined and their claims began to mount
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, the unraveling in its two-price example arguably stems from charging the young and the old different premiums -- so a voluntary system that instead charged one identical premium to everyone would largely avoid adverse selection.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Affordable Care Act and MediShield each escaped the adverse-selection problem, but by different routes. Which pairing does the chapter give?
options: The ACA subsidized every premium from tax revenues, while MediShield fined those who declined to enroll
The ACA compelled participation with fines, while MediShield set each cohort's premium to its own costs
The ACA set each cohort's premium to its own costs, while MediShield compelled participation with fines
The ACA charged the young reduced premiums to draw them in, while MediShield charged one rate to everyone
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, a mandate frees the policy-maker from caring whether anyone wants to join, leaving a single constraint: premium inflow must be enough to cover future claims. What does the chapter say would make even that constraint stop mattering?
options: Fines set high enough that nobody chooses to stay out and pay them instead
A pool of enrollees in which the healthy comfortably outnumber the sick
A premium schedule in which each cohort pays exactly what its members cost
A willingness to top the system up with tax revenues drawn from other sources
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, because MediShield was established as a voluntary system, its designers could not escape the adverse-selection problem by compelling participation; they instead had to price each age cohort's coverage to match that cohort's own costs and risks.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: The chapter lays out two escapes from adverse selection: compulsion and age rating. According to the chapter, what must the age-rating route accomplish that the compulsion route never needs to?
options: Freeing the system to fund payouts from tax revenues instead of from premiums collected
Letting the designer charge one premium across all groups without the healthy fleeing
Guaranteeing solvency automatically, so no actuary need check that inflows cover claims
Winning each cohort's enrollment by charging it no more than people like its members cost
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did the original MediShield's voluntary participation rate compare with health insurance coverage in the United States?
options: It exceeded both the pre-ACA American rate and the rate the ACA later reached by fining non-participants
It exceeded the pre-ACA American rate but fell just short of the rate the ACA eventually reached through its fines
It amounted to essentially universal coverage, the goal the ACA pursued with its fines but never managed to reach
It trailed both American rates until participation was finally made compulsory under MediShield Life
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: The chapter sets MediShield's voluntary participation rate beside two American coverage figures: the share of Americans insured before the ACA, and the share after the ACA had spent years fining those who declined to join. According to the chapter, what is this three-way comparison meant to establish?
options: That Singaporeans value insurance more than Americans do and volunteer for coverage at rates no premium design could produce elsewhere
That compulsion does raise enrollment, but only when fines are set high enough to make remaining uninsured the costlier choice
That voluntary enrollment always exceeds compelled enrollment, whatever premium structure the voluntary system happens to charge
That a properly designed voluntary system can out-enroll a poorly structured one even after that system resorts to compulsion
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: The chapter grants that 6 percent of Singaporeans carried no MediShield coverage, yet tells readers to count that figure as success rather than failure. What reasoning does the chapter give?
options: The opt-outs are believed to be well-off, holding employer coverage or the wealth to self-insure, so no vulnerable group was left outside
The premiums had been priced on the assumption that a small share would never enroll, so the gap was already built into the arithmetic
The opt-outs were overwhelmingly the young and healthy, whose exit costs the premium pool little because people like them file so few claims
The opt-outs stayed free to enroll in any later year, so the gap marked a delay in joining rather than any lasting exclusion
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, the 6 percent of Singaporeans who went without MediShield were presumably in much the same circumstances as the Americans who lacked health insurance before the ACA, with the two countries differing mainly in how large the uncovered share was.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, how are MediShield's annual premiums for each age cohort sized?
options: To charge every cohort an identical amount, with general tax revenue covering any shortfall that opens up
To collect just enough each year to pay for that year's healthcare spending by the cohort's own members
To price each cohort a bit below its expected costs, with investment earnings on the fund making up the rest
To build up a reserve across each member's working years that pays for that same member's care in old age
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does age rating stop politicians from turning a health insurance system into a channel for moving wealth between generations?
options: Each cohort's premium covers only its own members' spending, leaving no slack to overcharge one group and discount another.
In a voluntary system the young would simply refuse to enroll if their premiums were pushed above what people like them cost.
Regulators cap how far any one cohort's premium may be set above or below the average premium charged across all the cohorts.
Premiums paid in by each member are credited to a personal account that only that member can ever draw down to pay for care.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: The chapter grants that some will call the ACA's community-rated design fair, since the young who are overcharged now are to be undercharged decades later, in their old age. According to Flynn, what further assumption is that fairness verdict making?
options: That healthcare costs will stay stable enough for the premium schedule to hold roughly steady over those decades.
That politicians will keep the system solvent across the decades before today's young get their turn to pay less.
That today's older enrollees paid their own way when young and are now drawing out what they banked back then.
That younger enrollees can comfortably afford the inflated premiums out of what they earn in their working years.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn doubts that the young who are overpaying under the Affordable Care Act will get back all they have been promised, because the pressure to win elections biases politicians toward overpromising now and underfunding later.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: Ida May Fuller, the first person ever to receive Social Security benefits, collected vastly more over her retirement than she had ever paid in. According to the chapter, what fact about Social Security made that possible?
options: It is an age-rated program: each cohort's taxes are sized to cover that same cohort's later benefits
It is a transfer program: taxes from today's workers go straight out as benefits to today's retirees
It is a savings program: each worker's taxes accumulate in a personal account until that worker retires
It is an endowment program: benefits are paid from investment returns on a permanently invested fund

items.stem: The chapter calls Ida May Fuller's experience equivalent to that of an early investor in a Ponzi scheme. According to Flynn, what makes that comparison hold?
options: Her payout came from investment returns the program had promised its participants but never genuinely earned
She entered early enough that her own small deposits had decades to compound before she began drawing on them
She misstated what she had paid in, so the program's administrators computed her benefits from contributions she never made
Her payout was funded by those who entered after her, and the design fails once withdrawals outgrow deposits

items.stem: According to the chapter, falling birth rates presumably threaten MediShield just as they threaten Social Security, since both programs ultimately depend on a steady supply of younger participants paying in.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter predicts that falling birth rates will eventually leave Social Security unable to keep its promises. On its reasoning, why does the birth rate decide that program's solvency?
options: Younger workers are the healthiest participants, so their absence removes the low-cost members whose payments balance the costly ones
Benefits for retirees come out of what current workers pay in, so a shrinking workforce cannot cover promises already made
Each worker's taxes are invested on that worker's own behalf, and a smaller economy earns weaker returns on those accounts
Smaller birth cohorts reach retirement with longer life expectancies, so each retiree's lifetime payout outgrows what was projected

items.stem: In the chapter's thought experiment, a voluntary insurance system charges the young a high premium and the elderly a low one. According to Flynn, what happens once sign-up opens?
options: The elderly stay out of a plan priced suspiciously below their needs, while the young enroll heavily.
Both groups enroll in full, since the premiums were built on the assumption of universal sign-up.
The young stay out while the elderly enroll heavily, leaving the system with its costliest members.
Neither group enrolls, since a voluntary system cannot attract members at any pair of prices.

items.stem: In the chapter's two-price illustration, the premiums for both the young and the old are set as if the entire population will choose to enroll.
options: True

items.stem: Flynn argues that community rating -- charging every member one identical premium -- tends to break down in any voluntary system whose enrollees differ in their cost profiles. According to the chapter, why?
options: The plan cannot observe which applicants will be costly, so it cannot price anyone correctly and stops accepting new members.
The costliest members resent being priced no differently from the healthy and withdraw, taking the premium base with them.
Healthier members see that everyone pays the same up front while payouts run mostly to the costliest, so they leave the pool.

items.stem: The chapter walks through two voluntary pricing schemes -- a high premium for the young paired with a low one for the old, and a single community-rated premium for all -- and in both the young end up staying out. options: In each, the young see that few other people have enrolled and avoid committing to an unpopular plan.
In each, the young are offered thinner coverage than the old in exchange for the same premium payment.
In each, the premium is set at a level no group can afford, so the young and the old alike decline to join.

items.stem: A marina association proposes a voluntary haul-out-and-repair pool for its slip holders: join and the pool pays your towing, haul-out, and repair bills in full. Anyone may join for one modest annual contribution, which the organizers set by spreading the pool's projected payout load across the entire slip roster. The berths hold owners of recently built hulls, whose boats need a yard visit perhaps once in several seasons, and owners of decades-old hulls, whose boats need yard work several times in a season. According to the chapter's adverse-selection logic, what should the association expect once sign-up opens?
options: Holds, with the modest fee drawing in both groups
Unravels, with the older-hull owners dropping out
Unravels, with the newer-hull owners staying out
Holds, with the older-hull owners sustaining it alone

items.stem: A freelance translators' guild runs a voluntary fund that covers a member's arbitration costs when a client contract turns into a dispute. Dues climb band by band with the number of contracts a member registers each year: the busiest translators pay the steep top band, while members who register only a handful of contracts pay the low bottom band. Disputes arise almost entirely out of contracts signed, so the busiest members also generate most of the fund's payouts. This season the guild forum is loud with complaints about the top band's cost, renewals have dipped, and a handful of members have quit. According to the chapter's adverse-selection logic, what should the guild expect?
options: Holds, with both bands staying enrolled
Unravels, with the steep top band emptying out
Unravels, with the bottom band drifting away
Holds, with participation made mandatory
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: For years a ski club has run a voluntary gear-breakage pool: members pay one yearly fee, set from the club's own history of snapped poles and delaminated skis, and broken equipment is replaced from the pool. This season the club votes to open the pool, at the same fee, to the regional racing circuit, whose training regimen wears through equipment at a pace recreational skiing never approaches. Racers accept in record numbers, and the administrators celebrate the largest membership in the pool's history, noting that risk is now spread across far more shoulders. According to the chapter's adverse-selection logic, what should the club expect?
options: Unravels, through the racers' wave of entry
Holds, through risk spread across more members
Unravels, through the recreational members' exodus
Holds, through the fee's long proven record
items.source_anchor: Chapter 15 → MediShield Encourages Participation and Fairness with Age-Rated Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, who were the six percent of Singaporeans who carried no MediShield coverage believed to be?

Well-off people with employer plans or the wealth to pay their own medical bills
Young workers who judged themselves too healthy for any premium to be worth paying
Recent arrivals who had not yet lived in the country long enough to qualify to enroll

items.stem: Four fishing ports run voluntary tow-and-rescue funds, and a maritime weekly has just ranked them by enrollment. At Brinsport, 84 percent of working boats are enrolled; those outside are trawlers whose packing-house charters keep a rescue tug on retainer for them. At Calder Narrows, 97 percent are enrolled; those outside are older skiffs whose owners applied but could not raise the joining fee. At Dunlow, 91 percent are enrolled; those outside are first-season crews who are sure they will never need a tow. At Edgewater, 88 percent are enrolled; those outside are boats held on a waiting list until new moorage opens in spring. Judged the way the chapter reads participation figures, which fund's record stands as a success?

Edgewater
Dunlow
Calder Narrows

items.stem: Two fruit districts run voluntary hail-damage mutuals, and in each, roughly one grower in ten stands outside. At Ashvale, those outside are the district's smallest growers, whose packing cooperative folds storm cover for members' fruit into its handling contract. items.stem: A translators' guild runs a voluntary fund that replaces income when illness interrupts a member's contracts. Judged the way the chapter reads participation figures, the growing share outside the fund marks --

A case for compelled membership
Contributions priced above their worth
The early stage of an unraveling

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.16.1: Identify the layers of Singapore's healthcare-financing safety net as the chapter orders them -- the direct subsidy program (general tax revenues funding grants to public hospitals and clinics, discounting poorer patients' bills by as much as 80 percent) standing in front of the 3Ms, and MediFund, the Medical Endowment Fund, as the final component, an endowment whose investment returns flow as grants to approved facilities (hospitals, polyclinics, nursing homes) to pay the healthcare costs of the indigent, joined by MediFund Silver for the indigent elderly -- together with the two-stage eligibility test: an applicant must already be a subsidized patient, and must additionally demonstrate difficulty affording the subsidized bill despite MediSave and MediShield.
learning_objectives.16.2: Explain why the chapter presents the direct subsidy program as a "pay-it-forward" safety net that makes MediFund only rarely needed: by subsidizing prices in advance, the program is in place before patients ever have health issues, pre-emptively removing funding pressure from the 3Ms and making it much less likely that a poorer person will run out of MediSave money to begin with.
learning_objectives.16.3: Explain how ward-class pricing produces the self-sorting the chapter calls extremely useful -- every ward class receives identical doctors, nurses and medical care, prices differ substantially on creature comforts alone, and physicians on fixed annual salaries have no financial incentive to cater to the rich -- and the two payoffs the chapter credits to it: richer patients voluntarily pay more, which hospitals recycle into subsidizing poorer patients' prices, and the poor's self-selection into spartan wards lets hospitals concentrate direct subsidy funds exactly there, so the well-off are unlikely to receive any benefit from the program.
learning_objectives.16.4: Explain how the chapter argues that MediFund is both a real promise and a rarely needed one: medical social workers at every approved facility advocate for the indigent from inside the system, approvals happen at the lowest sufficient level so the vast majority of cases clear in under an hour while only highly unusual ones wait about a month for a local committee of independent volunteers, over 99 percent of applications are approved with 93 percent of those paid in full -- and yet the fund accounts for under 1 percent of Singapore's total healthcare spending, which the chapter reads as the rest of the financing system working so well that the last layer is barely needed.
learning_objectives.16.5: Explain the chapter's case that the safety net's funding is sustainable where Medicare's is not: today's elderly were already middle-aged when MediSave began and so had only a few accumulating years, which makes the current under-1-percent MediFund share "even more extraordinary" and means -- against the intuition that aging brings strain -- the pressure will decrease as full-career savers replace the transition cohort, while the savings-driven symmetry (individuals saving through MediSave, the government saving through the MediFund endowment) funds future needs, against a Medicare whose trust fund is projected to run dry and whose long-horizon outlays far exceed its income.
learning_objectives.16.6: Given several described subsidy-delivery designs, determine which one works the way the chapter says Singapore's ward-class system works -- the core service identical across tiers, prices differing only on amenities, and beneficiaries sorting themselves -- so that the subsidy reaches only the needy, as against designs that differentiate the care itself or assign tiers administratively.
learning_objectives.16.7: Given a novel layered-assistance system reporting that its last-resort fund pays only a tiny share of total costs, determine whether the chapter's logic supports reading that figure as the upstream layers succeeding or as the backstop rationing by denial, and which facts about the fund's operation distinguish the two readings.
learning_objectives.16.8: Given a savings-based program young enough that its current draw-down cohort was already mid-career when it began, determine what that maturity stage implies for how to read the program's current backstop usage and for the direction of future funding pressure.

Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidi.text: Grants from general taxation go to public hospitals and clinics so they can charge the needy less, and because they arrive before anyone falls ill, savings are less likely to run out. Wards differ in comfort but not in treatment: the same surgeon, the same care. So wealthier patients choose the comfortable rooms and pay more, which helps fund the cheaper ones and lets the grants be aimed where poorer patients have already chosen to be.

Chapter 16 → MediFund.text: An endowment pays only from its investment returns, which flow as grants to approved hospitals, clinics and nursing homes, with a second fund added later for the elderly poor. An applicant must already be receiving subsidies, then show the subsidized bill is still beyond reach despite savings and insurance. Social workers prepare the case; local volunteers decide it, settling straightforward claims the same day and sending rare hard ones to the next meeting.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's direct subsidy program can cut the bills of the neediest patients by as much as 80 percent. How is that help financed and delivered?
options: Workers' compulsory savings flow into individual MediSave Accounts, which the government tops up so poorer patients can pay their bills.
General tax revenues flow to public hospitals and clinics as grants, which the facilities turn into lower prices for poorer patients.
MediShield insurance payouts settle the bulk of each hospital bill, with the government covering poorer enrollees' premiums for them.
Returns on an invested government endowment flow to patients as cash, which reimburses poorer households after they settle their bills.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, a Singaporean applying to MediFund must clear a two-stage eligibility test. What are the two stages?
options: Already fall under a national income ceiling, and also show that no family member can be made to take over the bill instead.
Already qualify as a subsidized patient, and also show the discounted bill would strain them despite MediSave and MediShield.
Already hold an emptied MediSave Account, and also show that MediShield has formally refused to pay for the treatment at issue.
Already have reached retirement age, and also show enrollment in MediFund Silver, the chapter's fund for elderly applicants.

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediFund - formally the Medical Endowment Fund - is an invested endowment whose returns are paid out as grants to approved facilities (hospitals, polyclinics, and nursing homes) to meet the healthcare costs of the indigent, and a second endowment, MediFund Silver, adds funding for the indigent elderly.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, when does the help provided by Singapore's direct subsidy program actually reach a poorer patient?
options: On review: the program settles the remaining bill after a committee has examined the application.
Afterward: the patient pays the full bill first and the program then refunds the subsidized portion.
Up front: the patient is charged a reduced price from the start, before any illness occurs.
At exhaustion: the program takes over payments once the patient has emptied their MediSave Account.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does the direct subsidy program relieve funding pressure on the 3Ms before that pressure ever builds?
options: Patients on subsidized prices are excused from MediShield premiums, freeing that money to accumulate in their MediSave Accounts.
Lower subsidized bills draw down a poorer patient's MediSave balance more slowly, making it far less likely the account ever runs dry.
The program's tax revenues flow into the MediFund endowment, so the final layer's investment returns outgrow the claims made on it.
Hospitals recover the discount from richer patients' MediSave balances, so poorer patients' accounts are refilled as fast as they drain.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: Flynn calls the direct subsidy program a 'pay-it-forward' safety net. According to the chapter, what about the program earns that description?
options: It obliges those it helps to fund the same help for others later, each rescued patient underwriting the next one's discounted care.
It advances the money for a patient's bill as a loan, which the patient gradually pays back out of future MediSave deposits.
It acts ahead of need: the discount already sits in the prices poorer patients face before any of them has a health problem.
It lets richer patients pay extra for comfortable wards, money the hospital then recycles into cheaper care for poorer patients.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediFund ends up rarely needed presumably because its gatekeeping is tight, with most requests for last-resort help being turned down.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, how are the physicians who staff Singapore's public hospitals paid?
options: They are paid by seniority grade, with the most senior doctors assigned to the premium wards.
They receive a base salary plus a share of the charges their patients' wards generate.
They bill on a fee-for-service basis, earning more with each additional procedure they deliver.
They draw a fixed annual salary, so a wealthier patient brings a doctor no extra income.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: On the chapter's account, every ward class in a Singapore public hospital delivers the same medical care from the same doctors and nurses, yet the classes carry substantially different prices. Why, according to the chapter, does this arrangement sort richer and poorer patients into different wards without anyone assigning them?
options: Because a bed in the plainest wards requires MediFund approval, which demands documented hardship that a better-off patient cannot credibly show.
Because the higher price buys comfort alone, patients sort on what amenities are worth to them — the rich typically pay up, the poor keep the savings.
Because physicians guide their well-off patients toward the costlier classes, where the hospital rewards doctors for the revenue those stays generate.
Because admissions staff review each arriving patient's finances and place higher earners into the costlier classes, keeping the plainest wards open for the needy.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: The chapter claims Singapore subsidizes its public hospitals in a way that makes a prosperous patient unlikely to ever see a benefit from the direct subsidy program. On its account, how do the subsidies end up reaching only the needy?
options: The discounts attach only to bills that MediFund is already paying, and richer patients cannot qualify for MediFund assistance in the first place.
Hospitals verify each patient's earnings before quoting a discounted price, so no bill is ever subsidized for anyone above a set income cutoff.
Poorer patients, sorted into spartan wards by their own choice, sit exactly where hospitals aim subsidy money — wards the wealthy opted out of.
The subsidies reach patients as post-discharge reimbursements, and only those able to document genuine hardship complete the application paperwork.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, one payoff of the ward system's self-sorting is that richer patients willingly hand hospitals more money — they choose the costlier wards of their own accord — and hospitals then turn that extra revenue into lower prices for their poorer patients.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is the role of the medical social workers available at every MediFund-approved facility?
options: They hold the final authority over every application, convening monthly as an independent panel to rule on each case the facility receives.
They write the general approval criteria that each facility applies, adjusting the eligibility rules as local community needs change.
They manage the endowment's investments and decide how large a grant from each year's returns their own facility will receive.
They guide indigent applicants through the process, handle the forms with them, and make the case that paying unaided would be a hardship.

items.stem: The chapter reports that over 99 percent of MediFund applications are approved, yet the fund accounts for under 1 percent of Singapore's total healthcare spending. How does the chapter argue that these two facts fit together?
options: The approvals are near-universal only because strict eligibility screening turns most would-be applicants away before they ever formally apply.
The fund approves nearly every application but pays only a small fraction of each approved bill, keeping the total outlay low however many applications come in.
The endowment's returns are capped in advance each year, so once the budgeted grants are spent, later approvals are recorded but go unpaid until the next cycle.
Near-universal approval shows the fund genuinely pays when asked, and the tiny spending share shows the upstream layers work so well that few ever need to ask.

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediFund's under-1-percent share of Singapore's total healthcare spending largely reveals the fund to be an empty promise, a last layer that reassures on paper but seldom actually pays.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do the vast majority of MediFund cases clear in under an hour while only a few wait about a month?
options: Every application goes before the local committee, which fast-tracks the straightforward ones and holds the unusual ones over until its next monthly meeting.
Facilities approve all applications provisionally within the hour, and the month-long wait applies only to applicants appealing the size of their award.
Applications are decided at the lowest level sufficient for the case; only the highly unusual ones must wait for the next meeting of the local committee.
Cases clear quickly when the applicant is already a subsidized patient, and slowly when the facility must first arrange direct subsidies before it can rule.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Singapore's current cohort of elderly citizens accumulate comparatively little in their MediSave Accounts?
options: The program began only after they were already middle-aged, leaving just a few working years to build a balance.
Their balances were steadily drawn down across the years by the premiums charged for their MediShield coverage.
MediSave contribution rates were set far lower for their generation than for the younger workers who entered after them.
They were exempted from making MediSave contributions during their working years under the program's phase-in rules.

items.stem: The chapter says MediFund's small share of Singapore's total healthcare spending is 'even more extraordinary' than it first appears. What makes it so, on the chapter's account?
options: MediFund Silver handles the indigent elderly on a separate ledger, so their costs never show up in the main endowment's share of national spending.
The direct subsidy program pays most of the elderly's bills before MediFund is ever reached, so the endowment is rarely asked to cover their care at all.
The low share holds even while the group most likely to exhaust MediSave — savers given only a few accumulating years — is drawing on the system now.
The endowment's investment returns have grown faster than national healthcare spending, shrinking the share that MediFund represents each year.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the funding pressure on Singapore's healthcare safety net will decrease as the population ages, because retirees who had only a few years to save under MediSave are being replaced by cohorts who saved across their entire working lives.
options: True
False

items.stem: How does the chapter argue that Singapore's safety-net funding is sustainable where Medicare's is not?
options: Singapore saves in advance on both sides — individuals through MediSave, the government through the MediFund endowment — while Medicare's projected outlays far outrun its income.
Singapore spends so much less per elderly patient that the same pool of money stretches across decades of care that Medicare's revenues could never reach.
Singapore limits how much assistance any one patient can draw from the safety net, while Medicare's open-ended benefit promises let spending run far ahead of its funding.
Singapore's safety net draws on general tax revenues that grow along with the economy, while Medicare is tied to a dedicated trust fund that cannot be replenished once it is spent down.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how do Singapore's public hospitals make sure their subsidized ward prices go to the patients who most need them?
options: Admissions staff review each patient's financial records and assign the patient to whichever ward class matches them
Subsidies are paid out as cash reimbursements to patients who apply for them and qualify after they are discharged
Patients must present proof of a low income before they are allowed to book a bed in a lower-priced ward
Ward prices that differ sharply on comfort lead richer and poorer patients to choose different wards on their own

items.stem: According to the chapter, because Singapore's direct subsidies are paid to public hospitals that serve rich and poor alike, the program's benefits presumably flow to patients at every income level.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, why can Singapore's public hospitals aim their direct subsidy money at the lowest-priced wards and be confident it will mostly reach patients who need the help?
options: Well-off patients move themselves into costlier wards once prices differ, leaving the cheap wards mostly to those of modest means
Hospital rules bar anyone above a set income level from taking a bed in any of the lower-priced wards
Richer patients' higher payments are what supply the subsidy money, so none of it ever has to be routed back toward their own wards
The lowest-priced wards deliver a reduced standard of medical care that well-off patients are unwilling to accept for themselves
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does it matter to Singapore's poorer patients that richer patients willingly pay the much higher prices charged for the comfortable wards?
options: Hospitals turn that extra revenue into lower prices for patients staying in the inexpensive wards
That revenue shows the government the hospital qualifies to have its direct subsidy grants renewed
That revenue frees MediFund's investment returns to pay poorer patients' remaining subsidized bills in full
That revenue covers the physicians' fixed annual salaries without drawing on the direct subsidy grants

items.stem:
A city wants its meal-assistance budget to help the residents who most need it, and is comparing four subsidized cafeterias. Flynn's chapter describes the subsidy design Singapore's public hospitals use.

Millbrook: one kitchen, two menus; the carpeted room charges a high cover for made-to-order dishes, the bare hall a low one for a bulk-cooked meal; diners pick whichever room they prefer; the city's meal discount applies in the bare hall.

Eastgate: one kitchen, one daily menu for every diner; the carpeted room charges a high cover, the bare hall a low one; caseworkers check pay stubs and issue cards; only cardholders may use the bare hall, where the discount applies.

Harborside: one kitchen, one daily menu for every diner; the carpeted room charges a high cover, the bare hall a low one; diners pick whichever room they prefer; the city's meal discount applies in the bare hall.

Delmar: one kitchen, one daily menu for every diner, served in one hall at one posted price; the city's discount is built into that price itself, so every resident, whatever the household earns, pays the same reduced amount.

Which cafeteria is built the way the chapter says the hospital design is built?
options: Harborside
Delmar
Eastgate
Millbrook
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem: An island ferry line sails one fleet on one schedule: every passenger crosses on the same boats at the same times. A seat in the panelled upper lounge — armchairs, a steward, hot drinks — costs several times a bench on the open lower deck, passengers book whichever they want, and a county grant, meant for the island's poorer commuters, holds lower-deck fares down. The board is weighing four changes. According to the chapter's account of the design Singapore's hospitals use, which change leaves the ferry line still running that design?
options: Refit the lounge with plusher chairs and raise its ticket price further
Move lounge ticket-holders onto a faster boat that halves their crossing time
Require lower-deck passengers to show proof of income when buying their fares
Extend the county's fare grant to lounge tickets as well as lower-deck tickets
items.source_anchor: Chapter 16 → MediFund and Direct Subsidies: Singapore’s Amazing Healthcare Safety Net

items.stem:
Four towns subsidize children's music lessons. A state auditor must flag the program whose aid money is most likely being collected by families who could pay full price.

Brampton: one teaching staff and one curriculum for every pupil; its refurbished studio, with a parents' lounge and cafe, costs triple the plain studio; families book whichever studio they wish; the town's aid lowers plain-studio fees.

Corvell: one teaching staff and one curriculum for every pupil; its refurbished studio, with a parents' lounge and cafe, costs triple the plain studio; an annual lottery assigns families to studios; the town's aid lowers plain-studio fees.

Ashford: one teaching staff, but its plain studio teaches large combined classes while the refurbished studio, with lounge and cafe, keeps lessons small at triple the price; families book whichever they wish; the town's aid lowers plain-studio fees.

Linden: one teaching staff and one curriculum for every pupil, in a single studio at a single fee; families who file income papers at the town office receive a vetted discount; the town's aid funds those discounts.

Given the chapter's account of what makes this kind of subsidy targeting work, which town should the auditor flag?
options: Corvell
Ashford
Brampton
Linden
