items.stem: According to the chapter, how does MediFund respond to the applications it receives?
options: It approves most of them, but pays a fixed share of each remaining bill so the money reaches more applicants.
It approves over 99 percent of them, and most approved applicants have the whole remaining subsidized bill paid.
It holds each of them for the next meeting of a volunteer committee, where most are eventually approved.
It refuses most of them at the first stage, because few applicants can show they are already subsidized patients.

items.stem: According to the chapter, medical social workers are available at every MediFund-approved facility to help indigent applicants work through the process, complete the paperwork, and show the hardship they would face if made to pay unaided.
options: True
False

items.stem: MediFund pays under 1 percent of Singapore's total healthcare spending. A skeptic could read so small a figure as proof that the fund turns away or shortchanges the people who come to it. According to the chapter, what closes off that reading?
options: Applications are decided by committees of independent local volunteers, who have no institutional motive to protect the fund's balance at applicants' expense.
Applicants must already be subsidized patients, so anyone the fund might have reason to refuse was screened out well before an application could be filed.
The endowment is so large, and its returns so steady, that the fund has no financial reason either to refuse applicants or to trim what it pays them.
Almost every application is approved and most approved patients have the whole remaining bill paid -- the small total can only mean little was left to cover.

items.stem: The chapter grants that the million-plus MediFund applications approved in a single year 'may seem like a lot,' yet still presents the fund as barely used. How does the chapter square the volume of approvals with that claim?
options: Each approval pays only what is left of a bill already cut by subsidies and the applicant's own accounts, so even a million of them total a sliver of spending.
The headline count folds in MediFund Silver's cases for the indigent elderly, which the chapter treats as spending by a separate endowment outside the total.
The volume is a passing bulge from the cohort who had few working years to save, which the chapter expects to disappear from the figures within a few years.
Most of the approvals are quick reviews of repeat applicants, so the count of applications runs far ahead of the number of people actually drawing on the fund.

items.stem: Four private colleges each price tuition on published family-income bands, require every student to pay into a term-time savings account, and stand a last-resort completion fund behind both; at each college the fund pays out well under 1 percent of all tuition charged. At Northdale, the fund fields thousands of requests a term and grants nearly all of them, clearing whatever balance remains. At Southbrook, requests are rare, since the forms run long and no staff member is assigned to help a student finish them. At Eastmere, the fund grants nearly every request, but caps each grant at a flat sum well short of most remaining balances. At Westcliff, an alumni volunteer board turns requests around within days, and the fund's invested reserve has grown every single year. Read the way the chapter reads a backstop's small share, which college's record shows the upstream layers succeeding?
options: Northdale
Southbrook
Eastmere
Westcliff

items.stem: A county legal-aid ladder works in layers: the public law clinic bills clients on a steep sliding scale, with the poorest owing only a small portion of the posted rates; every client also keeps a modest retainer in escrow; and a last-resort Access Fund stands behind both. A newspaper columnist finds that the Access Fund's grants average a few hundred dollars in a county where private lawyers bill tens of thousands for comparable matters, and concludes that the fund is 'approving petitions, then fobbing people off with token help.' On the chapter's logic, what is the flaw in the columnist's inference?
options: It reads a yearly average as a ceiling, when a few large grants could sit behind the small mean.
It concedes the grant rate, which is the figure that settles whether a backstop is rationing help.
It measures the grants against a price no petitioner was facing by the time the fund saw the case.
It ignores how quickly petitions are decided, which is what separates a real fund from an empty one.

items.stem: A consortium of nonprofit landlords scales rent to income -- its lowest-income tenants pay deep discounts funded by a levy on its market-rate units -- and requires every tenant to hold a small escrowed deposit against arrears. A last-resort Arrears Fund stands behind both. At a board meeting, a director cites two figures as proof that the discounts and the escrow are doing their job: the fund pays out under 1 percent of the consortium's rent roll, and it grants nearly every petition it decides. On the chapter's logic, which fact, if true, would do most to unseat that conclusion?
options: No one on the consortium's staff is assigned to help a tenant assemble and file a petition.
Final say on petitions rests with a rotating panel of volunteers, not with housing professionals.
The fund's invested reserve lost value this year, and its managers expect leaner returns ahead.
The number of petitions filed with the fund has fallen in each of the past three years.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why is a Singaporean who is now eighty-five much more likely to exhaust their MediSave account than a fellow citizen a generation younger?
options: MediSave arrived when they were already in their fifties, leaving only a few working years to pay in.
The medical bills of late old age are heavy enough to drain even an account built over a full career.
Their generation's accounts were depleted early by the hospital prices that prevailed before subsidies.
Their balances depend on the endowment's investment returns, which have fluctuated with world markets.

items.stem: According to the chapter, because Singapore's population is aging, the strain on its savings-based healthcare funding will presumably intensify over the coming decades.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter notes that MediFund pays under 1 percent of Singapore's healthcare spending even though MediSave has existed for only part of today's retirees' lives. According to the chapter, how does the program's age bear on how that small share should be read?
options: The figure is produced under the hardest conditions the program will face, so it understates the mature system's strength.
The figure comes before most citizens are old enough to draw down, so it flatters a system whose real test is still ahead.
The figure mostly shows that a young program is not yet widely known, so usage should climb as word of it spreads.
The figure reflects an endowment that has had little time to compound, so grants are still running below their eventual level.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what should be expected of the funding pressure on Singapore's savings-based healthcare system as its population ages, and why?
options: It should build, because a larger elderly population draws down more savings than a smaller one.
It should hold level, because grant payouts are pegged to the endowment's investment returns.
It should ease, because each new wave of retirees will have paid in over nearly a whole career.
It should build, because subsidized prices invite heavier use of care year after year.

items.stem: Fourteen years ago, Alderline University began crediting each semester taught into a personal release-credit account, which professors spend on a lighter teaching load in their final years before retirement; a dean's bridge fund covers anyone who reaches those years short of credits. A faculty career there typically runs thirty to forty years. Bridge-fund outlays have now risen for five consecutive years, and campus projections show annual retirements climbing for another decade. Applying the reasoning Flynn's chapter uses for savings-based programs and their backstops, how should the planning committee read the bridge fund's trajectory?
options: A shortfall that will keep widening
A surge that will crest and pass
A permanent step-up in demand
An accrual rate set too low

items.stem: Twelve years ago the town of Pelham Narrows began requiring every homeowner to pay monthly into a roof-replacement escrow attached to the house; roofs there last about twenty-five years. When a failing roof's escrow cannot cover its replacement, the town's resilience fund pays the difference. The share of roofs in town older than twenty years is at a record high and still rising. Applying the logic of Flynn's chapter on savings-based programs and their backstops, what should the council expect of the resilience fund's future burden?
options: Growing, as repair prices climb
Cyclical, following the storms
Growing, as the stock keeps aging
Shrinking, after a passing peak

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.17.1: Identify the ward-class ladder the chapter describes in Singapore's public hospitals -- A1+ and A1 at the top, then B1, B2+ and B2, down to Class C -- what falls away as the price falls (single rooms give way to shared open bays, air conditioning to ceiling fans and then open windows, private bathrooms, televisions, telephones and meal choice drop off), and the fact the chapter leads with: the medical care, the doctors and the nurses are exactly the same in every class.
learning_objectives.17.2: Explain how the chapter says direct subsidies are kept aimed at the poor: richer patients' self-selection into the pricier classes fills the open-bay B2 and C wards almost entirely with poorer patients, which historically let the Ministry of Health use ward class itself as the basis for distributing subsidies; means testing was later added, excluding higher earners entirely even when they stay in B2 and C and scaling the subsidy with need up to 80 percent for the poorest; and a subsidized patient must spend the money on care, not a nicer ward -- which is why B2 and C are known as the subsidized wards -- while two booking rules force identifiably richer patients into the full-price A1+ and A1 wards: anyone having inpatient cosmetic surgery, and anyone treated by a visiting consultant rather than a staff physician, on the chapter's stated ground that only richer people employ visiting consultants.
learning_objectives.17.3: Explain the mechanism the chapter calls a largely voluntary redistribution of wealth from rich to poor: the rich eagerly pay for nicer lodgings at prices that massively exceed what those lodgings cost to provide, the resulting surplus is recycled toward poorer patients' bills, and the chapter claims the only reason C and B2 charges are so low is that richer people pay so much for the fancier wards.
learning_objectives.17.4: Explain how the chapter's first-class airline analogy maps onto the ward system and what it is built to establish: the airline's profit on first-class passengers lets it price economy seats lower as it competes for economy customers, so without first class, economy fares would have to rise -- the role the A-class wards play for the subsidized wards -- capped by the chapter's Robin Hood twist, that here the rich are happy to be overcharged.
learning_objectives.17.5: Explain the fairness argument the chapter closes on: many Americans recoil at rich patients in suites while poor patients share nine-bed unair-conditioned wards, and US hospitals accordingly offer nearly everyone a private room with full amenities; the chapter presents Singapore's Ministry of Health as rejecting that view -- a healthcare system's purpose is to deliver healthcare, not hotel amenities -- so that rich and poor get equal access to top-quality care while the rich pay much more for it, an arrangement Flynn says is in his opinion more "fair" than giving everyone first-class comforts.
learning_objectives.17.6: Given a novel multi-tier service arrangement and a proposed change to it -- leveling the tiers in the name of equal treatment, capping what the premium tier may charge, or barring the operator from premium offerings -- predict the consequence the chapter's cross-subsidy logic implies for the cheap tier's price or the subsidy it supports, tracing the effect through the surplus the premium tier generates rather than through the apparent savings from eliminating luxury.
learning_objectives.17.7: Given a described program that distributes a subsidy through an observable choice rather than income verification, determine whether the chapter's self-selection logic says it will reach mainly the needy -- judging by whether the better-off would voluntarily shun the subsidized form, not by the subsidy's generosity or the strictness of its paperwork.

Chapter 17 → Singapore’s Multiple Ward C.text: Every class gets the same doctors, the same nurses, the same operation; what differs is comfort — room size, air conditioning, privacy. Price follows comfort, so those who can afford more choose the better rooms and pay well above cost, while those who cannot choose the plainest and pay far below. The surplus from the first group helps fund the second, and subsidies can be aimed at the plain wards because that is where the poorer patients already are.

AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS FIELD SAID ch18 CARRIED ZERO, and that was an artifact of a narrow predicate list rather than a fact about the chapter: widening the list to cover solvency, motive, competence and cost verdicts found three FDA verdicts here that the first list did not recognise. The null survives the correction and is better measured for it, but the earlier ZERO must not be quoted. ch18 has no application-tier objective whose subject is the FDA verdict (18.6 is disclosure, 18.7 approval architecture generally, 18.8 account design), so a zero at Tier 3 remains equally consistent with the clause working and with the objectives simply not being political. The one live sub-test, whether 18.7's items would touch FDA content as a contrast case under an objective not about it, came back negative at 0 of 7. THIS BANK IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT CLAUSE 13 DOES ANYTHING and must not be cited as such.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.18.1: Identify the three main drug-subsidy programs the chapter describes and what each covers: the Standard Drug List of drugs assessed as both cost-effective and essential, split into SDL I, costing subsidized patients a token flat weekly charge no matter the market price, and SDL II, carrying a 50 percent subsidy; the Medication Assistance Fund Plus, subsidizing up to 75 percent of the market price of expensive drugs assessed as clinically necessary, depending on the patient's financial need; and the Inpatient Drug Subsidy, a MediFund-like grant scheme in which each public hospital's own local medical committee allocates government money to inpatients needing costly Non-Standard Drugs — plus CHAS, whose outpatient subsidies for lower- and middle-income households include drug coverage for fifteen chronic conditions.
learning_objectives.18.2: Explain how, on the chapter's account, Singapore's approval design hands the verdict on a drug to the market rather than the regulator: the Health Sciences Authority typically licenses any drug already approved by a major foreign regulatory agency, demands proof of safety but never of efficacy, and leaves effectiveness to doctors and patients — so a drug survives only by consistently attracting paying customers as word of mouth about whether it works spreads.
learning_objectives.18.3: Explain why Flynn argues the FDA's efficacy requirement, enforced since 1962, should be dropped while the safety requirement stays: proving efficacy on top of safety takes many years of massive double-blind randomized trials, which he calls a primary driver of the high cost of new drugs — the estimates he cites put a single approval at over a billion dollars and a decade — while the Peltzman quotation he offers claims the pre-1962 market was already weeding out ineffective drugs within months of introduction, leaving the regulation little room to improve on market forces.
learning_objectives.18.4: Explain the manipulation logic the chapter organizes its whole account around: drug companies profit by pairing low supply with high demand; the most effective supply-side tactic — rigging the approval process so rivals are denied — is made impossible by the wide-open licensing design, and advertising, though legal toward both the public and doctors, is unlikely to raise any one firm's relative demand because rivals counter it, while it alerts patients to competing options and so produces bargain shopping and price competition.
learning_objectives.18.5: Explain how each defense built into the drug-subsidy program blocks the remaining route to higher demand, subsidy capture: stocking the SDL with many low-price generics so a cheap option is usually available at prescribing time; publishing no information on how drugs are selected for the lists, so there are no explicit rules for lobbying to expand or carve exceptions into; folding SDL I, SDL II and MAF+ drugs into one combined alphabetical list, so the published list reveals nothing about which drug receives which subsidy; and capping daily MediSave withdrawals, so patients who would rather spend MediSave money than other cash opt for generics the account can fully cover.
learning_objectives.18.6: Given a novel disclosure choice by a benefits or subsidy program — publishing or withholding its selection criteria, its tier assignments, or the prices of what it covers — determine which consequence the chapter's logic predicts, judging by whose decisions the disclosed information would feed: price information in buyers' hands fuels comparison shopping, while criteria and tier information in sellers' hands gives lobbying a concrete target to work against.
learning_objectives.18.7: Given a described drug-approval or subsidy architecture that differs from Singapore's design in one respect, determine which manipulation channel the difference opens or forecloses — restricting supply through a gate that can exclude rivals, or inflating demand through the subsidy system — and hence what the chapter's logic predicts firms will attempt there.
learning_objectives.18.8: Given a novel earmarked-account design with a per-day spending cap, predict the effect the chapter's logic implies: users who prefer drawing on the earmarked balance shift their choices toward the options the account can fully cover, rather than demand simply falling, the cap denying care outright, or users indifferently topping up from other cash.

Chapter 18 → Pharmaceuticals in Singapor.text: Regulators there license what safety trials support, and generally accept approvals already granted by major foreign agencies; whether a drug actually works is then settled by prescribers and patients choosing, with subsidies ensuring the poor can obtain essential medicines. Flynn contrasts this with requiring proof of effectiveness before sale, which he argues drives approval costs up for little gain, citing an economist's finding that the market had been discarding ineffective drugs quickly on its own.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Medication Assistance Fund Plus (MAF+) is one of the Ministry of Health's three main drug-subsidy programs. What does MAF+ do?
options: It pays up to 75 percent of an expensive, clinically necessary drug's market price, depending on the patient's financial need.
It hands each public hospital a pool of grant money that a local medical committee allocates to inpatients needing costly drugs.
It subsidizes outpatient medical, dental, and drug care for lower- and middle-income households treated at private clinics.
It delivers drugs to subsidized patients for a flat charge of $1.40 per week, no matter how high each drug's market price runs.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Standard Drug List - drugs assessed as both cost-effective and essential - is split into SDL I and SDL II. How do the two subcategories differ in what a subsidized patient pays?
options: An SDL I drug costs the patient just a flat $1.40 per week however high its market price; an SDL II drug carries a 50 percent subsidy.
An SDL I drug is dispensed to the patient completely free of charge; an SDL II drug costs a flat $1.40 per week whatever its market price.
An SDL I drug carries a 75 percent subsidy and an SDL II drug a 50 percent one, with both percentages scaled to the patient's financial need.
An SDL I drug is a low-price generic the patient buys at its market price; an SDL II drug is a brand-name drug subsidized at 50 percent.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Inpatient Drug Subsidy - one of the Ministry of Health's three main drug-subsidy programs - is a grant scheme in the mold of MediFund: the government funds each public hospital, and a medical committee local to that hospital decides how to divide the money among inpatients needing costly Non-Standard Drugs.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what must a pharmaceutical company prove to Singapore's Health Sciences Authority (HSA) before its drug may be sold there?
options: That the drug is both safe and effective, each demonstrated in clinical trials.
That the drug is cost-effective and essential enough to join the subsidized lists.
That the drug is effective for its intended use - safety is watched after release.
That the drug is safe - the HSA never asks for proof that it actually works.

items.stem: According to the chapter, once the HSA has cleared a new drug as safe and it goes on sale in Singapore, what determines whether that drug succeeds or fails?
options: Whether the Ministry of Health assesses it as cost-effective and essential enough to join the Standard Drug List.
Whether the foreign agency whose approval opened Singapore's door keeps the drug licensed in its own home market.
Whether the HSA's own post-market reviews confirm, from patients' outcomes, that the drug performs as its maker claimed.
Whether it keeps attracting paying customers as doctors and patients try it and word of its effectiveness spreads.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's approval design is market-based through and through: the Health Sciences Authority presumably demands proof of nothing, leaving safety, like effectiveness, for doctors and patients to sort out once a drug is on sale.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter contrasts Singapore's drug-approval design with the approach it attributes to the US Food and Drug Administration. On its account, how do the two regulators differ in what a drug maker must prove?
options: The HSA requires proof that a drug works but not that it is safe, while the FDA demands safety alone and lets the market pass judgment on efficacy.
The FDA demands proof of safety and efficacy from every applicant, while the HSA waives both proofs once any major foreign regulator has signed off.
The two demand identical proofs, but the HSA decides far sooner because it accepts a foreign agency's trial records instead of running fresh ones.
Both demand proof of safety, but the FDA also requires efficacy shown before sale, while the HSA leaves that verdict to doctors and patients.

items.stem: The chapter contrasts Singapore's approach to drug approval with the FDA's. What change to the FDA's rules does Flynn say he favors?
options: End the safety requirement as well, leaving the market to screen new drugs entirely.
End the efficacy requirement while keeping the safety requirement in force.
Replace FDA review with automatic licensing of drugs cleared by major foreign regulators.
Keep both requirements but shorten the clinical-trial phase to cut approval costs.

items.stem: Flynn argues that the FDA's efficacy requirement, in force since 1962, is chiefly responsible for how expensive new drugs are. What mechanism does the chapter give for this?
options: Proving efficacy obliges firms to advertise heavily to doctors and patients before approval is granted.
Firms that clear the efficacy bar gain gatekeeping power they use to keep rival products off the market.
Showing a drug works demands years of large randomized trials, far costlier than showing it is safe.
Each approval triggers subsidies that lower patients' out-of-pocket costs and bid up market prices.

items.stem: To argue that the efficacy requirement gained the public little, Flynn quotes economist Sam Peltzman. According to the chapter, what was already happening in the drug market before 1962?
options: The FDA's own safety reviews were catching drugs that failed to perform as their makers claimed.
Medical societies were publishing ratings that steered doctors away from ineffective products.
Drugs that did not work were losing their sales within a few months of reaching the market.
Drug makers were pulling weak products voluntarily to protect their standing with doctors.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn's case against the efficacy requirement weighs cost against benefit: the requirement adds enormous expense, since demonstrating that a drug works takes years of massive randomized trials beyond what proving safety demands, and it adds little benefit, since the market before 1962 was already driving drugs that did not work out of circulation within months of their introduction.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, drug companies would rather manipulate the pharmaceutical market than let supply and demand operate freely. What combination of conditions does the chapter say they aim for?
options: A small base of loyal customers willing to pay steep niche prices
Maximum sales volume at whatever price level the subsidy schedule sets
Scarce supply of their own product alongside strong demand for it
Abundant supply sold at cut-rate prices to capture the entire market

items.stem: The chapter says the most effective way for a drug company to restrict supply is to arrange the approval gate so that its own products pass while rivals' products are refused. Why, on the chapter's account, is this tactic impossible in Singapore?
options: The government fixes each drug's price directly, so controlling which drugs win approval would not let a firm charge more for its own
The Ministry of Health publishes no criteria for its subsidy lists, leaving firms no explicit rules through which to lobby against rivals
Rival firms would answer any exclusion attempt with advertising campaigns large enough to cancel the excluding firm's advantage
Licensing is wide open: approval by a major foreign regulator typically earns a license, so the gate cannot be made to exclude rivals

items.stem: In Singapore, the chapter notes, drug companies may legally advertise both to the public and to doctors. Why does Flynn nonetheless think advertising is unlikely to hand any one firm a lasting lift in demand relative to its rivals?
options: Advertising is so costly that no single firm can afford a campaign large enough for the buying public to take any notice of it
Subsidies already hold patients' out-of-pocket costs so low that no advertising campaign could push their demand noticeably higher
Whatever one firm spends on campaigns, rivals are likely to answer with campaigns of their own, cancelling the relative gain
Campaigns tip patients off to rival products, so firms conclude that advertising is not worth the expense of running

items.stem: According to the chapter, because Singapore lets drug companies advertise to both the public and doctors, advertising presumably gives each firm a dependable tool for raising demand for its own products at its rivals' expense.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's Ministry of Health built a set of deliberate defenses into its drug-subsidy program so that drug companies could not use the subsidies to push up demand for their own products. Which option states the defenses the chapter names?
options: Many cheap generics kept on the Standard Drug List, no published account of how listed drugs are chosen, one merged alphabetical list that hides each drug's subsidy tier, and a daily cap on MediSave drug withdrawals

A ban on advertising prescription drugs to the public, a rule that doctors must try a generic before any brand, publicly posted admission criteria so firms cannot game the lists, and annual open hearings on tier assignments

Bulk-purchase contracts negotiated directly with manufacturers, a fixed retail markup for every licensed pharmacy, routine audits of physicians' prescribing records, and an import tariff on brand-name drugs

Efficacy trials required before any drug can be subsidized, one government-set price for every listed drug, a ceiling on the number of listed drugs each company may hold, and quarterly public review of tier assignments

items.stem: The chapter quotes a former health minister saying that visiting drug-company CEOs talk about one thing: getting their new drugs onto the subsidy lists. According to the chapter, why does the Ministry of Health respond to this pressure by publishing no information about how drugs are selected for the SDL or MAF+ lists?
options: A published standard would give lobbyists something definite to work on — rules to press wider or carve exceptions into — while silence leaves CEOs able to ask only in general terms
Written criteria would legally oblige the ministry to subsidize every drug that meets them, turning a discretionary assistance program into an open-ended entitlement it could not afford
The selection criteria rest on confidential price concessions from manufacturers, and publishing them would let rival companies see one another's offers and coordinate their pricing
Patients who could read the criteria would press their doctors toward whichever qualifying drug carries the deepest subsidy, raising utilization across all three of the lists

items.stem: Singapore's Ministry of Health publishes the SDL I, SDL II and MAF+ drugs together in one combined alphabetical list rather than as three separate lists. How, on the chapter's account, does this merged format weaken drug-company lobbying?
options: Nobody reading the list can tell which subsidy a given drug receives, so a firm cannot learn where its own product stands and lobbying loses its concrete target
Alphabetical ordering scatters each company's products among thousands of entries, leaving the list too unwieldy for any single firm to analyze systematically
The combined list conceals whether a drug has been listed at all, so a company cannot even confirm that its product passed the ministry's assessment for inclusion
Merging the lists lets the ministry reassign a drug's tier without announcement, so whatever a lobbyist wins in one round can be quietly taken back in the next

items.stem: According to the chapter, the daily limit on MediSave withdrawals for drug purchases restrains demand because most people would rather pay with their accumulated MediSave balances than with other cash, so they often choose a low-price generic that MediSave can cover in full over a costlier drug whose price would run past the daily cap.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does Singapore's Ministry of Health publish the drugs covered by its three subsidy tiers - SDL I, SDL II, and MAF+?
options: As a single alphabetical list combining all three groups, with nothing to indicate which subsidy any drug receives
It publishes no list at all; patients learn whether a drug is subsidized only when the pharmacist rings it up
As a list ordered by subsidy generosity, from the fully covered drugs down to those receiving the smallest discount
As three separate lists, one per tier, so that patients can see in advance what share of a drug's price they will owe

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's deliberate obfuscation presumably extends to retail drug prices as well, which are kept from the public so that no part of the pharmaceutical market can be gamed.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter reports that the Ministry of Health deliberately publishes nothing about how drugs are selected for its subsidy lists. What purpose does Flynn say this opacity serves?
options: Published rules would give drug companies something concrete to push against, so with none public, executives can press their case only in general terms
Opacity shields the officials who assemble the lists from being courted one at a time by pharmaceutical company sales representatives
Unpublished criteria leave the Ministry free to reshuffle its selections quietly as market prices move, without having to justify each change in public
Concealing the selection process keeps patients from insisting on expensive name-brand drugs, so demand for the costliest listed medications stays in check

items.stem: The chapter describes two opposite disclosure practices in Singapore's drug system: the Ministry of Health will not reveal which subsidy tier any listed drug falls under, while the Pharmaceutical Society of Singapore publishes the lowest and highest per-dose prices pharmacies charge for common chronic-disease medications. On the chapter's account, why do these two practices point the same direction rather than contradicting each other?
options: Subsidy tiers stay fixed long enough for secrecy about them to be enforceable, whereas prices change so often that concealing them was never a realistic option

The two reflect the habits of two different bodies - a ministry that happens to prefer confidentiality and a professional society that happens to prefer openness - with no shared principle behind them
Subsidy assignments are commercially sensitive information belonging to the manufacturers, whereas retail prices are already visible to anyone who walks into a pharmacy
Each is judged by who would act on the information: tier assignments would chiefly arm drug companies seeking subsidies, while posted prices chiefly arm patients deciding where to buy

items.stem: A city subsidizes after-school programs: sites that clear an internal review are admitted to the scheme, and families then pay reduced fees at any admitted site. The review's scoring rules have never been made public. A newly elected council member, who campaigned on open government, proposes posting the complete scoring rubric online so that families can finally see what the city looks for in a program. According to the chapter's logic, what is the most likely consequence of posting the rubric?
options: Weak sites exit rather than face public scoring
Operators work to bend particular rules in their favor
Reviews become more consistent from one year to the next
Families choose sites on a better-informed basis

items.stem: A regional authority pays part of the cost when a household hires an approved insulation contractor. Writing its disclosure policy, it is weighing two documents. One is the internal checklist used to admit contractors and set how much of each one's work the program reimburses. The other is a periodic survey of the installed prices contractors have charged households across each district. A news story about an admitted contractor with a history of shoddy work has fueled calls to open the admission process to scrutiny, while several contractors object that a price survey would unfairly shame firms working in costlier terrain. Which disclosure policy does the chapter's logic recommend?
options: Release the checklist and withhold the survey
Release the survey and withhold the checklist
Release the checklist and the survey alike
Withhold the checklist and the survey alike

items.stem: For a decade, the board that runs a tuition-voucher program has posted each accredited provider's fees for the most commonly funded courses. The providers' association petitions to end the posting, arguing that courses differ so much in quality that a bare fee table misleads the public; a student advocacy group agrees, calling the table too crude to capture what matters about a course. The board ends the posting. Which consequence does the chapter's logic predict?
options: Little changes for either students or providers
Fee competition among providers slackens
Fees spread out to track quality differences
Pressure on the accreditation standards eases

items.stem: According to the chapter, a drug company that sets out to manipulate a market for higher profit aims to bring about which pair of conditions?
options: Expanded supply alongside reduced production costs
Restricted supply alongside elevated demand
Restricted supply alongside weakened demand
Expanded supply alongside elevated demand

items.stem: According to the chapter, drug companies would rather manipulate a market than leave price-setting to open competition, because competition between firms tends to wear their profits away.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does Singapore's approval design leave drug companies unable to restrict supply by getting rival products kept off the market?
options: Licensing is nearly automatic for drugs already cleared by major foreign regulators, leaving no discretionary gate to capture
The Ministry of Health fixes each drug's price, so engineered scarcity would not lift what a firm could charge
A refused applicant may resubmit without delay, so even a successful exclusion would hold a rival off the market only briefly
Efficacy must first be demonstrated before independent review panels whose membership drug firms are not permitted to influence

items.stem: The chapter recounts drug-company CEOs pressing Singapore's health minister to place their products on the subsidy lists. On the chapter's account, what would a listing actually do for the firm?
options: Cut what patients pay out of pocket, and artificially low out-of-pocket cost pulls demand up
Commit Singapore's public hospitals to purchasing the drug in volumes negotiated in advance with the Ministry
Shield the drug from price pressure by keeping generic equivalents off the same list
Let the firm bill the government at a rate above the price the open market would bear

items.stem: A state registers home-solar installers. For years, any installer holding a certificate from one of several national trade bodies was registered as a matter of course. The state also runs a popular rebate fund that pays homeowners a large share of an installation's cost — applications pour in, the fund is the centerpiece of the governor's energy agenda, and installers' sales teams mention it on every call — though the agency has never published how it decides which systems qualify, and awards appear only as one combined list. This year the legislature ended automatic registration: a board of appointees now reviews each new application and may turn away installers it judges the market does not need. Under the chapter's manipulation logic, where should we expect established installers to direct their effort?
options: Working the board's reviews against new entrants
Outspending rivals on homeowner-facing advertising
Discounting installations to lock in market share
Lobbying to broaden the rebate fund's qualifying terms

items.stem: A school district pays most of the tutoring bill for lower-income families at two support levels, and it publishes a rubric stating which service features earn a provider the higher level. To operate at all, a provider must clear the district's vetting: fingerprinting of every tutor, an annual on-site audit, insurance checks, and a safety file reviewed each term — a process providers call the toughest in the region, and one that washes out several applicants a year. Any provider that completes the checklist is enrolled automatically; the district has no authority to refuse one that passes. Under the chapter's manipulation logic, which route to higher profits does this design leave open, and so where should we expect providers to press?
options: Undercutting rival providers on hourly rates
Pushing the district to vet competitors more harshly
Saturating parents with advertising for their brand
Campaigning to stretch the rubric's tier terms

items.stem: A national aid program reimburses part of the cost of approved laptop models for students from poorer households. Any manufacturer may sell in the country without restriction. For a decade the agency published three reimbursement levels and the exact model list for each, and manufacturers fought hard over placements — one firm's government-affairs office tripled in size, and two placement decisions were reversed after sustained pressure. This year the agency stopped: it now releases a single alphabetical list of every covered model, with no level markings and no published placement criteria. Under the chapter's logic, what should we expect of manufacturers' efforts to work the program now?
options: Effort shifts to blocking rivals' market entry
Lobbying persists but blunts into generalities
Lobbying intensifies through informal back channels
Firms abandon the program and compete on price

items.stem: According to the chapter, what restriction does Singapore's Ministry of Health place on MediSave accounts as one of its tools for holding down drug demand?
options: A ceiling on the total balance the account is permitted to build up over the years
A yearly quota on the number of prescriptions the account is allowed to help fund
A restriction on which retail pharmacies are entitled to accept the account's money
A limit on how much money can leave the account in a single day for drug purchases

items.stem: The chapter gives one reason the daily MediSave withdrawal limit succeeds in restraining drug demand. What is it?
options: Doctors are required to keep every prescription's total cost beneath the daily limit
Pharmacies are not allowed to charge more than the daily limit for any one medication
The government tops up the accounts only of patients who stay beneath the daily limit
Most people would much rather pay for drugs with MediSave money than with other cash

items.stem: The chapter says the daily withdrawal limit often leads a patient to pick a low-price generic over a costlier non-generic. On its account, what produces that choice?
options: The Health Sciences Authority permits account money to be spent on generic medications and nothing else
The generic's whole price can come out of MediSave, and patients would rather not reach into other money
The subsidy tiers refund a far larger fraction of a generic's market price than of a non-generic's price
The combined alphabetical drug list nudges prescribers toward generics by masking each drug's subsidy tier

items.stem: According to the chapter, the daily MediSave withdrawal cap presumably holds down drug spending by putting any drug priced above the cap out of a patient's reach.
options: True
False

items.stem: A software firm loads a meal card for every employee each month, spendable only at the office food hall, and caps how much of the card can be used on any one day. The hall's set lunches price under the cap; its chef's specials price a little over it, and the staff, who are well paid, could easily make up the difference out of pocket. Which outcome does the chapter's logic imply?
options: Orders shift toward dishes the card can pay for by itself
Staff add the small difference in cash and order as before
Visits to the food hall drop off as staff eat elsewhere
The chef's specials pass out of reach of card-holding staff

items.stem: A city issues each sixteen-year-old a culture wallet, an app balance spendable only at registered bookshops, cinemas and music venues. After a season of heavy spending on collector box sets and arena tickets, the council adds a daily redemption cap sitting below those big-ticket prices but above paperbacks, screenings and club shows. The budget office forecasts that teenagers will simply redeem less. Which outcome does the reasoning of the chapter imply?
options: Box sets and arena tickets fall out of wallet-holders' reach
Teenagers chip in pocket money for big items as readily as ever
Teenagers redeem noticeably less from their wallets overall
Purchases shift toward items a day's allowance fully covers

items.stem: A regional rail operator credits every season-ticket holder with an annual travel balance, spendable only on its own fares, and caps the credit that may be applied on any one day. Standard off-peak fares sit within the cap; first-class and peak express fares sit above it. A passengers' association warns that the cap will shut credit holders out of the express services. What does Flynn's reasoning in the chapter imply?
options: Credit holders cut back their travel on the network overall
Riders pay the excess above the cap from their own money as usual
Credit holders are in practice barred from the express services
Bookings drift toward fares the day's credit meets in full

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.19.1: Identify the chapter's accounting of who pays for Singapore's healthcare: what makes each of the 3Ms privately funded on its telling — MediSave funded by private savings, MediShield's premiums, deductibles and copays paid with private money much of which flows from MediSave accounts, and MediFund paying the indigent's bills from the interest of an endowment operating independently of the government — and the 2013 breakdown it reports, the 3Ms together just 8 percent of total national healthcare spending, government spending (mostly direct subsidies) about 38 percent, and other private sources (supplemental insurance plans, employer coverage and benefits, and consumers' own cash) the remaining 54 percent.
learning_objectives.19.2: Explain why the chapter says the 3Ms' small share "completely contradicts" the misperception that they are Singapore's substitute for a national health service: that misperception assumes all medical payments run through the 3M structure of individual savings plus high-deductible insurance plus a safety net, while the reported shares show the 3Ms at under a tenth of spending, dwarfed by both government spending and other private spending.
learning_objectives.19.3: Explain why the chapter calls the opposite, naive reading of the same figure — that a component this small could be done away with while keeping the system's low costs and high quality — "a grave error": the 3Ms are the part of the system that actively promotes competition and prudence, because MediSave gives even the poor skin in the game, money they do not spend is theirs to keep, so patients consume only when benefits exceed costs and their spending decisions force second parties to compete on price and quality.
learning_objectives.19.4: Explain how, on the chapter's account, first-party spending decisions are amplified by third-party payments: a subsidized patient may spend only a small amount of his own MediSave money, but a hospital receives the much larger government subsidy revenue that comes with treating him only by first convincing him to be treated at its facility rather than a rival's, so where the patient's own small payment goes determines where the substantial third-party money goes too — the modest 3M spending acting as a small lever controlling a huge crane, forcing hospitals to compete intensely for the combined volume by pleasing first parties, rich or poor.
learning_objectives.19.5: Explain how the chapter extends the gains from first-party comparison shopping to the payers who never shop, and what its ounce-and-pound conclusion is built to establish: the low prices that competition produces are available to everyone, including the government when it pays direct subsidies for the poor, so a healthcare system does not need to be cash-and-carry end to end — an ounce of first-party spending is all that is needed for competition and prudence to yield a pound of efficiency benefits.
learning_objectives.19.6: Explain how the chapter turns the MediSave stockpile into a long-run solvency argument for an aging population: over S$80 billion already sitting in MediSave accounts — enough, it says, to run Singapore's entire healthcare system for over four years without a penny from any other source — means the baby boomers' future care is already paid for, so aging is not a financing problem for Singapore, while other developed countries' boomer health-spending commitments must on Flynn's telling either be broken or be kept through massive tax increases he expects to damage growth and productivity.
learning_objectives.19.7: Given a novel funding design in which users spend only a small amount of their own earmarked money while much larger third-party flows pay most of each bill, determine whether that design forces providers to compete on price and quality — judging by whether the large third-party flow reaches a provider only by way of the first party's choice of where to be treated, rather than by how big the users' own share of total spending is.

Chapter 19 → The 3Ms Dominate Incentives.text: The 3Ms are privately funded and come to only about a tenth of national health spending, far less than government subsidies or other private payments. That refutes the idea that they are Singapore's whole system, but dropping them would be a grave error: a patient's own small outlay decides which hospital earns the far larger subsidy that travels with them, so providers must compete for that choice. Flynn adds that accumulated balances pre-fund an ageing population.

items.stem: According to the chapter's reported 2013 figures, how did Singapore's total national healthcare spending divide among the 3Ms, government spending, and other private sources?
options: The 3Ms about 54 percent, government spending about 8 percent, and other private sources about 38 percent
The 3Ms about 8 percent, government spending about 38 percent, and other private sources about 54 percent
The 3Ms, government spending, and other private sources each accounting for roughly one-third of the total
The 3Ms about 38 percent, government spending about 54 percent, and other private sources about 8 percent
items.source_anchor: Chapter 19 → The 3Ms Dominate Incentives, Not Payments

items.stem: The chapter counts MediFund among Singapore's privately funded programs. On its telling, where does the money that pays the indigent's healthcare bills come from?
options: Interest from an endowment that operates independently of the government
Balances that recipients have accumulated in their own MediSave accounts
Annual appropriations drawn from the government's general tax revenue
Premiums, deductibles, and copays collected from covered policyholders
items.source_anchor: Chapter 19 → The 3Ms Dominate Incentives, Not Payments

items.stem: According to the chapter, much of the private money that covers MediShield's premiums, deductibles, and copays flows out of MediSave accounts.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter reports that some people hold a mistaken view of the role the 3Ms play in Singapore's healthcare system. Which statement captures that misperception as the chapter describes it?
options: The 3Ms are financed out of general tax revenue, with the government topping up accounts whenever private contributions fall short
The 3Ms are a transitional arrangement, due to be wound down as government subsidies take over a growing share of each hospital bill
The 3Ms stand in for a national health service, with every medical payment moving through savings, insurance, or the safety net
The 3Ms serve only Singapore's indigent patients, with everyone else paying for treatment through employer plans or their own cash

items.stem: According to the chapter, the 3Ms' small share of Singapore's total healthcare spending "completely contradicts" the belief that they are the country's substitute for a national health service. Why, on Flynn's account, does the reported share contradict that belief?
options: A true substitute would operate as one unified program, yet the chapter splits the job across three separate schemes covering different kinds of expenses
A true substitute would be publicly financed, yet all three programs run on private savings, private premiums, and endowment interest outside the government
A true substitute would hold reserves on a national scale, yet the balances inside the 3M accounts could not fund the whole system for any length of time
A true substitute would carry nearly all medical payments, yet the 3Ms carry under a tenth and are outweighed on both the government and the private side

items.stem: According to the chapter, the 3Ms are dwarfed both by government healthcare spending and by other private spending. In Flynn's rebuttal of the claim that the 3Ms substitute for a national health service, why does it matter that they are outspent on both sides?

It shows the two bigger payers squeezing the accounts, since public subsidies and private insurers both grow by absorbing payments the 3Ms once made
It makes the mistaken picture fail twice over, since that picture allows for neither a large public payer nor large private flows outside the accounts
It suggests the two larger payers could between them absorb the accounts' small remaining share, leaving the 3Ms close to redundant in the system

items.stem: Four provinces fund civil legal help for low-income residents, and in each the public money covers most of what the clinics spend. In Alder, a resident puts up a small sum from a personal legal account at whichever clinic takes the case, and the province then pays that clinic a much larger set fee for each case on its books. In Birchfield, residents pay a share of every bill from their own wallets, a share they genuinely feel, and the province rounds out clinic budgets with appropriations still pegged to the caseloads reported a decade ago. In Crestline, residents pay nothing at all toward a case at any clinic willing to take it, and the province finances each clinic through an annual grant scaled to the number of lawyers it employs. In Dunmore, residents draw a token payment from court-issued case accounts when a matter is opened, and the province supports each clinic with a lump sum settled each spring by the floor space it occupies. On the chapter's reasoning, in which province do clinics come under the strongest pressure to compete on price and quality?
options: Birchfield
Alder
Crestline
Dunmore

items.stem: A country overhauls its funding of adult job-training academies. For years, trainees had paid a stiff share of every course fee from their own savings while each academy drew a fixed annual grant set by its classroom capacity -- and the academies were notoriously complacent, with stale courses and ignored waiting lists. The reform makes four changes at once: the ministry stops the grants and instead releases a set payment to an academy for each trainee enrolled there; trainees' own payments shrink to a token sum drawn from newly created personal training accounts; whatever sits unspent in a trainee's account at year's end stays the trainee's own money to keep; and the ministry starts publishing a yearly league table of academies by graduate job placement, posted in job centers and quoted in the press. Within two years, academies are competing hard on fees and course quality. Applying the chapter's reasoning, which of the four changes forced them to compete?
options: The published placement rankings
The cut in trainees' own payments
The rollover of unspent balances
The switch to per-trainee funding

items.stem: Two neighboring regions subsidize youth sports clubs, and in both the public money is most of what the clubs spend. In Harlow, a family registering a child puts up a token sum from a council-issued activity account, and the regional fund then pays the club a far larger yearly amount for each child on its register. In Veldt, families pay a seasonal membership fee from their own money that is big enough to budget around, and the fund finances clubs through fixed allocations tied to the pitch and hall space each one maintains. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should be expected of the clubs?
options: Veldt's clubs court families harder than Harlow's
Clubs in neither region have much reason to court families
Clubs in both regions face similar pressure to court families
Harlow's clubs court families harder than Veldt's
